TO A SEA-SHELL.—A SONNET. 0 sea-shell, singing, as if in thy soul, In a melodious low-voiced monotone' ; Of sounding shores where foam-bright breakers roll, Of sunlit seas where but wave-songs are known! Drank crimson-wreathed ear, in days long flown, deep the wondrous music of the sea. And now thy heart, with mingled mirth and moan, Still sighing swells with ocean's melody. I A. shell, upon life's morning.shore like thee, The sad soul, severedlfrom its natal bays, , Yet holds high treasured in dear memory The glorious cadence of love's early lays, And pleased in sorrow, listens to the low Heart-holden symphonies of long ago. • 45—Cassell's Family Magazine.
J. W. M.

, THE LAND OF COUNTERPANE. When I was sick and lay abed, I had two pillows at my head, And all my toys beside me lay, • To keep me happy all the day. And sometimes for an hour or so I watched my leaden soldiers go, With different uniforms and drills, Among the bedclothes, through the hills. And sometimes sent my ships in fleets All up and down among the sheets; Or brought my trees and houses out, 1 And planted cities all about.

I was the giant great and still That sits upon the pillow hill, And sees before him, dale and plain, The pleasant land of counterpane/ • ' •—•.4 Child's Garde* of Verses. R. L. STEPHENSON.

- A Rev. Mr. Itobbin once entered a shop and bought among other things, some eggs. One of the bystanders, observing him put them into his pocket, told him to be careful not to sit on them. "Yes,' said the divine, "but did you ever know &robin sit on hens' eggs and hurt them." A foreigner, in learning the English language, and lading that the word "plague" is a monosyllable, while "ague," which contains only the last four letters of • plague," is a dissyllable said he wished that the plague would take one-half of the language, and the ague the other half. A woman was brought before a police magistrate and asked her age. She replied, " Thirty-five." . The Magis- trate: "I have heard you have given that same age in this court for the last five years." The woman: "No doubt, your honour. I'm not one of those females to Say one thing to-day and another to-morrow." "I've gone about as high in masonry as anybody can," said a labourer. "Is that so? How high have you gone ?" "Well, I worked on the top ofiWashington lionument ass mason." 4," Well, that's not taking any -degree in masonry." "It isn't, eh? "Well, you'd a thought it was if you'd been there, with the thermo- meter at thirty-one degrees below zero." A witty as well as a soft answer will sometimes turn sway wrath. Charles Burleigh, the abolitionist, in the midst of an anti-slavery speech was struck by:a rotten egg full in the face. Pausing to wipe away theleontents of the missile, he said calmly, "I have always contended that pro-slavery arguments were very unsound." The crowd roared, and he was no longer molested. A ten-year-old boy, bound by rail from Rochester, New York, to Troy, in the same State, became hungry before 11 o'clock, and began to eat the broiled chicken which his mother had placed in his luncheon-box for him. A gentleman who sat behind him was moved to say, "See here, my son! If you eat much now, you won't have any appetite for your dinner." To which the little fellow slowly replied, "Well, I guess if I haven't any appetite, I shan't want any dinner." The friendly traveller had no snore to say.

BISMARCK'S SONG. • Oh, I'm leading all Europe a lively dance! Now it is England and noir it is Fran', And now it is Spain. But I'm first in the field. A fig for their anger! They grumble—and yield. Bonus pocus, Fit Fo! Fum ! Political honesty's all a big hum. ' At Spain I just twiddle my finger and thumb, I'm King of the Caroline Islands !—Punch. • There is nothing more unfavourable to female beauty than late hours. 'Women who spend most of the day in bed, and the night at work or dissipation, have always a Tale, faded complexion, and dark-rimmed, wearied eyes. Too much sleep is almost as hurtful as too little, and is , .sure to bloat the person with a pallid and unwholesome -fat. A gross and excessive indulgence in eating and , drinking is fatal to the female charms. The appetite should never be wasted during the intervals between meals on pastry, confectionery, or any other tickler of the appetite which gratifies the taste but does not sup- port the sy-steni, Exercise is, of course, essential to -female beauty. Tnons.—lt may be worth mentioning that the late' Mr. Thorns was fond of saying that, though he cauld not have been quite three years old at the time, he had a distinct recollection of seeing Charles James Fox, and he *used to add that he believed that he remembered the tea- ' ' ditional blue coat and buff waistcoat, but he could not be quite sure of that. Another anecdote, which admir- ably illustrates the character of the lamentedantiquary; relates to a conversation he had with Lord Macaulay in the Library of the House of Lords. Mr. Thorns men.: toned to Lord Macaulay that he could quite understand why Pope had satirised Dryden in the " Dunead." Lord Macaulay said that Mr. Thorns mist be mistaken, and, with his usual energy and eloquence (before a score of Peers), he spoke for nearly half an hour in support of his &pinion, and proved beyond all doubt that it was impos- sible that Pope could or would have lampooned Dryden. Mr. Thorns had all this time a copy of "The Dunciad" in his pocket, with the page turned down at the passage. He was, however, much too kind and too well bred to produce the volume.—Atheneuna. THE VANITY OF WOMML—With all her love of dress and finery, and her anxiety and concern for her personal appearance, woman is not, vain—not vain, that is, with the vanity of a fop or coxcomb. It is true she loves, above all things, to see herself reflected in a mirror, or In teed in anything that reflects without distorting. It is true that she cannot pass along the street without looking for her own dear image in every shop window that happens to reflect her. But this is not vanity, but merely solicitude for her external well-being. The two things, though apparently the same, are in reality:verY different. A man—that is, a vain man—will look at himself in a glass with supreme complacency, will stroke his chin with ridiculous self-approval, and gravely thank heaven that he is gifted with so charming an exterior. This is vanity, pure and simple—the vanity of a cox- comb, the vanity af man. But this is not the case with women. They may, it is true, look long and earnestly into their mirrors, but it is not to applaud themselves, and exclaim "How beautiful r but to find some defect that may be remedied; not to please themselves, but to see that there is nothing there to displease another. And this is mere solicitude, the solicitude—not a vain, but a praiseworthy solicitude, or, if you will, the vanity e! a woman. THE IRISH JUDGE AND THE PRISONERS.—Rather a good story which is going the rounds was wont to be a standby of Justice Porter, the well-known :legal bon vivant Of Dublin. It concerns a rare old Irish Judge on the Nortri-west Circuit, who loved the hunting-field more than he did the stupid, sleepy court-room. His clerk was like-minded, and a joyous pair they made. One fine morning the clerk whispered to the Judge yer Honour, old Billy Duane's meet's to-day at • Ballykill- mulligan, an' they've a fine dog-fox." "How many's in the docket?" asked the Judge excitedly. "Twenty, for rioting and breach of peace, yer Honour." "Tim," said the Judge, "do you think you can get the first fellow to plead guilty without a jury trial, and me to let him off with a week in goal ?" "The easiest thing in the world," a&swered the -faithful clerk. "Make haste, then, and bring the whole gang; and, I say, Tim, tell Jerry to saddle the mare meanwhile. The twenty Fenians were brought into Court—a defiant gang, nineteen of them prepared to fight with counsel and jury to the bitter end. The twentieth had been interviewed by the clerk. He was called by the clerk. "Guilty or not guilty of the 'crimes charged?" demanded t Judge, with a propi- tious smile. "Guilty, yer HonSur ; God help me," said the crafty prisoner. "Well," said the Judge, glancing benevolently about the room. "I fancy I can let you off with a week." The man thanked the Judge, and Stepped &Nen to the bailiff. There was a terrific sensation arming the other defendants. Why, none of them ex- pected to get, off with less than five years. in limbo. Bore was a chance to profit by "his Honour's" pleasant mood. One and all manifested an earnest desire to fol- low the example of their comrade and acknowledge the crimes in a batch. "Do you all plead guilty?" de- manded the Judge eagerly. "We do r shouted the enthusiastic neteen in chorus. "Fourteen years' trans- portati rd on apiece," exclaimed the Judge, with a click of ji jaw—" Jerry, is the mare saddled yet ?" •-• BRIDAL BOUCrusr limos!, for beautifying the eom- p!exion It imparts exquisite beauty to the face, neck, arms, and hands. A correspondent of the New York Tribune reports that he is milking a two-year-old heifer that has never calved, and is not in calf. Recently he found that a younger heifer running with her was sucking her, and that her bag had the appearance of having milk in it. He separated them, and is now getting two quarts Of milk a day from her. Her milk is very rich, showing in the test-glass 26 per cent, of cream. A missing bullock was recently found at Sevenoaks under extraordinary circumstances. Ths animal had not been seen for twenty-one days, and it was supposed that it had been' stolen, but it was discovered in a hol- low tree at the back of the White Hart Hotel. It is sup- posed that it got into the tree to escape from the flies, and was prevented from getting out by a branch. When found, the bullock was much emaciated, but is expected to recover.

GREAT num rig Suairs.—A feature of the season is the drop in price of store sheep. Thus, at Overton fair, where 30,000 were penned, prices were 3s. to 4s. below those at Stockbridge; and at VVeyhill fair the quotations were is. to 2s. per head lower than at Overton. At Dor- , chester, where 10,000 sheep were shown, Down ewes sold at 30s. to 425., and wethers at 355. to 455, prices considered to range 10s. or 12s. below the corresponding figures at the same lair last yeaf.AVflsley fair the trade was one of the dullest known, and prices for Down lambs were 10s. to 15s. lower than last year. At Lanark, where 24,000 Leicester cross and grey-faced lambs woire shown, prices fell 3s. per head during the holding of the fair; and it is estimated that in two years lambs have fallen in value one-third, and in some cases nearly one- half.

PROTECTION OF DAITIYING INTERESTS IN AMERICA.— New York dairymen, for the purpose of protecting their rights, have had a law passed by their State Legislature, which is as follows :,—Section 1. No person Shall offer for sale butter or chetse branded or labelled as to the quality of the article or the county or State in which the article is made. The New York State Dairy' Commissioner ;is hereby authorised an& directed to procure and issue to the cheese manufactories of the State, upon proper ap- plication therefor, and under such regulations as to the custody and use thereof as he may prescribe, a uniform stencil brand bearing a suitable device or motto, and the words, "New York State Fall Cream Cheese." Every brand issued shall be used upon the outside of the cheese and also upon the package containing the same, and shall bear a different number for each separate manufac- tory, and the Commissioner shall keep a book in which shall be registered the name, location, and number of each manufactory using the brand, and the name or names of the persons at each manufactory authorised to use the same. It will be unlawful to use'or permit such stencil brand to be used upon any other than full cream cheese or packages containing the same. Who- ever violates the provisions of this section is guilty of a misdemeanour, and for each and every cheese or, package so falsely branded shall be-punished by a fine d not less than 25 dole. nor more than 50 dols., or imprisoninentof not less than 15 nor more than 30 days. Sec. 2. This Act shall take effect immediately. ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—FARM PRIZR9 IN 1866. In Connection with tho Norwich meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society of England the following prizes, amounting in the aggregate to £360, have been offered by the Norwich Local Committee, viz. :—Class I.—For the best managed arable anclgrass farm exceeding 550 acres, £100; for the second best, £5O. Class 2.—For the best managed arable and grass farm exceeding 250 acres and not exceeding 550 acres, £75; for the second best, £25. Class Z.—For the best managed arable and grass farm above 100 and not exceeding 250 acres, £5O; for the second best, £25. Class 4.--For the best managed arable and grass farm not exceeding 100 acres in extent, £25; for the second best, £lO. • The competition is con- fined to the counties of Norfolk and Suffolk. Though so large an entry as at Preston can hardly be expected, still a keen competition may resialt for the farm pre- miums which the Norwich Local Committee have placed at the disposal of the Royal Agricultural Society. The judges, when appointed, will be again authorised to re- commend to the Council the award of certificates.to any really deserving persons employed on any of the com- peting farms for distinguished merit in the discharge of their duties, these recommendations to be accompanied by a certificate of good character and length of service from the competing farmer. Various recommendations to this effect have been made by the judges of the farms competing for the last two years, and the certificates granted by the Council have been highly appreciated by their the recipients. Docitnio HORSES.—Doctors will disagree, to a proverb, but for an out-and-out wrangle nothing can beat the veterinary profession, and a case in point occurred at the Become general meeting of the National Veterinary Association. The subject was that of docking horses, and the question at issue was whether the operation is a necessary one, because if it is necessary it cannot be called cruelty. Dr. Fleming and Professor Pritchard spoke very earnestly against the practice; they do not say that docking is never necessary, but they say that as,a rule it is not necessary, that it serves no useful pur- pose, and that therefore, it is cruel Professor Axe, Pro- fessor Williams, and a host of lesser lights say that dock- ing is necessary often,that it does serve a useful purpose, and that, therefore, it is not cruelty. And so the matter rests. It is pretty sure, however, thi‘t Mr. Colam, on be- half of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, will prosecute any veterinary surgeon for per- forming the operation without any apparent necessity for it, and the law will have to decide whether docking is or is not cruelty to animals. Professor Pritchard de- clares that a horse is much less likely to get its tail over the reins if it is not docked. Professor Axe says it is pet a question of getting the tail over the reins but of get- ting the reins from under the tail, and, therefore, the shorter the tail the more easily the reins can be got , away. Professor Pritchard says the dock is always tender. Professor Axe says that, "as a matter of fact, when a horse has been .docked, the cicatrice at the end of the tail never afterwards has the physiological sensi- bility peculiar to the undocked tail" Professor Wil- liams says that docking is not cruelty; "some little pain is inflicted, but it, causes the animal little or no in- , convenience."

THE Reavner.—Our agricultural contemporary, the Mark Lane Express, published on Monday a further esti- mate of the yield of the crops in the harvest now being gathered. The final conclusion is, in one respect, some- what more favourable than the earlier reckonings. Wheat is shown to be over average in every division of Great Britain; but barley seems to be under average in England, though over average in Wales and Scotland; oats and pulse crops under average in each case. The estimated yield of wheat is 30 bushels to the acre, which is exactly that of last year; but our contemporary ex- pects that on full information it will not prove to be more than 29 bushels. On this reckoning, the yield for 2,478,318 acres, which was the area sown with wheat in Great Britain this year, gives a total crop of 8,947,650 quarters. Adding the 70,874 , acres in Ireland, where the wheat crop is a very good One, and the 5,660 acres in the Isle of Ilan and the Channel Islands, the total crop of wheat comes out as 9,223,710 quarters, of which a million quarters will be needed for seed, leaving 8,224,000 for sale. Now, the top value of white wheat in Mark-lane on Monday was 355., and of red wheat 325. Taking a mean between

This is only. one crop among many, and its value is worth noting as indicating the immense importance of agriculture as an element in the national welfare. There has been a con- siderable falling off in the number of acres sown with wheat, but pasture has usually been laid down in its stead. The decrease of the production of wheat- has consequently been simultaneously, with a great increase of the number of cattle. The land not devoted to corn growing has prodUced cattle, to nearly fotir times the value of the discontinued crops. . - CLEANLINESS IN MILKING—The National Live Stock Journal (Chicago) remarks, under this heading, that to insist on cleanliness in every operation connected with the dairy is like repeating not a "twice-told," but a "thousand-times-told" talc, and yet every day's receipts of butter in the Chicago market urge its repetition. Pure milk and good butter are as incompatible with unclean- liness as truth is with falsehood, and yet there seem to be just as many people seeking to make good dairy pro- ducts without due regard to the .cleanliness as there are seeking to maintain a reputation for truthfulness, while indqlging occasionally in a little departure from it The old adage, " Cleanliness is next to godliness," is nowhere more strictly applicable than to the dairyman, who handles milk, and makes bUtter and cheese. The dairy- man owes It to the public, as well as to his pocket, to exercise extreme care in handling his product, as much to the physician or apothecary, who handles medicines, where a slight inattention may entail serious results. His attention to cleanliness must begin in the cow-house and with the milking. The cow-house itself must be kept clear of accumulations of steaming manure, the odour of which the milk Would quickly absorb, and the ventilation of the house must be such as to keep the atmosphere sweet and wholesome. The milking pail must be examined before each milking, to see that it is per- fectly free from impurity or dust which may have found its Way in since it was scalded after the last milking. The udder and teats of the cow must be carefully wiped clean of hairs, dust, or other impurity before milking. The scrupulous attention to the cleanliness of the milk- ing pail must be extended to every other vessel used in the dairy. It is only by such carefulness that butter or ; cheese can be made marketable, much less palatable. The slovenly dairyman is constantly working for half- I pay. LORD TOLLEMACHS AND SMALL HOLDINGS FOR LA1301713- Bro.—A good deal of evidence was given before the Royal Commission on the Housing of the Poor, to show that ' nothing can be done to improve the 'condition: of the: rural labourer, but Lord Tollemache disputes this view. lit a hitter to The Times, Mr. F. Impey, hone, rary secretary, to the Allotments and Small Holdings As- sociation, writes:—" So strong was Lord Tollemache's opinion that he drew up a series ot resolutions, which he invited large landowners to sign. This document is, I venture to say, unparalleled in its sagacious perception of the points at issue and honest avowal of the only means of meeting them. This remarkable challenge of one of the great English landowners, and the one of all others who understands the need of the labourer as well as of the farmer, was unheeded." The following is a copy of the document:—

We, the undersigned, intend to offer to any agricultural labourer residing on our estates in a dairy district land suffi- cient to keep a cow, or in an arable district half an acre attached like a garden to his cottage. All agricultural labourers when once admitted to a cottage, on the recommendation of a neighbouring farmer, will become at once the tenant of the landlord, and not of the farmer. The number of small farms and holdings on our estates shall be double the number of farms above 100 acres, provided tenants can be procured for them. In future all applicants for small farms and holdings under thirty acres must show that they have some additional occupa- tion from which to derive profits besides farming, to support them and their families. Any respectable person with sufficient , means can have on our estates half an acre on a lease of ninety- years, or for ever, as a sitefor a good and comfortable house, to which will be added land, if required, at a rack rent. With respect to farms. above 100 acres, all respectable tenants will, on application, be given a lease for twenty-one years, on con- dition that they will secure to the landlord a good system of husbandry, and to the tenant a comfortable and convenient farmhouse, with suitable buildings attached. The foregoing rules to be carried out on our respective estates without any unnecessary loss of time. ToLLEMAGKE OH HEMINGHAM. PLouGHING 'STOBBLE.—ArabIa farmers cannot be too strongly advised to put the plough into their stubble as soon as possible. All who have had experience of ploughing Immediately after harvest and ploughing in the winter will, I am perfectly sure, endorse this recom- mendation, and for many' reasons. In the first place, upon most soils the strength required is less • land which requires three horses in the winter can be very well ploughed with two at the present time. In the next place most, except the lightest soils, after having been sodden with rain, turn up in anything but a friable form; they lie cold, heavy, and thick, on. are readily baked, even by a moderate winter sun. It is quite true that frost does a large amount of good, but in the mode- rate winters which we have had even that does not sufficiently penetrate the heavy cold clods in the fur- rows; whereas had they been ploughed when they were still friable, they would have been sufficiently fractured to allow of the penetration of the slightest frost. Another point is that insect life at the present time lies near the surface of the soil and is brought to • the top, being killeil as the nights become colder and the early frosts appear; but if allowed to remain where it is, it secures itself deeper in the ground, and is not affected by the weather at all, but comes up again in its destructive form another season. There is certainly no plan of ob- taining a fine friable surface soil which can equal that of ploughing now, and again ploughing in the spring. It must be evident, too, that land can be cleaned very much better at the present time by harrowing than in the winter, when it isiffipessible to drag the weeds, atid especially those with lorigtranthing roots, out of heavy land, ,which has been -ploughed wet, and which is fre- quently trodden into a disagreeable and unworkable mass by the horses. I am quite aware that it is often difficult to commence work of this kind immediately after harvest; but it is chiefly because the system of the farm does not permit. _ That system can be altered, and another year it will come in in the regular way, and there will be no difficulty about it whatever... There ,is no question that in the future labour musthe curtailed, and I take it this is one of the best methods of curtailing it.—Manchester Guardian. ' ENSILAGE FOR SMALL- FARMS.—A USEFUL Sounasriox. —There is .no better time than the present for calliht the attention of the smaller class of farmers and persms oCcupping a few acres of land to the value of the green food, if we may so venture to call it, growing,-upon the sides of the road. In some parts of the country the larger farmers monopolise everything that grows front- ing their fields. If they do not mow it they take care to send their sheep over it at least once a week, and where this practice is admitted bythose who are in charge of the roads ef a district there is little chance for the work- ing man or anyone else who has an eye to the point about to be suggested. The 'valise of ensilage is now too well understood to be disputed, and there is no reason why the labourer with his. pig, the peasant occupier with his cow, or the cottager with his .goat, should not preserve in a miniature silo something in the way of en- silage for winter use just as well as the landowner or the late farmer. To enable him, however, to do this it is necessary to obtain a number of tubs or barrels, all of which should be water-tight and air-tight, at all events at the sides and bottom. If there is any doubt about this point they should be tarred when they are filled. There is nothing better than a barrel for the purpoie, and small as it is it will take a large quantity of green material if it is thoroughly well pressed down, and this it certainly should be, for upon the perfection of packing and pressure depends the preservation of the food. There are, however, some persons who have brick pits or similar conveniences, which will do as well as barrels and hold a much larger quantity. Indeed, after all, it is far better to have one large silo than a number of small I ones, the surface exposed to the air being relatively I smaller. A brick pit lined with cement very slight in thickness is as good as anything, provided it is covered I with boards which fit well, and which in their turn are weighted down by bricks or stones. It is scarcely neces- sary to refer to more elaborate systems of pressure, more especially at the present moment, as they are not all perfection, constantly giving trouble and sometimes causing expense to those who adopt them. The class of persons these remarks are intended for should not de- spise the weeds, and everything in the shape of green material growing in the hedges and ditches, or upon the roadsides, if not actually poison, should be fish for their net, for it will almost invariably make good ensilage'.— J. L." in the Manchester Guardian.

It is about the same costume.that Rubens wore—black vervet breeches,- marine-blue stockings, a tvelvet vest trimmed with red sille,and 'a large felt hat—a costutne that the late Count Lalance, of Brussels, persistently wore. It is mounted on wheels so as to bestride a: cotton row, and the machine is double stroirto glean each side of therow. 'Hugh Brown, the Ayrshire poet, has just died in Glas- gow, at the age of 85 years. The deceased, whose first productions appeared 60 years ago, was best known as the author of" The Covenanters." He was a hand-loom weaver when the Scots Magazine published, in 1825, • his noticeable poem to the memory of Lord Byron, who had died in the Pievious year.' Mown became a rustic schoolmaste4ll 1828, a calling which he pursued forup- wards of 40 years.. He gragnally' declined in circum- stances; until towards the end he was dependent upon the bounty of friends for support. The Christian Leader of Glasgow states that a few months ago a brother poet, Mr. A:B. Todd, ventured to bring Brown's claims under the notice of Mr. Gladstone, who generously responded by forwarding a cheque for £so.—Times. A BODY Liouricum-Ron.—Mr. Delane, inventor of the Synchronous Telegraph, has devised a lightning-rod for wearing on the person. This idea is not very novel, but it has a fresh interest in connection with the accidents to electric light men from accidental shocks, especially, as in America, where the dangerous naked wires are some- times used. The rod, as may be-. imagined, consists of copper cords which branch along the arms and legs, where they are connected to metal plates on the soles of the boots, and thus reach the earth. In the event of both feet being off the ground at once, a short length of metal chain or braidmight be allowed to drag on the ground.. We are Dot aware that any ono has practically tested this device in a lightning-storm; but experiments could be made with it on electric light currents, for which Mr. Delane wishes 'it to be a safeguard.—Cassell'i Magazine. TUE RECESSION or Niicans.—Sir Charles Lyell, in 1841 and 1842, estimated the gradual recession of Niagara Fall by the undermining of its brink at the rate of about lft. per annum. Recent investigations of the subject by a Commission for the establishment of a State reservation at the Falls have, however, shown that this and other estimates are more or less erroneous. A map, based on surveys of the Philos made in 1883 by Mr. Thos. Evershed for the New York State Surveyor, have shown that in the 41 years ending 1883 the annual rate of maxi- mum recession has been 6 1-6 ft. For the eight years ending 1883 this rate is given at 18ift., so that the rate of recession has been higher of late. These results were obtained from the Canadian Fall, white the American Fall was found to have receded at the rate of 10in, per annum during the 41 years ending /883. It has been shown by the surveys that these two falls were once united; and supposing the rate of recession to continue, the Niagara gorge will be cut through in some 10,000 years. Lyell's estimate was 35,009 years. Of course, these attempts to calculate the cutting of the entire gorge, which terminates at the heights near Lake On- tario, assume that the hardness of the shale and lime rocks' volume of water, and height of the fall continue much the same as they are now.—Engineering.

No. XIL—SUPERSTITIONS OF SAILORS. -- There is but a plank between a sailor and eternity- perhaps the occasional realisation of that fact may have had something to do with the broad grain of superstition at one time undoubtedly lurking iii his nature. But whatever the cause, certainly the legendary lore of the sea is as diversified and interesting as the myths and traditions which haunt the imagination of landsmen, and, it is not surpriaing that sailors, who observe the phe- nomena of nature under such varied and impressive aspects, should be found to cling with tenacious obstinacy to their superstitious fancies. The winds, clouds, waves, sun, moon, and stars, have ever been invested with propitious or unlucky signs; and 'within, a score of years we have met seamen who had perfect faith in the weather-lore and traditions acquired during their ocean wanderings. We know by experience with how much solicitude the mariner looks for a fair wind, to speed along his craft; and this anxiety must have been more marked' before the adoption of steam as a propelling • pawer, when ships were often detained by a contrary wind for weeks at tlie harbour's- mOuth. At such times, the superstitious sailor would endeavour to obtain a fair breeze by buying one ; and not many years ago it was customary for a prudent skipper to purchase a favourable wind before putting to sea. And the selling of winds has prevailed from the early days of the world's history. Pomponius Mela,,an, 45, mentions certain Druidesses on the coast of Gaul who could raise storms and tempests by their incantations. In the "Discovery of Witchcraft," 1584, Reginald Scot affirms that "no- one endued with common sense but will deny that the elements are obedient to witches, and at their command, or that they may at their pleasure send rain, hail, tempests, thunder, and lightning." Shakespeare, in "'Macbeth," alludes to the superstition :- Ist Witch. Her husband's to Alleppo gone, master o' But in iasieve I'll thither sail, [the Tiger;. And like a rat without as tail, . I'll do, I'll &aril do. 1 2nd Witch. I'll give thee a wind. 3rd Witch. .And I another. . Ist Tack. . And I myself have all the-other. And the very ports they blows. All the quarters that they know I' the alupman'a card, I will drain him dry.as hay; . Sleep shall neither night nor day Hang upon his pent-house lid; He shall live a man forbid: Weary seven nights, nine times-nine, ,Shall he dwindle, peak and phie;: Though his bark cannot be lost,. Yet it shall be tempest tosa'd. Look what I have. . , 2nd Witch. Show me, show me. Ist Witch. Here have I.a pilot's thumb,. Wreck'd as homeward he did come. The possession of a pilot's thumb by witches and others would seem to indicatethbfr power of controlling- storms.; and it frequently occurred that a dead man's hand and other human relics were carried to sea as charms against shipwreck. It was customary to suspend a child's caul in the cabin of a ship to save her from sinking, and these curious membranes were much sought after by credulous mariners. - In ancient times sacrifices were 'universally azade to Boreas and to/Jupiter by the Greeks and Romans. A milk-white ewe, the western winds to please. And one coal-black, to calm the stormy seas. It was the cuatom of the Persians and Athenians to offer human sacrifices to "invoke the sea gods and in- vite the wind." Navigators of the middle ages obtained a blessing on their ships before starting on a voyage, and days were set apart for feasts and prayers, when the sailors would prostrate themselves before the altars and pray for favourable winds. This custom is by no means extinct; and it was common, seemingly, with many nationalities. 'lt is observed on the island of Capri, in honour or Madonna di Carmela, by the coral fisherso.pre- vipus to the departure of their fleet every spring. A somewhat modified form of the ceremony is observed by the Canton and Foochow sailors who call at the island of Pootoo, in. the Chusan Archipelago, on their passage up and down the China Sea, where they pray for fair wind and a prosperous voyage. liwunang is their chief divinity, seemingly amalgamated with the "queen.' of heaven," and as goddess her peculiar delight is to save those that are in danger by sea. She can assume thirty- two different shapes, and proceed to different parts of the world on her missions of mercy. I. Buddhism the holds the highest place as a saviour of 'mankind. The same deity is also worshipped by Japanese sailors, and during a storm they occasionally throw money in the sea to buy fair weather and a favourable breeze. Chinese sailors observe various customs for producing a fair wind.' On leaving port they attract the attention of their divinity by the loud beating of a gqng, the burning of fire crackers , and incense sticks' and casting food- offerings in the water. 'All this is to ward off_evil in- ' fluences., , When. starting on a,voyage they consider-it unlucky and the forerunner of foul weather to expec- torate over the bow of the vessel. A southerly (or ,favourable) breeze can be obtained by holdings cap high 'up against the wind; and the lives of a boat's crew would be endangered by repeating the word frig or wind.' -The Chinese have a strange custom of painting eyes on the bow of their craft, large or small, which are supposed to have the gift of sight by the superstitious.; and when asked to explain the utihty of the practice; they stop turther inquiry by responding, "Suppose no bale eyehow can see?' , . • . It was a'aridespread superstition among sailors that 1 Finns and Lapps were leagued with the Devil, and they were supposed to have the power of provoking storms and contrary winds. In Dana's excellent book, "Two' Years Before the Mast," is-a story of an old seaman who had sailed in a ship that was so hing beset by head heads, that a Finn' on board was suspected of being, the cause. He was aCcused and threatened by the captain, and, so completely terrified that he produced a favourable breeze within a very few hours! Lapland waseatpecially noted for its 7itches, who caused storms by Incantations and charms. Congreve refers to the superstition, "11l marry a Lapland witch as soon. and live upon selling winds and wrecking vessels." In-Ireland and -Denmark, alto, witches sold winds to mariners. Winds were sold less than fifty years ago itt the Orkney Islands; and at the present day occasionally the whale-fishers of Scotland, before leaving their harbours, burn effigies to promote a lucky voyage. Witches sold winds in the Isle of Man during the seventeenth 'century; and a State paper of 1834 records that nineteen women were under trial for conjuring up' a storm against a. ship of Charles, the First's. The patroil saints of sailors were St. Nicholas, who-was once in danger of Shipwreck, siad St. Christopher who was a ferryman; and St. Antonio also distributed his favours to fnanners. The padrone in the "Garden Legend " Eva : Now all is ready, high and low, ' Blow, blow, good saint Antonio. Whistling at sea was regarded, with special displeasure when a breeze was blowing, as the practice was supposed to provoke a gale. At the present time the habit is held to be a highly reprehensible one, and juniors, indulging it are often sharply told to " stop that whistlidt." But the credulous sailor believed also that whistling, in a guarded way, during a calm would induce a favourable breeze to spring up; and "whistling for a wind" is by no means a forgotten custom, even at the present day, during that patience-trying period when the sails hang idly-against the masts, and the ocean's surface is smooth and unruffled, like a polished mirror. Longfellow refers to this common belief Only a little while ago I was whistling to-Saint Antonio For a capful of-witid to fill our sail, But instead of a-breeze he has sent &pale. Captain Basil Hall, in hilt "Voyages," menttOns a case of whistling for the wind; during a calm in-the-Yellow Sea, which occurred 'on board his own ship. One of the . sailors undertook to prodUce a breeze; and Whilst in- credulously permitting-the practice to convince the men of the foolishnessof the.superstition, the captain remarks that a favourable breeze did spring up immediately after- wards. It was also a very general belief that a breeze might be produced by scratching the mast:. A wide-spread superstition prevailed that Friday was a very unlucky, day for a vessel to leave • port, and the prevalence of the belief is confirmed by frequent mention of it in old-fashioned ditties of the sea—. On a Friday she was launched;, On a Friday she set sail, On a Friday met a storm, Ancl was lost too in a gale. Pertinent-to the foregoing rhyme, L Fennimore Cooper relates an anecdote of a Connecticut merchant who devisedas plan to show the folly of the superstition. He had built a fine vessel, the keel of which was laid on a FridaY ; the ship was launched on a Friday; was named' the Friday; a Captain Friday had command of her; and she sailed on a Friday, freighted with a valuable cargo,. bound for China. .Strange to relate, no tidings of ship or crew were ever afterwards received; and we can well believe that such an event would strengthen the credu- lous mariner's faith in the superstition. Other instances of disaster, following the sailing of vessels on Friday have occurred; notably the West India steamer Amazon, , which foundered in the Bay of Biscay, when upwards of t a hundred passengers were lost,. Eliot Warburton among ^the number, who, strangely enough, had written "since the days of steam navigation the Bay of Biscay was no longer formidable ;" the Golden Gate, between San Francisco and Panama; the troopship Birkenhead, off the Cape of Good Hope; and; more recently, the English man-of-war Captain. Friday was also linked with the mermaid superstitions. Under certain circumstances the apparition of a mermaid was a favourable omen to' 'seamen; and a tempest-tossed vessel, "spoken" by a mermaid on a Friday, would assuredly reach her destined harbour in safety. The picturesque legend of the Flying Dutchman has been well utilised by learryatt and other nautical writers; but the tradition is worth repeating. /about three cen- turies ago, Mynheer Vanderdecken thy some named , Barron Fokke, a. Dutch skipper sailing between Holland land Java), the captain of a Dutch Indiaman, after a long 'season of adverse gales, swore that be would round the

div.p: 'Calk of Good Hope fir the face of a contrary wind, even itho'should be compEted to sail till the day of judg- 'inentr"Of course be falled to accomplish his object, and -for'his obstinacy and impiety, Vanderdecken and his crew were doomed to sail for ever in the latitude of the stormy Cape. So in the night watch, the superstitious sailors used to arm that they had seen the phantom ship, borne along by the gale over the tempest-lashed , waves, her spectral crew working the sails in response to the orders of her ghostly commander. The early navigators had a very general belief In ap- paritions and evil spirits, who were supposed to show themselves to the terrified sailors during a storm. The Cape of Good klOpe, or Cape of Storms, as it was for- merly called, is associated with many of these myths of the sea; and even the thick gray cloud which occa- sionallY obscures the top of Table Mountain, named the Tableclothris the premonitor of stormy weather. Camoens, in his immortarpoem, describes the kobold of the Cape.: Robust and vigorous n the air appeatod,. Enormous and' of stature very tall, The visage grimy arid with squalid beard,. The eyes were hbllow and the gesturmall Threatening and badi the colour pale andsear'd. Carmilhan was the phantom ship on which theapectre sat, when he appeared to doomed vessels. Sir Walter Scott, in "Rokeby," refers to the superstition— that phantom ship, whose form Shoots like a meteor* through the storm, And well the doomed, spectators know 'Tis harbinger of wreck and woe. We shall complete these traditions of the sea in a future chapter.

THE "PALL MALL" ABDUCTION C A.SE. Rebecca Jarrett was charged on remand at Bow-street, on, Monday morning, with four offences is connection with the alleged abduction of Eliza Armstrong. Five other defen- dants also appeared, namely, Mr. Stead, editor, and Mr. J'acques, a member of the staff of the Pall Mall Gazette; Mrs. Coombe, Mr. Bramwell Booth, of the Salvation Army; and Madame Mourez.—lt may be explained that the case arises out of the Pall Mall Gazette exposure of the way in which children were obtained for immoral purposes. The girt Armstrong was, it is alleged by the defendants, " sold " by the mother for a purpose of this kind; and the girl was abducted, though not criminally assaulted, to show how easily such a transaction coald be carried out.—Mr. Poland, for the prosecution, opened the proceedings by detailing the history of the case, and then called Eliza Armstrong, who said she first saw Mrs. Jarrett on the Tuesday before last Derby day, at Mrs. Broughton's. Jarrett asked her whether she would like a place. Afterwards Jarrett called her mother, who would not at first let her go, but eventually cenaented. Jarrett bought her a new dress, hat, and boots, and she wished her mother good-bye. They first went in an omnibus to the Marble Arch, and then to a house in Albany-street, where there was another lady. They had tea there. In the even- ing witness was taken to a house in Milton-street, Dorset- square, kept by Madame Mourez. Witness was then taken to a little room by the latter. She descried what took place. Soon afterwards Jarrett took her away in a cab to Poland-street. Two men followed them up the street to a house near a ham and beef shop. Mr. Jacques was one of the men. She was then taken into a bedroom, and Jarrett made her undress and get into bed. Soon after witness heard a man come into the room, and she called out. Shortly afterwards Jarrett said they must go away. Wit- ness described her removal to Paris. Her cross-examination was deferred.—Mre. Jarrett said she distinctly understood that Armstrong was going out to service.—Mre, Armstrong was afterwards examined, but her evidence was not com- pleted when the court adjourned —ln applying that Jarrett might be admitted to bail, her counsel said he was in- structed that there would be a miscarriage of justice if she was not allowed out. She had made a statement to Mr. Stead, to which she still adhered, and they could only arrive at the truth if he were at liberty.—All the defendants were liberated on bail.

Mrs. Armstrong was further examined, and gave an in- teresting account of the negotiations for the restoration of the child. She denied that she "sold" her daughter. The little girl herself was afterwards cross-examined, and was questioned as to her home surroundings. She admitted that she was well treated after she was sent abroad. Mr. Stead, who is not represented by counsel, did` not cross- examine the witness. Ile said be was satisfied with the truthful manner in which she had answered the questions pat to her. The inquiry was adjourned to Saturday.
GREAT EXCITEMENT IN WALES ABOUT A MARVELLOUS CURE.
LIVING SIX TRAM 'WITHOUT GOING TO RED.
Mr. EDITOR.—WhiIe spending a few days at the pleasant seaside town of Aberystwith, Cardiganshire. Wales. I heard related what seemed: to rEu3 either a fabulous story or a mar- vellous cure.

The story was theta poorsnfferer who had not been aNe to lie down in bed for six, long years, given up to die by all the Doctors, had been sceedily cored by some Patent Medicine. It was related with the-more implicit confidence from the clreum. stance, as was said, that the Vicsr of planrystyd was familiar with the facts, and could vouch for the truth of the report. I Raving a little ourhoity be knew how such stories grow in I travelling, I took theliberty while at the village of Llanry.tyd tonsil upon the Tiber, the Rev. T Evans, and to inquire abo u this wonderful more. Though& total stranger to Lim, both he and his wife most graciously entertained me in a half hour's con- versatlon,-princlpally touching the case of Mr. rush, in which they seemed to take -a deep and sympathelc interest, having been familiar with his sufferings, and now rejoiced In what seemed to them a most remarkable cure.

The vicar remarked that he presumed his name had been eonnected with the report from his having mentioned the case so Mr. John Thomas. a chemist, of Llanon. He said Mr. Pugh was formerly a rsAdent of their parish, but was now living In the parish of Lianddeinol.

Hs strongly vouched for Mr. William Puth's character as a respectable farmer and worthy of credit. I left the venerable Vicar with a livelier sensephf the happy relation of a pastor and people, feelinz that be was one who truly sympathised with all who are afflicted In mind, body, or estate.

On my return toaberystwith, I was impressed with a desire to see Mr. Pugh, whose reputation stood so high. His farm Is called raucous-Mawr, signifying above the dingle," situ- ated near the summit of a smooth round bill, overl.oking beautiful valley in which is situated the lovely ivy.mantled Church of Llanddeinol. I found Mr. Pagh, apparently about 40 years old, of medium height, rather slight; wits a pleasant and Intelligent face. I told him I had heard of his great afflic- tion and of his remarkable and almost tairseulous relief, and that I had come to learn from his own ilpe what there was of truth in the reports.

Mr. Pugh remarked that his neighbours laad taken a kindly nndevmpathetiodnterest In his case for many years, but of late their interest had been greatly awakened by a happy change in his condition. What you report as having heard abroad, said he, is substantially true-with one exception. I never under- stood that ray case was ever given up as hopeless by any PhY- siclan. I have been treated by several doctors hereabouts, ra good as any In Wales, but unfortunately so prescription of theirs ever brought the desired relief. Fifteen years ago, he said, I first became cotscious of a sour and deranged stomach and loss of appetite, vFlaich the doctors told me was dyspepsia. What food I could hold in my stomach seemed to cm me no good, and was often thrown up with painful retchings. This was followed after a time with hoarse- ness, and a raw soreness of the throat. which the doctors called bronchitis, and I was. treated for that, bat with little success. Then came shortness of breath and a sense of suffocation, es- pecially nights, with clammy sweat, and I would have to get out of bed and sometimes open a door or window in winter weather to-fill my lungs with the coldalr.

About slaryears ago/ became so bad, that I could not sleep in bed, but had tdtake my unquiet rest and dreamy sleep sitting in an armelmir. My affliction seemed to be working downward into my bowels as well as upwards into my lungs and throat. In the violent coughing spasms which grew more fr•quent, my abdomen would expand and colia,pe and at times It would seem that I should. suftotate. All this time I was reduced ;In strength so that I could perform na hard la- bour and my spirits were con,equently much depressed.

Early In this last spring I had aztin more severe Ppasmodie attack, and my family and neighbours became alarmed. be- lieving that certainly I would not survive, when a neighbour, who had some knowledge, or had heard of the medicine, seat to Aberystwith by the driver of the Omnibus Post, SOM seven miles distant, and fetched a latttleot Mother Siegel's Curative Syrup.

This medicine they administered to me according to the directions, when to their surprise and delight no less than my. own, the spasm ceased, I. became at ease, and my sto- mach was calmed. My bowels were moved as by a gentle cathartic, and I felt a sense of quiet comfort all through such, as I-had not before realised In many years. I mull walk' around the house and breathe comfortably in a few hours after L had taken the medicine. I have continued to take the medi- cine daily now for 80IT ebbing over two months, and I can lay down sad Sleep sweetly at nights and have not since had a r•carrence of those terrible spasms and sweating,. I have been so long broken down and reduced in my whole system that I have not tried to perform any very hard Out-door labour, deeming it hest to be prudent lest by over-exertion / may do myself injury bsfore my strength IS fully restored. I feel that my stomach and bowels have been and are being thoroughly renovated and renewed by the medicine. In feet I feel like a new man.
__------ I have been much congratulated by my neighbours. especi- ally by the good Vicar of Llannrystyd, who with his sympa- thetic wife have come three miles to shod tears of joy on my recovery.__
I bade Mr. Pugh goodbye, happy that even one at least among thoulands had iouna a remedy for an aggravating din- ease
Believing this.remarkable ease of Dyspeptia Asthma sh-uld be known to the nubile. I beg to submit the above facts as they are related to me.

The CHAIRMAN, who was received with appleeese, said that although a number of the delegates Ilea not yet ar- rived, he thought that as the time announeee ,for the meet- ing to commence had expired, they hed better begin busi- ness. In the first place, they must allow him to tender a very cordial welcome front the people of Warrington to all the delegates present. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to see that the conference was confined to two very important resolutions—one dealing with the land and one with local government. There was so much for the Liberal party to do, and there was so much upon which they were all united, that it was desirable they should undertake these subjects first. He believed that all Liberals, both the moderate and the more extreme, were thoroughly united on the desirability of these two reforms. A. great reform in the land laws—some would go a little further and some would go not quite so far—a large reform in the land laws was advocated by all genaine Liberals, and also a reform in local government. (Applause.) They had a short time ago a very weighty speech from one of their greatest leaders— ha meant Lord Hartington—(cheers)—and they would have that evening a great treat indere.d, atlethey would have amongst them one of their most advanced leaders—Mr. Chamberlain. (Loud cheem) Between the lines laid down by Lord Hartingten' and those they might fairly ex- pectto be laid down by Mr. Chamberlain that evening, the Liberal party might march steadily to victory. (Applause.) , The leadership and presence ,of such men as Lord Elarting- ton and Mr. Chambertain were both required and both were necessary to the Liberal party. (Hear, hats e And then presently they would no doubt have, after a long silence, a few but weighty guiding words from—the two gentlemen he had named would not object to his saying it—a greater man than either. He meant the Grand Old Man. (Loud and continued cheers.) 'Their opponents fully expected—, perhaps the wish was father to the expectation—that the, Liberal party would be divided—(" No 'e)—and that it would be impossible ler the moderate Liberals to work with the Radicals and the Radicals with the moderate Liberals. They had been disappointed in that expectation before, and they were to show them that they would be disappointed in It again. (lime hoar, and applause.) He would not longer occupy their time. Lamm, who was received with applause,, moved the following resolution :—"That, in the opinion of. this conference, the reformed Parliament which will be ' elected next November should direct its earliest efforts to a thorough and drastic reform of the laws which relate to the tenure and transfer of land, (I) IF the abolition of primo- geniture, enteil, and other eemnacts of feudalism, which have the effect of keeping the soil in the hands of a com- paratively email number of persons; (2) by the simplifica- tion tif the transference of land; (3) by giving to occupiers security ef tenure and full compensation for improvements effected by them; (4) by facilitating the acquisition of land by corpoiations and other public bodies, who will hold and use it forthe benefit of the people; (5) by the enfranchise- ment of urban leaseholders; and (6) by promoting allot- ments to labourers and artizans, and encouraging the growth of peasant proprietors." (Applause.) He said he thought he could congratulate them upon the terms in which the resolution was framed, because it laid down no abstract Vrineiple on which they might possibly differ, but limply pointed Oat the evils which every Liberal wished to see remedied. He could tell them that at the present moment be had no wish to lay down any specific remedy. Tell him •if they could the quantity and the quality of the Liberal majority in the enetting• Parliament, and then he would tell them what remedies the Liberal party ought to aim at. If they could get a Parliament that would be strong enough eby its Liberal majority to Intimidate the House of Lords and prevent them frustrating Liberal measures, if they -could get such a Liberal majority in the House of Com- mons as would benddown all obstruction, and prevent the landowners la the House of Commons combin- ing with the landowners in the House of Lords, and so thwarting the wills of the constituencies, then • they might 'aim .at large results.
