The Chairman then, before calling upon Mr. McMinnies to propose the first resolution, announced that letters, includ- ing one from Mr. Daniel Adamson, had been re- ceived from gentlemen who were unable, to be present. (Applause.) Mr. MeMuneres, who was received with much applause, said; Mr. Chairman and gentlemen,—l beg to move "That this meeting heartily welcomes the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, M.P., and ex- presses its unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone and the members of the late Government, thanks them for the great measures passed during their tenure of office, and especially for the Acts for the Extension of the Franchise and Redistribution of Seats, which have secared for the people a wider and more equitable share in the government of the eountee." (Cheers.) There are two reasons, gen- tlemen, why a Liberal meeting like this should pass a resolution such as I have just rot& The first reason is that it is fitting and"proper for us to ex- press our recognition of the services of the late Goyernnient, and our thankfulness to themfor what they have done during this Parliament. (Applause.) The second reason is that we should contend against that contention of the other side, that the Tories have passed all the good measures that have been passed during the last Parliament. We have been told over and over again that all the good measures, —all the reformmeasures—that have been passed have been passed by Tory Governments and by the: Tory party. We, of course, know-ennless we have been contending with imaginary foes for the last' 50 Tears—that the Tories have been the most strenuous opponents of those measures that we thank the late Government for having passed. Now, the late Lord Beaconsfield was the 'father of thisTalsehood, for when certain measures had been. forced upon a Tory Government, either' because the chiefs of that Government had been converted or because that Government coult not any longer resist the demand for reform, he taught his followers to say that those were Tory measures passed by the Tory party. Well, I must say his followers were as at to lea= as he was apt to 'teach this falsehood. ltt is very easy to pass from 'falsehood in reference to measures to falsehood in reference to men, and there are certain Tory speakers and writers, Dot all though, but certain ones who, when they come to deal with an oploonent, the first thing they do is to tell it lie about him—(applause)—and the next thing they do is, when the lie has been disputed and disproved, to repeat it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Now we have on this platform a very distinguished victim of this mode of warfare. The late Mr. O'Connell used to say he was the best abused man in Europe, andl think we may say of our friend Mr. Chamberlain that he has been the object of more misrepresentation and inaccuracy than any man in the three kingdoms. (Applause.) Well, he seems to me to beef the teniperament of the man whom the late Lord Derby used to speak about. That man was a great burly brawny Cornish miner, and he had a little wife who ased to beat him. (Laughter.) On one occasion when he was being reproached by his companions for allowing this, he said, "Well, it don't matter ;• it pleases she and it don't hurt me." (Laughter.) Well, now Mr.. Chamberlain acts quite :like this man and he acts quite rightly in disregarding this mode of attack. ' It does not seem to hurt him. (Applause.) What gives rise to no little surprise is that notwithstand- ing these daring lies, he himself :does not seem a 1 penny the worse. (Laughter and applause.) And. he is no worse; he is better. (Hear, hear.) There is only one man in this country who is more popn- lar among the rank and file of his party—(hear, hear)—and we know that. -We who have had the , getting up of this conference to-day and this meet- ing to-night know it, and we know perfectly well that when we welcome Mr. Chamberlain here to- night we are speaking the s entiments of the great Liberal party in the district by which we are sur- rounded. (Applause.) We can assure Mr. Chamber- lain on their behalf, and his .late colleagues also, that we thoroughly appreciate what they have done for us during the Parliament which is about to er- pre, and we look forward with confidence to. their future efforts to promote the interests and prosperity of the three kingdoms. (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. WILLIAM CIIOSFIEL1). ( Liberal candidate for Warrington,) who was received with loud applause, said: Mr. Rigby, ladies, and go mtlemen,—it has been said that a thing well begun is half done. (Hear, hear.) In the spirit of that pr overb Ithank you for having . already so far ace° raplished the object of my rising to second this resolution. It is my duty, as seconder of the first resolution, to en- courage you and emphasize the welcome which you have given to Mr. Joseph :Chamberlain (cheers) and, if it needed. it, it would also be my duty to endorse the expressions of confi- dence which you have already given, though not in the words of the resolution, to the acts of her Majesty's late Government. (Hear, hear.) We are here to night mainly to hear an address, which we know will be one of greatsnoment, from a member of the late Government, and I wish as strictly. as I can, without looking at my watch, to follow out the injunction of our chairman, that injunction which he enforced by a breach on his own account. (Laughter and applause.) We are here to welcome Mr. Chamberlain, one—it would perhaps be invidi- ous to say how near the front, but -one of our leaders. (Load. cheers and a voice: "Our future Prime Minster") The LiberAl party does not march in the solid phalanx • the platform of the Liberal party is sufficiently :broad to hold all those who have the best interests .ot the people at heart, and who seek to pursue these interests Iby improving the condition of things as we !go along. I look upon Mr. Chamberlain as a general of division. (Hear, hear.) Some people may take that in the sense which don't mean it. I don't 'Mean be is one who necessarily divides us, but I mean in the ordinary sense of the term, lie is a general of division. It is no weakness to an army that there is in one branch of the' service a general who is at the head of the engineers, another who is at the head of the cavalry, and another who has a harder work, and stands at the head of the foot regi- ments. (Hear, hear.) It is in that sense that ,I. I speak of Mr. Chamberlain as a general of division, and he in that sense is loyal to his commander-in-. chief. (Loud applause.) And we, therefore, wet-. come him and thank him and the late ministry' through him, for the work which they have done. (Hear, hear.) They have done a vast amount of work which has put es in a superior position to what the Liberal party occupied five years ago. It -may be that yea and Ido not think that we have lad quite as much of our own way as we deserve, but perhaps, if we had been standing in an impar- tial position, we should have seen things rather OH- lerently. However that may have been during the past, we hope that our deserts will be met to a greater extent in the future than in the past. (Hear, hoar.) We tha,nk them not only for what the have accomplished but for what it was their intention to accomplish. (Hear, hear.) There was a vast num- ber of very good measures thrust aside through no fault of the late Government. They have been met by those who considered it .was the duty of the Opposition to oppose, and therefore we have found that very many measures which we, as Radicals would have wished to -see passed have been put on, one Side, and, for the time being, put on the shelf. We thank Her Majeetyes late Government for what the present Government has accomplished—(ap- plause)—during the last few weeks of the session. They heNe shown to those who consider that the Opposition must always oppose that there 'is another and a better way, and that, the motto of their action has been that It is the duty of the Leg- islature to legislate. (Hear, hear.) Believing this I second the resolution with great heartiness, and I ask you to support it. (Loud cheers.) The resolutwe was then put and carried by loud acclamatioll- - Right Hon. Josmat CHAMBERLAIN next addressed the meeting, and was received with loud cheers. Ile said he was glad to have the opportunity of fulfilling at last a 'itemise which he made long ago to hiafriend Mr. Mc.Minnies. He did not think in the last Parliament there was a more loyal, a truer, or a more unselfish Liberal than their representative, and he was sure it was a matter of regret to his colleagues that he had decided to relinquish Parliamentary life. As he had done so, he hoped and believed Mr. Crossfield would take his place, and would follow in his footsteps and represent worthily the Liberalism of that borough. (Applause.) He understood that the occasion of that meeting had been taken in order to ihvite representatives from the widely surrounding district, and therefore it was representative not only of the Liberalism of War- rington, but also of the borough and county constitu- encies within a considerable radius.' The time at which they had gathered together lent to ft an additional en- pertance. For the first time in the history of our country the Parliament whioh would shortly meet at Westmin- ster would be representative, in the full sense, of the people of the obuntry—(hear, hear)—and great numbers
[abi4

lof the population hitherto ignored and passed - over would now be invested with their full political rights. (Hear, hear) The change was a momentous one, and unparalleled in the annals of reform. Two millions of voices, hitherto silent or unheard, now demanded attention, and the claims that they made, the wants that they expressed, and the rights upon which they insist, would be potent factors in future legislation. , There were, however, some people who seem to think that the revolution—for it was no less—which had just been accomplished was an incident complete in itself which was to have no future consequence. They seemed to think that the franchise was a toy, which was con- ceded to a childish demand. Now that had been given everything would go on as ' before, and the ' old watchwords were to do duty, and the old platitudes were to be trotted out, and a grateful nation was , to return a Liberal Government to power without ask- 1 ing impertitent questions (laughter) —or exacting inconvenient pledges. (Laughter and applause.) Well, that was not the view which he entertained of the situation. (Hear, hear.) The great agitation which had set the seal upon popular government in this country was the work of the Radical party—(cheers),— which now constituted the great majority of the Liberal party--(hear hear),—and the arm chair politiciens who looked on with indifference while they were bearing the heat and the burden of the day, had no claim and power to deprive them of the effects of that victory. The programme which satisfied a limited electorate, of which, perhaps, not more than one-third belonged to the working classes, was much too restricted for the new coastituencies, in which the working classes formed three- fifths, or three-fourths, of the whole voters. This was so obvious a fact, that it had even attracted the notice of the stupid party—(laughter)—and the Tories were now building their hopes upon expectations of division in the Liberal ranks, and of a great secession from the Liberal camp. (Laughter.) Well, in a speech which was recently delivered at Sheffield—(laughter and ap- plause)—he observed that Lord Randolph Churchill— (hisses)—with considerable ingenuity, pointed out the irreconcileable differences in the Liberal party. After an exhaustive criticism of a recent speech of Lord Hart,- ington at Waterfoot, after proving the incapacity, in- consistency, and the ineptitude of the noble lord, Lord R. Churchill gave to him and his friends a patronising in- ' vitation to leave the party with which, by their history and their traditions, by their past services and past sacrifices, the Whigs had been identified in order to join the party of union----(laughter),—of moderation, of consistency, and of patriotism—(renewed laughter),—of which Lord Randolph Churchill was a conspicuous member. (Lend laughter.) In vain was the net spread in the eight of any bird! Lord Hartincton WAS the last man In the world to be caught by the chaff of Torydemocraey. The Tories were founding themselves again, as they had ' done in the past, on expectations that were doomed 1 to disappointment. Liberalism was broad enough I and free enough to include within its borders all the friends of progress. (Applause.) Although they might differ among themselves, as they had done in every period of their history, as to order, or even as to the nature of the measures that they should take from time to time to give effect to their principles, those difficul- ties they would settle among themselves -- (Ap- planse)--end without Tory assistance. (Applause.) life did not think that there were any of them who would be tempted to desert their own cause and their own party, in order-to make a new alliance with that hetero- geneourecombitiation which styled itself the Constitutional party, and which included in its ranks Free Traders and Protectionists, Ulster Orangemen and English Roman Catholics, licensed victuallers and Established Church- men—(laughter),—Tory democrats and fossil reactionists, —(renewed laughter)—who united their discordant 'voices in order to form a mutual protection society for ensuring to each of its members place, and privilege, and power. (Cheers.) He thought there were two rea- sons why the moderate-Liberals would resist the tempta- tions that were addressed to them. The first was because the proposals of the Radical and advanced section a the party were so moderate and so reasonable—(hear)— that no sensible man would see in them cause for a dis- ruption • and the second reason was because, whatever might be the alarm which timid people felt as to some of the propositions which were ascribed to the Radical party, it was nothing at all in comparison with the disgust and indignation which they must entertain of the speeches and the actions of the present Tory Government. (Applause.) It was quite true that in the speech •to which he had referred Lord Randolph Churchill gave a clear and concise account of what would be the policy of the Government ef which he was so distinguished a member, and he declared that it would be to oppose in every point the domestic policy of Mr. Chamberlain. (Laughter.) That was all very well. But then this promise -came rather late in the day—(laughter),—for it catneeter the Tory Government had conceded to Mr. Chamberlain every single point upon which he had .the misfortune to differ with the moderate Liberals. (Ap- plause.) Just let him recall to their mind what those points were. He was in favour of the immediate exten- sion of the franchise when the Tories and some of the moderate Liberals thought it might with advantage be indefinitely postponed. (Hear, hear.) He was in favour of the equality of the franchise throughout the three kingdoms as well as to Great Britain; he advocated equal -electoral districts, and he was denounced as a red Republican and a revolutionist for doing so. (Hear, hear.) He was opposed to the minority vote in any shape or form. (Hear, hear.) He objected to the continuance of exceptional legislation in Ireland after the emergency which alone justified it had passed away, and he was in favour of granting to that country, as well as to England and to Scotland, the largest possible measure of local government consistent with the integ- rity of the empire. (Loud applause.) He objected to disqualification for medical relief—(hear, bear)—and he 1 was in favour, when it became necessary to raise addi- tional taxation to cover the expenditure on foreign ex- peditions, of throwing that expenditure upon the shoulders of those who were best able to bear the bur- den. (Hear, hear.) In the first instance the Tories were against him upon everY one ef those points; there was not a single Tory speaker, with the exception of Lord Randolph Churchill, who ever-said one word in favour of any one of those propositions, and even Lord Randolph Churchill said as much against them in one day as he said in their favour on the other. (Laughter.) But, now, without a word of acknowledgment, without a shadow of reason, except party exigencies and party interests, they had appropriated every item of his pro- gramme--(hear, hear, and laughter)—they claimed it as their own, and they had stripped him of his policy and left him bare and forlorn till he could invent another. (Re- newed laughter and applause.) Let them not mistake him. He did not complain of the theft, but was distressed at the ingratitude of its perpetrator's. (Loud laughter.) He read, a short time ago, an account of the forcible entry which had been made into a gentlemaa's country man- sion, and the people who effected it carried off the plate ' and the valuables; then they turned to the cellar and the pantry, and they made a hearty supper; before they left, they put upon the tables a note which was con- ceived in terms somewhat to this effect :—" Your pork- pies and champagne is first class. but your beer is beastly—(loud laughter)—and if you do not alter your tap, we won't corns again." (Renewed laughter and ap- plause.) Well, that was exactly the position of Lord Randolph Churehill.• (Laughter, mad hoar, hear.) He and his friends had gorged themselves with the political food which he (Mr. Chamberlain) had provided for them and they turned round and abused him, and said they would drop his acquaintance unless he changed his tap. (Loud laughter and applause.) But it was not only, he thought, in connection with domestic policy, that the moderate Liberals would see little reason ta change the party to which they now belonged for the party to which they were invited. (Hear, hear.) In the time of the late Government, they had on more than one occasion to deplore the apathy and teen the desertion of mem- bers of their party on the occasion of the numerous votes of censure which were moved against them. What were their grounds of disaffection? It was that they thought their policy was not sufficiently vigorous and decisive. He said the Government were yielding too readily to the claims of other nations; that they were altogether too conciliatory in their deal- ings with them. He was not going to argue that point then. He asked the moderate Liberals what satisfaction they had found in the change, and how much better they were now that a Tory Government was in office? The financial agreement in Egypt, which was condemned as being humiliating and inadequate, had been carried out. (Applause.) The retirement fromehe Soudan had been proceeded with, and no attempt had been made to relieve the garrisons in equatorial Africa; no attempt had been made to complete the railway to Berber • no- body ever talked about it now. Even Sir Henry Tyler, with whom it was the subiect of pathetic excitement, believed in silence now. The negotiations had been going on on precisely the same lines that were laid down, and the peace, which Lord Randolph Churchill denounced as terrible news, would be the peace for which the late Government had arranged, and which their Tory suc- cessors would be only too glad to carry into effect. Those negotiations had been undisturbed even by the extraordinary incidents of which they heard just before Parliament was prorogued, when a British consular official was said to have been arrested by the 'Russian authorities and flogged in order to extort information from him. Let them just consider for a moment what I would have been said if such an occurrence had hap- pened in the time a the late Government. Let them just imaeine—their imagination was equal to it—what 1 would hive been the frantic outcries of Mr. Asheneasl Bartlett—(laughter),—the outraged patriotism of .Sir Henry Drummond Wolff—(renewed lauebter)—the simu- lated indignation of Sir Michael Hicks• Beach—at the unparalleled disgrace inflicted on the British name. But under a Tory Government they heard nothing of that. The incident passed without observation; it did not for a moment ruffle the meek complacency of the men who had not even yet got over their astonishment at finding themselves in office. (Laughter.) The Jingo in his wild and natural state of independence and of opposition was a very furious creature indeed when he simulated the lion's roar, but when he got into the toils of office, and was domesticated on the Treasury Bench, he was per- fectly inoffensive. (Laughter.) But there was another point of more serious importance than any to which he had hitherto called their attention. They would, no doubt, recollect how angry the Tories were at the supine- ness of the late Government when Germany annexed a portion of New Guinea. The territory was a vast one,

Inhospitable, unhealthy, in which we had no settle- ! mints and no present interests, but, notwithstanding thilt, there was no limit to the virulence with which they were assailed for having "truckled" to Germany, and betrayed British interests; but now Germany has been suffered, without protest, to outrage the feelings of the 1 Sultan of Zanzibar, under whose authority and influence ' a vast and increasing trade had sprung up, which had done something considerable for the prosperity of Man- chester and all the surrounding elistsicts, but which was now imperilled and threatened. A dozen New Guineas would not compensate us for the loss of the markets secured to us by the independence of Zanzibar, yet they had not heard a single word of opposition from the Government and from the party which professed to be the special guardians of British rights and British in- terests. As to South Africa, the only change had been that the commander who, without the loss of a single life, restored to the province of Bechuanaland peace and prosperity had been recalled, and they heard not of any steps to be taken in order to prevent the return to anarchy of the vast province which he had redeemed from riot and disorder. Under all the circumstances, he thought they might declare that the evidence accumu- lated that the stop-gap Administration was a Govern- ment of vast promises and small performances—(hear, hear)—brave words and poor deeds, letting, as Shak- were said, " ' I dare not' wait upon 'I would." (Ap- plause.) He would come to anotherpoint which he said affected more deeply the integrity of the empire and the interests of its populations than our relations with any foreign country. He referred to the relations which were to subsist in the future between Great Britain and Ireland. (Hear, hear.) He supposed the moderate Liberals had some opinion upon that matter, but upon it Lord Randolph Churchill, although he spoke for an hour and a half at Sheffield, was significantly silent. In view of the most important declaration which had ever been made by any. Irish leader, Lord Randolph Churchill, the most influential member of the Tory Government, uttered not a ward, gave not a sign to show what would be the attitude of his party—the party which he has led and educated— (laughter)—in view of the,unhesitating and uncompro- misin demand of Mr. Parnell for the dismemberment of the British Empire. He might say that his (Lord Ran- dolph Churchill's) reticence was at least as eloquent as speech, and the moderate Liberals must be blind indeed if they did not see in it the natural consequence of the Ma,amtmsna alliance and of the tacit compact by which the Tories had purchased office. Now, he was not going to imitate the reticence of the Tory Minister. (Applause.) ilt was necessary that every man should speak out on that matter. He owed it as much to the Irish people as to the Engl sh and Scotch. (Hear, hear.) There should be no ambiguity in his utterances on a matter which so vitally affected the interests of the country. He (Mr. Chamberlain) thought he might claim in some measure to be an impartial witness. He had tried to be a friend to Ireland. He had a deep sympathy with the Irish ' people in their struggle against oppression and unjust faws—(hear, hear),—and embarrassed with a system of government which was alien to their own national senti- ment, and under which many of her best, ablest, and most patriotic sons had been excluded from the practical work of administration in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Even in the speech referred to he saw that Lord Randolph Churchill went out of his way to say that when Mr. Foster resigned—it appeared that now he approved of the administration of Mr. Foster—it was in conse- quence of a discreditable intrigue which was principally the work of Mr. Chamberlain. Well, they knew that there was no intrigue at all, and that Mr. Foster left office because he could not agree to the release of Mr. Parnell and his companions from Kilinainham' where they were confined without trial. He (Mr. Chamberlain) would only say on that that he thought subsequent events had amply justified the policy of the Government which he (Mr. Chamberlain) gave his hearty support to. He would not refer to it then, because he hoped that among many other things it showed that he had notbeen an opponent of Mr. Parnell or a prejudiced opponent of the cause to which he had devoted his life. Before he spoke of the main points of his recent declaration there was one Matter upon which he thought scant justice had hitherto been done. On many previous occasions they had regretted that the Irish leader had not used the in- fluence which he had deservedly acquired with his own people in order to repudiate and denounce the out- rages that had disgraced and staintd an agitation in many other respects worthy of admiration. But when he spoke the other day at Dublin he used language, which for firmness and definite con- viction left nothing to be desired, and he showed the folly as well as the wickedness of the crimes which had done so much to prejudice the Irish nation in the eyes of all honourable and honest men. He (Mr. Chamber- lain) was glad to acknowledge that that was a point of good augury. But what was Mr. Parnell's programme? He (Mr. Parnell) said that in his opinion the time had come to abandon altogether all demand to obtain remedial measures or subsidiary reform, and to con- centrate the efforts of Irish representatives upon the securing of a separate and independent Parliament, which was to consist of a single chamber, and whese first object was to be to put a protective duty against all English manufactures. ("Never.") Then he said, in the second place, that he • expected that Whig and Tory would vie with one another in helping him to a settlement on his own terms. He said, lastly, if any party sought to make that object impossible, he and his friends would make all things impossible for them. Ile (Mr. Chamberlain) was not a Whig—(laughter)—he was certainly not a Tory—(more laughter) ;—but speaking for himself he said that if those, and these . alone, were the terms on which Mr. Parnell's support was to be obtained, he would not enter into them. (Cheers.) If his claim were conceder{ they might as well for ever abandon all hope of maintaining a united king- dom, and we would establish within less than 30 miles ,of our shores a new foreign country animated from the outset with unfriendly intentions towards England. It was a policy that would be extremely disastrous and ruinous to Ireland; it would be .dangerous to the se- curity of this country, and under.these circumstances he held that we were bound to take every step in our power to avert se great a calamity. They would appeal in the first place to the Irish people. He could not being himself to believe that they were so prejudiced by the recollection of past wrongs that they would not recognise the anxiety of the present generation of Eng- lishmen to do them justice—(hear, hear)—to remove every tangible grievance, to establish equal laws in the three kingdoms—(hear, hear)—and he thought if they ' were persuaded of this they would be unwilling . to sever themselves from the common history of • the United Kingdom, in which Irishmen had taken so great and glorious a part. ( Cheers. ) , Be would not dwell on the threats with which Mr. Par- nell accompanied his demand. He supposed they *ere intended for Irish consumption—(laughter,—but he thought they were unnecessary and uncalled for. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Parnell seamed to him to forget the change which had come over our constitutional system. He had no longer to deal with interests and class representa- tion in the British House of Commons, altogether out of proportion to their number, but he was face to face with the whole population of England and Scotland, rein- forced as it would be by at least one-fifth of the popula- tion of Ireland itself, and to threaten 32 millions of people with the vengeance of four millions—why that was rhetorical artifice utterly unworthy of Mr. Parnell's powers and influence. (Hear, hear.) It was said by him that justice required that they should concede to Irishmeu the absolute right to self-government, He would reply that was a right which must be considered in rela- tion to the security and welfare of the other countries in juxtaposition to which Ireland was placed, and with whose interests hers were indissolubly linked. (Hear, hear.) He could not admit that five millions of Irish- 1 men had any greater inherent right to govern them- selves without regard to the rest of the United Kingdom 1 than would have the five millions of persons inhabiting I the Metropolis. (Hear, hear.) God had made us neigh- bours, and he would to heaven our rulers had made us friends. ' (Loud cheers.) But as neighbours neither one nor the other had any right so to rule his own house- hold as to be a source of annoyance or danger to i the other. (Hear, hear.) But subject to that limitation, 1 he for his part would concede the widest possible rues-; sure of domestic government to the Irish people, as he ' would concede to the people of England and Scotland. ' (Hear, hear.) Some time ago—nearly twelve months I ago—he prepared a scheme with this object, which, in . addition to providing for the population a representative i authority in every district throughout the three king- I doms for the purpose of dealing with exclusively local work, proposed also the establishment of a National Elec- tive Council, to which might be referred the administra- tion, supervision, and control, which were now exercised by some of the departments in London, and by those de- partments of Ireland known commonly under the name of the Dublin Castle. He proposed to sweet) away the 1 network of Boards appointed by the English Govern- 1 ment, carrying with them the seal of English authority, whose interference had produced so much irritation, so much just annoyance, and even injury to Ireland. He had reason at the time to believe such a scheme would have been favourably received by the vast bulk of the Irish people. He had reason to know that it would have been accepted by the leaders of the National party, and by the chief representatives of public opinion in Ireland, as a full and satisfactory settlement of the question of Local Government. (Hear, hear.) No doubt there would have remained the national sentiment, which some persons said would never be composed by the con- eesssion of a separate Legislature: but if such , councils as he had suggested had been established j and in full working order; if the perpetual interference of foreign authorities had been for ever abolished he believed the whole sense of grievince would have gradu- ally died out and a new generation would have arisen which would have been willing and glad to accept the obligations as well as the advantages which the union of the three kingdoms for material interests was calculated to secure. (Hear, hear.) Well, his proposals, unfortu- nately, did not meet with the support of the moderate Liberals, and under those circumstances it would have been useless to proceed with it. ',Now, what had hap- pened? The opportunity had passed away; Mr. Parnell, encouraged by the Tory party, suddenly raised his terms, and the national leaders hadabandoned, at all events for a time, all care for local government properly so called, in the expectation that one or other of the great parties, either from fear or from interest, would concede their , demand for a national and separate legislature. Ile ;

wished he could think that the moderate Liberals ha • learned the lesson. They were now very much troubled by certain moderate proposals which had been made by • the Radical party for the settlement of the English land question. (Hear, hear.) He ventured to predict, if they were rejected, at no distant date these men would find themselves confronted by propositions much more"- extensive, more dangerous, and more questionable, and they would find themselves outbidden upers.-,, the land question as they had been upon the ques- tion of Ireland by the Tory party, whose indifference; to all political principle kept equal Pace with its eager; ness for power and for office. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) His second propositkm was that if the moderate Liberals joined with the Tories they would be jumping out of the frying pan into the fire. (Laughter.) His first conten- tion was that the proposals of the Radical party were moderate and reasonable. They went on the old lines of progress; to which every member of the party was pledged. We were face to face with a great struggle. He had very little doubt himself they would obtain a. majority at the next election. That was not enough if they were to derive much advantage from it. If the country was to be' saved they must have a majority which would render them independent of the cynical offer Mr. Parnell had made to any statesman who was willing to betray the interests of his country. Well, they would be confronted with all the forces of obstruc- tion; territorial and ecclesiastical influences would be brought to bear; they would meet with personal autho- rity, private blandishments, and these things could only be successfully combated if they secured some great. movement of popular opinion. What were the objects which they set before them? They were told that they must have inscribed on their banner "Local govern- ment and the cheapening of the transfer of land.' Theo, were good, most excellent things. He did not know whether they were of a nature to cause the hot blood of a Whig to course rapidly through his veins—(laughter)—but he must give it as his opinion that they would not inspire: the passionate fervour that he desired to see among the people. (Hear, hear.) They would have to go a great deal further before they could do that There were many candidates for county constituencies on that plat; form. lie asked-,Could tfey win on such a restricted issue? He was going to address great meetings in Scot- land next week, and he fully believed that if he was to tell those audiences that this was all the Liberal party had to offer them he would be hooted off the platforms, and he would deserve it. (Hear, hoar.) It was per- fectly futile for any Rip Van Winkle to come down from the mountain in which he had been slumbering and tell them that these things were to be excluded from the Liberal programme. The world was moving on while these dreamers had been sleeping, and it would be ab- surd to ignore the change in public opinion which the Reform Act had produced. He did not desire to raise his voice on political necessity alone. If they could not convince their allies pf the justice and reasonable- ness of their views, well then, with whatever relict. ance, they must part from them. (Hear, heat.) They would not fight alone. They would' appeal unict Caesar; they would go to the people from whom they came and for whose cause they were fighting; and although the verdict might be delayed, he, on his part, had no doubt as to the ultimate decision. (Cheers.) They had been looking to the extension of the, franchise in order to bring into prominence questions too long neg. lected. The great problem of our civilisation was un- solved. We had to grapple with the mass of misery and destitution in our midst, co-existent as it was with the evidence of abundant wealth and teeming prosperity. We at last would have a government of the people, and it would be made a government for the people—(cheers) —in which all should co-operate in order to secure for every man his natural rights. (Cheers.) He would be told that this was Socialism; of course it was. The Poor- law was Socialism; the Education Act was Socialism; every kindly act of legislation was Socialism, and it was none the worse for that. (Cheers.) Their object was the elevation of the masses of the people, a level- ling up which should do something to remove the inequality in our social condition which was one of the greatest dangers of the State. (Hear, hear.) For such a purpose he did not pretend that any one • specific would be found; they were bound to try experi-- ; meats, and let them try and try again until they sue.. • ceeded. What was the Radical programme? The most ; important of their proposals had reference to the ques- tion of land; the most urgent reforms centred on this ' subject. If they could do anything to multiply the number of those who had a direct interest in the soil that they tilled they would increase the production of the land; if they could find work for the larger propor- tion of the population in connection with the greatest and most important of our industries, and if they could make the lot of the labourer more hopeful and pros- perous they would have done much to bless both town and country,—(hear, hear)—and to add to the content- ment and prosperity of the whole population. What was their contribution to the solution of this problem? ' They proposed to extend the functions and powers of local authorities; they proposed to go on the lines already adopted in Legislation in the Irish Land Act, in. the Irish Labourers' Actvin the Artisans' Dwellings Act, and in some of the Public Health Acts, and they proposed to give to popular representative authorities the right to obtain land for puplic purposes at its fair value. They. also proposed that the local authority in every . district, under proper conditions, should have power to ' let land for labourers' allotments, for artisans' dwellings, ; and for small holdings. They proposed that the tenants should have entire security as long as they fulfilled the I conditions of their holding. In this way they would ; be doing something for the agricultural labourers, and ; something also for the towns, for it was not an agricul- I tural question alone. Every working man knew that ' towns suffered by the competition of the cheap labour 3 which came in from the country. He believed by such a proposal they would` do something to fix the 'labourers in the country, to tie them to the land. He thought the proposal was just, reasonable, • and moderate. Another important thing he would like I to see was Free Schools. His proposal would not, as 7, some thought, destroy denominational schools and reli- gious education, questions which would have to be dis- cussed on their merits at another time. At present, the ; total amount of fees receivable from all the schools in ; I the kingdom was l millions a year, and he believed that • an addition to the Income Tax of d.in the pound would be sufficient to provide the money. He claimed Freon I Schools as a great aid to the spread of education, and as a just concession to the necessities of the poor. The fee was the great bar to regularity of attendance,. t. and accounted for the vacant seats in the schooia lip read copies of letters sent to a schoolmaster by parents and proceeded to say that these letters Iwere not only pathetic, but they were tragic in character, and showed the misery some people suffered because of the L3lly and pedantry of others who imposed on them hardships under the pretence of preserving their independence. In the new Parliament they must provide for the children free for the advantage of the country. (Cheers.) He would also go in for a revisioja lof taxation; for a graduated taxation, a taxation whiok which was in proportion to the superfluities of the tax.„ ; payer. (Hear, hear.) Then there was the question of I the taxation of unoccupied land—(hear, hear)_oE ; sporting land, of ground rents, and of mineral royal.. ties. He advocated all those methods of taxa. tion, not because of the amount they brought to the j Exchequer, but because he thought they would' ' courage certain arrangements which haa been pro- ductive of much inconvenience and suffering to the . community. There was the question of the Game Laws. He could not believe that any popularly-elected I Parliament would tolerate the continuance of this anomalous, this barbarous legislation, intended to pro-- the just demand, for an inquiry tect the sports of the well-to-de; and lastly there the proposal, into the illegal appropriations of land—(hear, hear)__of public rights, and of public endowments, and if they be found to have takera,place within the last half-century there would be provleion for their restitution or for adequate compensation. He did not say that every one of these j points should necessarily and at once be made a cardinal article of the Liberal programme, but he said that any attempt to exclude them from impartial consideration would be fatal to unity and conduce to their certain ; defeat. The Liberal party in the past had been the popular party. It had been reinforced from time to time by successive Reform Bills, and now after the great. ; est of them all it would be false to its trust and un- worthy of its high mission if it did not strive to bring the institutions of the country 'into harmony with the wants and aspirations of the people; if it did not seek continuously the greatest happiness of the greatest num., ber ; if it did not serve the poor with, at least as touch skill as it brought to the protection of the rich, and if it did not enforce the obligations of property as strehtk, 'ously as it defended its rights. -- t Mr. CHAMBERLAIN' s speech at Warring- 'on, on Tuesday, was equal to the highest ve?tPectations. Looked at from any point of 'slew, it was magnificent—magnificent in its 44 dmogeniety, in its fertility and freshness 91 illustration, in its brilliant sallies of wit, its lofty scorn, tender pathos, and noble patri- Otism, and in the passionate desire which it tevealed for improving the lot of the lowly, !rrespective of race or creed. No one could near MT. CHAMBERLAIN on Tuesday night Viithout recognising not only that he was an ,i?lator, but that he was a great and good man. 4-le combines in himself qualities which may take him what the meeting denominated 4,!ni on Tuesday night—the future leader of he Liberal party. So long as Mr. GLAD- FONE is with us, no one can of course take the t,;„`l,ce which no one can so well fill; but ~"L'en, in the natural order of things, "the noblest figure of the nineteenth century" is Ziooved from the scene of his beneficent isQtkrks, Mr. JOSEPH CHAMBERLAIN will, there th;;!ry reason to believe, be found equal to 'sk of leading the Democracy of tHs -lit.ntrv. He is bold, resolute, and far-seeing ; lie nr 'as the tongue of eloquence, and the pen th th. e ready writer, and such sympathy with toslsilffering poor as will always attract them k, uini as to a magnet. What could be more t_lndly than the way in which he read the ,°ll,elling letters of parents who were begging II be excused from paying school fees when L'ieir children were wanting bread! He ti o 1 the difficult question of Free Educa- _ubn in a way w znds of mainy hich carried conviction to the dom who have, doubted the wis- Inalu f making a further advance in this direction. The Catholics have hitherto :lbws some fear _ educationof Mr,. CHAMBERLAIN'S proposals; but that would seem to e because they have not seen that there is bOne way of getting over d the denominational i fficulty which they have not previously con- sidered. The total amount realised by school Pence throughout the kingdom is a little over one and a half millions; and as this can be covered, as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN remarks, by an addition to the income tax of three far- things in the pound, it borders on the ridiculous that there should be any ques- tion of raising the Money. A matter nOf ten millions is treated as a mere 41 ea-bite when the issue is one of break- -1O g the heads of our neighbours. Is it asltc)t time that hld show ourselves ready we sou to spend money in getting know- into: the heads of our children? The t man Catholics of this country have a 4.lecial interest in considering. this question. hey have amongst them the poorest of the poor, and would derive the greatest benefit t°to education made free on the plan sug- gested by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. tbln approaching the question of Ireland, the orator reminded his hearers that e: had laboured hard and long in the inter- of the sister isle. In a sentence that electric in its effect, "God." he said, he,as made us neighbours, and I would to 13„'"ven that our rulers had made us friends " a't friendship may be obtained at too high hoprice—at a price which would be dis- t), nourable and degrading, and which would tlerefore defeat its own end. Mr. CHAMBER- the, Perceiving this, roused the audience to highest pitch of enthusiasm when he t(eela.red that he would not enter into any ) httiPact with Mr. PARNELL for the dismem- ethir,rnent of the empire. His utterance on as Point, as indeed it was on every other, pZ anal and unmistakeable. There was no sitt;eting with words in a double sense; no on the fence after the fashion of the skirY Democrat—ready to jump off on either thse; The courage which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN to P'ajed in this matter is in striking contrast tue cowardice of Lord RANDOLPH ho tskcRILL who, although he spoke for an *011„t and a half on Friday night, had not a ' of answer to the challenge of Mr. PAR. It comes apparently to this, that the iss:tn of his lordship is closed on this important wh.o because of an alliance with the party lc,h he coarsely denounced, not long since, Irish' the assassins of Phcenix Park." Let ttnen beware of Lord RANDOLPH Who" CHILL. The unprincipled politician hesi" now ready to betray England, will not ~ do ;`ate to betray Ireland when it suits him to Irej,°' And what have the Tories to offer snd ? vague promises which will resolve meats elves into thin air if by any accident

Lord SALISBURY should be returned to office. On the other hand, the Liberal party are pre- pared to give the widest scheme of local self- government, consistent with the maintenance of the integrity, of the empire. Irishmen are surely wiser than the dog in the fable; they will not drop the substance in order to snatch at the shadow. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in the course of his powerful speech dealt with other questions than those to which we have specially refer- red. He was merciless in his exposure of the hollowness of the Tories in meekly carry- ing out, on coming into office, a policy which they had loudly and bitterly condemned whilst in opposition. But he did more than this; he showed that they are not to be trusted in foreign affaics—that they have neglected British interests in Zanzibar, and slighted by recalling the commander from South Africa, "who, without the loss of a single life, has restored the great province of Bechuanaland to peace and prosperity." Coming to the programme of the future, he showed the pres- sing necessity of a thorough reform of the land laws; and of such revision of taxation as would adjust the burden to the back— rich and poor alike paying according to their ability. The meeting heartily responded to his remarks as to the taxation of unoccupied land, sporting land, ground rents, and mine- ral royalties ; and was not less with him when he touched upon the game laws, and the need of an inquiry into illegally ap- propriated lands, with a view to restitution to the public. The right hon. gentleman con- cluded an address which will largely deter- mine the Liberal programme by a temperate demand for full and fair discussion of the points he had raised, and by a stirring refer- ence to the mission of the Liberal party con- ceived in the spirt of the laureate's lines:— Forward, forward let us range; Lot the great world spin for over down the ringing grooves of change.

THE question of female drunkenness in Warrington was very properly brought before the licensing magistrates, last week, by a deputation from the local Temperance Society. The report of the CHIEF CONST- ABLE was quotf.d as containing the following significant passage :—" The 227 females pro- ceeded against are principally girls and young women who drink in private houses, the beer, &c., being mostly supplied by off. license holders." As might be expected, the I ladies who formed part of the deputation commented upon this alarming statement, and urged the Bench to take it into account with a view to lessening the number of licensed houses in the borough. Two of the magis- trates, Mr. GUEST and Dr. GORNALL, showed that they were fully alive to the situation, but the MAYOR (Alderman HARRISON) sought to minimise the statement. On Tuesday last, the matter was again referred to, at the ses- sion for applications for new licenses. Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, solicitor, showed himself commendably anximis for the good name of his native town; but—and we say it with all respect—we cannot but think that what he said would have come with a better grace, if he had not at the time he spoke held in his hand a brewers' brief—that of Messrs. GREENALL, WHITLEY, and Co. Taking his statements on their merits, apart from any regard to his anomalous position, we have to point out that his remarks were based on a blunder he had made as to the facts. Mr. DAVIES said "he had found that during the year 1885 there had been x7+ females who were summoned." The CLERK sought to correct him by 'saying " cases " ; but Mr. DAVIES said "he would make due allowance; 53 cases were dismissed, leaving the number x x." This total is altogether misleading; Mr. DAVIES has been look- ing at the wrong column in Mr. HUNT'S report ; he has deducted the number of cases dismissed from the total of con• vie/ions, instead of from the total number sum- moned, and it thus happens that, by his pro- cess, the 53 is twice deducted. Can it be that the Mayor had an eye to this when he quoted a celebrated authority as saying "there was nothing so misleading as facts, except figures ? " For our part, we do not see why the total given by the C HI BF CON- STABLE should not be taken as it stands, namely, 227 females proceeded against for drunkenness. It is little to the purpose that 53 cases Were dismissed, as it is notorious that in most instances the "letting off" is not because there is no case against the offenders, but because it is thought advisable to get rid of undesirable females. It would be scarcely creditable to the police, if it could safely be assumed that no conviction couldbe obtained in 53 out of 227 cases of alleged drunkenness. We take, therefore, the 227 as we find it, and we regret to have to say that it confirms the CHIEF CONSTABLE'S report, and what he had occasion IO say afterwards, namely, that "there is really more drunkenness among girls." There is an in- crease of x 8 cases in 1885 as compared with 1884. This is not much, it may be said, but it is sufficient to be alarming in view of the fact that there is a decrease of drinking among males—taking the results in Warring- ton for some time back. Mr. DAVIES pointed .out that "during ten years the number of charges for drunkenness had diminished from 1,033 to 715." Granted, and it is with pleasure that we note the fact as it relates to the inhabitants as a whole— /v.lle . is female. The mischief is— and this s the point which we wish to eMphasise—that, while during the past ten years there has been a large decrease in drinking among males, there has been an increase in the drunkenness of females. In 1876, the year quoted by Mr. DAVIES as giving a total, male and female, of 1,033 cases, there were 153 females only proceeded against for drunkenness; for the past year the number, as already stated, 15 227, show- ing an increase of 7+- Taking the cases against males for the same years, the numbers are 880 for 1876, as against 491 for 1885, showing a deciease of 309. In other words, whilst there is in Warrington a decrease in ten years of drunkenness amongst males to the extent of 35 per cent., there is an increase of drunkenness amongst females amounting to no less than +8 per cent ! Surely in the face of facts like these—facts taken from the public records—it is unwise to hide our heads, ostrich-like, in the sand, and declare that that does not exist which we do not for the moment see. Let the cause be what it may, it is truly deplorable to find that Warrington, with less that 50,000 inhabitants, has only ten fewer cases than Blackburn, with a popu- lation of over 110,000 ; or, to put it in another way, it is lamentable to learn that, in proportion to population, there are twice as many cases of female drunkenness in Warrington as there are in Blackburn. The i question arises—What s to be done ? Are we to conceal the truth under euphuistic plati- tudes; or acknowledge it, face the difficulty, and courageously endeavour to grapple with

it? We prefer the latter course, and we are therefore gratified to know that a Committee is being formed to deal in some way with this growing evil. The women of Warring- ton must bestir themselves; and the men must help them.

THE Miners of South-West Lancashire have set an example in the style of putting questions to Parliamentary candidates which other bodies of workmen would do well to imitate. The Scotch have a way of trying to get at the views of those who seek their suffrages by what is called " heckling " at a public meeting; but, useful as this is in its way, it is not equal to submitting written questions to which written answers are re- quired. As we pointed out in a recent issue, Sir RICHARD CROSS came out of the ordeal miserably, while Colonel McCoßQuo- DALE was, on the contrary, conspicuously successful. This week answers to the ques- tions which relate to the Miners' Pro- gramme have been received from Mr. SETON KARR, the Conservative Canditeiarp, for St. Helens ; and we commend thetNo the attention of working-men, especially those who, calling themselves Conservaave, have been disposed to persuade themselves that there is as much to gain from one side as the other. Let them go through the various answers of the Conservaave candidate, and then say, if even they can, that they are satisfactory. From beginning to end, Mr. KARR fences; he will consider this, and he doubts that, and he does not know what to do with the other. In no case does he say in a manly and hearty fashion—" Yes, if returned, I will vote for this particular thing that you desire." When he is emphatic, it is an em- ph tic negative, as in the matter of Free Education, and a thorough reform of the land laws. We are not of course surprised at this ; he wouldn't be a Tory if he didn't seek to block the way; but there has been so much profession of a desire on the part of Tory candidates to "do something" that it is quite right to bring them to book. The answer the miners of St. Helens have re- ceived settles two points; Mr. SETON KARR will not support them, and they will not sup- port Mr. SETON KARR.

Dn. ROBINSON or RUNCORN has been appointed medical officer to the Holy Trinity Provident Club. THE NEW PUBLIC OFFICES AT WIDNES.—OperatiODS were commenced on Thursday. The handsome building will occupy a position directly epposite St. Paul's Church. Winetes C.E.T.S.—An entertainment took place on Thurs- day evening at the National Schools, songs, Ac., being given by Mrs. Feirclough, Messrs. Hunt, Townley, and others. PRESENTP.TION AT RUNCORN.—The Rev. W. Preston, in- cumbent of Holy Trinity Church, has just been presented with a finely executed oil painting of the interior of that edifice. Miss Hankinson was the artist. PRIMITINE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, RUNCCOIN.—An enjeyable magic lantern entertainment was given to the members of this society in Regent-street School on Tues- day night. Mr. James Plimmer, of Liverpool, was the ex- hibitor. Miss Annie E. Chadwick, of Runcorn, passed firet class with honours in the junior division of the recent examina- tion at Manchester, ileld by the Society of Professional Musicians. Miss Chadwick had studied under Mr. E. France, of Leigh. Wesvoer POINT.—The Rev. J. J. Bryant, incumbent of Christ Church, Weston Point, has accepted the living of the vicarage of Lower Whitley, in the perish of Great Bud. worth, Northwich. The living is valued at £22, and is in the gift of Sir G. Chetwode. ACTION FOR SLANDER* ASATNST MR. R. SHAW, OF RUN. con-N.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, law clerk to the Board of Com- missioners, has issued a writ against the chairman, Mr. R. Shaw, for an alleged slander on the 6th inst. during a dis- cussion on the Ship Canal depntation. OPEN•AIIt CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—The Mill Brow Brass Baud gave the last concert of the season in the Market Hall on Wednesday evening, and there was a very large attendance of the public. The concerts during the summer have been greatly enjoyed and appreciated. WESLEYAN RECEPTION MEETING AT WIDNES.—A meet- ing of the Wesleyans of the Widnes circuit was held on Monday evening, when the Rev.. B. Burdon, the recently appointed superintendent, received a cordial and hearty welcome. Members of the press were not admitted. THE RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS. The B company (Ches- ter), and G company (Runcorn) of the 2nd C.R.V. tad the return shooting match on Saturday, and the Chester company was victorious by 655 points to 609. Sergeant Harvey (Runcorn) scored 90 points, the highest score on either side by seven. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WlDNES.—Smrinel Cullen, a young man, was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesdav, with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Tsveddle on the sth inst. It was proved that the pri- soner had kicked and struck the officer in a serious fashion, and he was ordered to pay a fine of 10s and costs for each offence, or go to prison for a month. THE LATE MR. JOHN HAZLEFIIIRST, OF RUNCORN The Rev. W. Preston, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity Church, on Sunday made reference from the pulpit to the late Mr. John Hazlehurst. The deceased gentlemau, he said, had the spirit of a Christian' as a Christian he lived, as a Christian he died, and he now reaped the Christian's reward—" The crown immortal and of glory that fadeth not away." SMITH'S ILLUSTRATED ALMANAC, 1836, AND DIRE*. TORY OF RUNCORN, WESTON AND HALTON —The atten- tion of the public is invited to this neeful publication, which will be issued early in December next. It comprises the most extensive and complete local postal directory ever published. Early applications for advertisements to be made to the agent, Mr. W. Brookes, 7, Waterloo-road, Run- corn —Advt. WIDNES BAPTIST CHAPEL.—The second anniversary of the pastorate of the Rev. Robert Yeatman was celebrated on Sunday by special services. The rev, gentleman preached morning and evening to good congregations, and the collections made in aid of the chapel funds amounted to upwards of £3. On Thursday evening Mr. W. B. Lock- hart preached a sermon to a fair congregation in connection with the anniversary services. NARROW ESCAPE FROM SUFFOCATION AT WIDNES.— William Furber, a married man, who lives at 103, Hurst. street, Widnes, was severAy " gassed" yesterday morning. He was employed at Mr. Aitken's works, Waterloo-road, mixing liquor in a tank, when he was overcome by the noxious fumes arising, and was insensible for a considerable time. He was attended by Mr. -Saul, assistant to Dr. Booth, and conveyed home. He is rapidly recovering. WIDNES SAMARITAN LODGE I.O.G.T.—At the weekly meeting, on Monday, Brother Machin, W.C.T., presiding, it was decided to hold an open air meeting to protest against the cledision in the Poole perjury case and to adopt a peti- tition for the release of Detective case, to the Home Secretary. A programme of songs, &a., was taken part in by the following:—Brothers Machin, Bullivant, Parker, Clarke, Webb, Wielders, Fox, Fairhurst, and Sister Lamb. EXTENSIONS AT TIIE WIDNES ALKALI COMPANY'S Worts.—The Widnes Alkali Company intend in future to manufacture their own salt cake, and men are now engaged erecting the necessary plant. Employment will be given to several hundred more men. It will be remembered tfiat works are in course of erection near Bitten for the Liver Alkali Company, of Liverpool. and the Broughton Copper ' Comyany. The prospects of the workingmen of the town appear to be brightening. DEPRESSION OF Taman AT Itureconer.—Notices have been posted up at the Weston and Runcorn works of the Runcr,rn Soap and Alkali Company, and at the works of Messrlr. WiLtg, Bros.' arid Steele, of a reduction of 10 per cent. in the wages of men in all departments. About 1,200 men will be affected. A few months ago several hundred men were discharged through the slackness of trade, and the remainder of the labourers were reduced 5 per cent. Mr. Claudet, one of the Weston managers, is about to leave the neighbourhood. FOUND DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT RUNCORN.—Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, on Thursday, held an inquest at the Norton Arms, Halton, upon the body of an old man which was found in the Bridgewater Canal between Astmoor and Green Bridge, Halton, on the previous day. The body was that of a man about 70 years of age, five feet 10 inches in height, grey hair, clean shaven face, dressed in dark-ribbed worsted suit, black silk neckerchief, brown worsted stock- ings, cotton shirt, and elastic side boots. Identification had not been proved, and a verdict of " Found drowned "was returned. A DISHONEST LODOER AT WIDNES —Before Lieutenant- Colonel Earle and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wedneeday, Patrick Fox, a herb vendor, was charged with stealing 2s Odd from a [edging-house Marsh- street, Widnes, the money of Michael Wood, labourer. The two men and others slept in the same bedroom on Monday light, and about three o'clock on Tuesday morning Wood found the prisoner with his trousers in his hands, and dis- covered that his money had been abstracted from the pocket.—A sentence of one month's hard labour was passed upon the prisoner. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES —At the works of the Widnes Alkali Company on Wednesday evening, a gang of men employed by Mr. Joseph Forshaw, contractor, were raising a tank weighing ten tons by means of "jacks," when the appliances failed, and the heavy mass fell. Two men were knocked a considerable distance away by a "jack," and to this circumstance they owe their lives, as the tank would otherwise have fallen upon them. James Naylor, a married man, had his hand and arm severely crashed under the metal, and at the suggestion of Dr. O'Neil, assistant to Dr. Booth, he was taken to Liverpool Infirmary. RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELxcriorr.—The corrected re- turn of the votes recorded at this election has been issued by Mr. Shaw, but differs only in a very sl.ght degree from the first declaration, The position of the candidates are unaltered. The Orange Lodge, which holds its meet- ings at Trinity School, has passed a resolution, to be for- warded to the Commissioners, to the effect that owing to the early closing of the poll, a considerable number of rate- payers employed at Weston and Widnes were unable to vote, and expressing the opinion that an extension to 6-30 or 7-0 p.m. would be an advantage to the working classes. ROYAMARCH MASONRY AT RUNCORN. The Bridge- water Chapter held their annual installation of chiefs and investiture of officers for the ensuing year at the Runcorn Masonic Hall on Wednesday night. There was a good at- tendance. The following companions were installed aid invested :—James White, Z; Edward Marwood, H; W. Mellor, P.Z., P.P.P.S., of Cheshire, as J.; T. H. Annett, S.E. ; George Bell, S.N.; T. H. Hitchen, P.S. ; T. Kirk- ham and Garnett, assistant S. The ceremony was per- formed in an efficient manner by Excellent Companion Stevenson, P.Z., P.P.J., of Cheshire, Birkenhead. The remainder of the evening was spent in an enjoyable man- ner. -

CATTLE DISEASE.—The Chief Constable of Che- shire has announced that twelve fresh cases of foot- and-mouth disease had occurred on two fresh farms in the parishes of Ashton and llelsby. There were 27 animals under treatment last week, of which 24 recovered, leaving, with the twelve fresh cases, 15 remaining under treatment.. Swine fever has broken out in the parishes of Ashley, Antrobus, and Pown- ' all Fee. A CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE WANTED FOR WID- NES.—Mr. Robert Pierpoint, barrister-at-law, having declined the honour of contesting the Widnes Par- liamentary Division in the Conservative interest, the statement has been extensively circulated during the past week that Mr. Edmund Molyneux Seel, of London, Who is a Catholic and a large owner of pro- perty in Lancashire, had agreed to tight the battle of the Tories. It appears, however, that Mr. Seel is not anxious to come forward, and his candidature has been officially denied. Apparently the Tories of the division would be delighted to see the Liberals also on the hunt for a candidate, and the rumour has been persistently adhered to that Mr. E. K. Muspratt had intimated his unwillingness to stand for the constituency. It is needless to add that there is not a word of truth in the asser- tmn.

ACCIDENT TO A Bo Y AT RIINCORN.—Henry Houghton, son of the apparitor at the Parish Church, on Saturday fell from the wall of Waterloo Bridge to the roadway beneath, a distance of about ten feet. He sustained a serious fracture

of the skull. FOOTBALL MATCH AT RIINCORN.—OR Saturday afternoon a match took place between the Recreation Club and the 2nd team of the Runcorn Football Club. The score at the conclusion was Runcorn two goals, one try, and several minor points to one dead ball. THEATRE ROYAL, RuNconte.—Mr. Thomas James, son of the proprietress of the Theatre Royal, asked the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, to fix a day for hearing an ap- plication for a new license.—Superintendent Leah said alterations were in progress at the theatre, and the appli- cant was told that Mrs Waldron, as manager of the theatre, must apply when the alterations had been completed and inspected by Superintendent Leah. CAMDEN WESLEYAN IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.— The members c,marnenced their winter session on Friday night by a fruit banquet and entertainment. Camden School had been decorated for the occasion, and the numer- ous persons present spent a very agreeable time. Mr. H. Randle, the president of the class, occupied the chair, and deliyered an address. Speeches were also made by the Rev. A. Percy Watsm, Messrs. Beckett, Shore and Nor- man. An interesting programme of music ar;cl readings

was gone through. A FATAL IMMERSION AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Woreley, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Grapes inn, Halton-road, touching the death of John Heath. cote, 48 years of age, of 2, Robert-street. The deceased was a boatman on the Snowdrop, belonging.to Messrs. Mills and Son, Brighouse, Yorkshire, and ou Wednesday he fell into the Bridgewater Canal at Hulme Locks, Manchester. He was immediately rescued, and wrapped is blankets in bed. He remained on the boat until Saturday, when it arrived at Runcorn, and Dr. MacDougall ordered his prompt removal home. The doctor said death resulted from congestion of the lungs. THuNDERSTORM AT RUNCORN.—During the brief storm. on Friday night last week, flighfield House, Halton-road, the residence of Mr. J. N. Lello was struck by lightning Large holes were made in the roof arid chimney stack, and the furniture in the room beneath was damaged by the fal- ling debris and the rain. The electfic fluid passed down the chimney into tbe dining room, seriously injuring the handsome suite of furniture there. One of Mr. Lello's sons sustained injury and was rendered unconscious by the shock. The chimney stack of the house in Albert-terrace, recently occupied by the Rev. Father Fennegy, was demo- lished, and the debris descended through the roof into the bedroom of the next house. The houses opposite the Town Hall were flooded by the rain. SHOCKING FATALITY AT KINGSLEY.-011 Monday Mr. Churton, the coroner for this division, held an inquiry at the Bed Bull Inn, Kingsley, concerning the death of Thomas Ravenscroft, son of John Ravenscroft, farmer, Hall-o'th- Hay, Kingsley, who died on the sth inst from the effects of wounds received some three weeks since. The deceased was at the time of the accident engaged in loading oats, and as the man below was reaching him a sheaf on the top of the load his foot appears to have slipped, and he fell upon the reacher's pitchfork, the prongs of which entered deceased's chest. It penetrated a portion of his lungs, and in spite of all medical assistance it caused his death. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned. He was much respected in the neighbourhood, and was a regular attendant at the Wesleyan Sunday school. S. PAUL'S CHAPEL, RUNCORN RE-OPENING OF THE ORGAN.—For several weeks the organ at St. Paul's Wes- leyan Chapel have been closed whilst extensive repairs have been made to the excellent instrument, which was re-opened I on Sunday. Special services, in which vocal harmony had a prominent place, were held to celebrate the event, and there were large congregations, especially in the evening. The Rev. George Wood, recently appointed to the circuit, occupied the pulpit in the morning, and his colleague, the Rev. A. Percy Watson, preached in the evening. Mr. Wm. i Grice presided at the organ, which is greatly improved in power and tone, and he performed the following as volun- taries :—"Quoniam," Farmer's Mass, B flat; Handel's "March of the Israelites from Eli ; " "Kyrie Eleison," from Mozart's 12th Mass; and Ilsydn's seventh symphony. The choir rendered Several anthems in a very tasteful fashion. Flamm OF A RUNCORN AND WIDNES GROCER. A meeting of the creditors of Joseph Pollitt, who carried on business as a grocer and provision dealer at Widnes and Runcorn, was held at the offices of the Official Receiver in Bankruptcy, Victoria-street, Liverpool, on Wednesday after- noon. Mr. Ring, deputy official receiver' presided; and there were seven credit Ora present. The statement of affairs shoved liabilities amounting to £lO6 is 4d, and a deficiency of £1,086 163 Bd. The debtor could not satis- factorily account for the goods he had received, and how they were disposed of. Mr. Ring said the debtor would be punished if he did not immediately find out what had become of his books and papers. It was no use of him try- ing to persuade his creditors that he was a fool, for they knew he was no fool. The debtor had no offer to make, and he was adjudicated a bankrupt. Mr. Ring said there were sundry rumours about that the goods had been re- moved from the place. The Official Receiver was appoin- ted trustee. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednes lay, Mr. Littler in the chair. Present— Messrs. James Handley, J.P., Whittaker, Coleburn, Moss, Rogerson, Imison. and Salkeld (secretary.) It was reported Tre thathspe sameoFtnhpideeni ran ineeda interments for the five months ending August 25 numbered 147, a decrease of two compared with the nor. responding periodooumnomtfeid t IttBeBoe4xr. recommended nh, emafeendedes cdrreeacsteehi vaotefd4a Idp4urr3eicsneg3pdtt.—hbee forwarded to the overseers for £l2O on slaking fund ac- count, and £lOO on general expenses accennt.—Mr. Moss moved, and Mr. Handley seconded the adoption of the re- commendation. Carried.—Mr. Moss said during the last year or two he had attended several public funerals, and on every occasion complaints had been made about the way in which Wright the sexton fulfilled his duties. No sooner had the final " amen " of the benediction been pronounced, and whilst the relatives of the deceased were taking a last look at the coffin, Wright went forward, took possession of ono side of the grave te the displacement of the mourners, and unceremoniously begins his operations of filling in the grave as though no one were present. This conduct had produced a painful impression on those present. He (Mr. Moss) had remonstrated with him on two occasions, but he had recently received strong complaints of this conduct, that be thought it was time the Board put a stop to it in an effectual manner by admonishing Wright in such a way that he would be more careful in future. He moved that Wright be instructed not to approach the grave side at an interment until the relatives had left, and that if any fur- ther complaints were made the Board would ideal severely with him.—Mr. 'liaison seconded the motilon.—Mr. Whit- taker said this conduct showed a great want of feeling in Wright—The motion was carried unanimously.
