A RUNCORN WOMAN AND THE GAME LAWs.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ann Stubbs was charged with aiding and abetting Charles Stubbs to poach and also with being unlawfully in possession of game. On Wednesday afternoon, the 26th nit, P.C. Cooper met the defendant walking along the railway towards Rocksavage, knowing her husband and son to be poachers, he asked her what she was conveying in her basket. She replied" Nothing but a few clothes," but the constable persisted in making a search and found four rabbits—The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined 103 and costs 9s ed. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, John Brown, boatman, Weston Point, was charged with being drunk and also with assault- ing P.C. Breeze. At 50 minutes past midnight, on Satter- day, he was lying asleep in Higheitraet in a state of intoxica- tion: He was with difficulty awakened, and then struck the constable on the head and chest with his fist, and a struggle took place on the ground. With assistance he was con- veyed to the police station.—The prisoner,, who said he was so drunk he had no recollection of the affair, was ordered to pay D. 7s 4d, or go to gaol for 21 days. SHORT WEIGHTS AT Relicorte.—Elizabeth Randles, keeper of a greengrocer's shop, Bridgewater-street, appeared before the Runcorn magistrates,. on Monday, to answer a charge of being in possession of an unjust weight. —Super- intendent Leah said on Saturday, ths 29tii of August, be visited the defendant's shop, and found a four-pound weight six drachms light, and several othera one or two drachms light. —Defendant pleaded guilty, and alleged that the four- pound weight had been l-ft at her shop by a young woman who sold fish.—Semerintenetent Leah said the woman denied the assertion.—A tine of 5s and costs lie 64 was imposed. Swoon's ACCIDENT TO A YOUNG MAN AT FARYGYORTH.— A few nights ago a young man employed at Harrison's sadlers shop, Church-street, Farnwerthment with the police- man on his beat. On returning home he fell into the cellar of a honse in Church-street, the grid which usually cow- ered the cavity having been removed. He shouted for help, but no one apparently heard him. and hfter the lapse of half an heur he succeeded in scrambling out. His arm is broken in two places. The policeman has been in the habit of wending upon this grid, and it is suggested that It was removed as a practical joke upon the officer. ROBBERY FROM A SCHOOL AT RUNCORN.--Yesterday afternoon, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. F. Rigby, Eliza Whit:ield, a married woman living at 5, Ewe's- court, Cooper-street, was charged with stealing a Paisley shawl, value 15a, the property of Eleanor Parr, wife of. Joseph Parr, of Bentinck-street. On Monday, Mrs. Parr'a girl took the shawl to school, and placed it in the cloak room. When the school broke up the shawl had dissap- peered, and on Thursday P.S. Nield found it in the pri- soner's house and took the prisoner into custody. She was remanded. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN MARINE STORE DEALER..—liefore Capttin C. W. Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Srssioo, on Monday, , Benjamin Scott, marine store dealer, Mersey-street, was charged with buying a buying a quantity of rope from John Thomas Rothwell, a boy under the age of 16 years On the 22nd August Police-Cerk Wallace was in Mersey. street, when he Saw Rothwell with some money in his bands, and ascertained that the boy had sold a bag and a quantity of rope for 3d to Mrs. Scott. A man employed on board the flat Annie of Chester had sent the boy with the material.-51r. J. W. Knowles of Widnes, appeared for the defendant, and pleaded that his client was ignorant of the law, and was unabl, to read and write.—The Beach imposed a fine of is and costs us 6d, and cautioned the defendant. A charge of not keeping a register was not gone into. STABBED BY A WOMAN AT RUNCORN.—Mary Ann Brick- nail, a woman of bad character with several aliases, was brought before Mr. J. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, on I Wednesday, charged with feloniously and maliciously I wounding Rose Pearle with intent to do her some grievous I bodily harm. A statement by Superintendent Leah showed that Pearle is a servant at the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms, Church-street. —Oa Monday night, at half-pest eleven, she went to the railway station in company with Francis Deere, a seamen on hoard the schooner (lulling Star, for the purpose of meeting her master and mistress, named Payne. On returning Pearle and Deere stopped on Waterloo Bridge to listen to a quarrel between the prisoner and several young men. The prisoner commenced to insult Pearls, and told her that if she came near her she had ramie- thing in her hand that would do her good. Pearle went to her, and the prisoner stabbed her three times on the body with an ordinary pocket knife, indicting two wounds on the back and one very serious wound in the region of the heart. , Pearle was taken home, and ordered to bed by Dr. Man- gan, who is in attendance upon her. On Tuesday morning P.S. Neild apprehended the prisoner, who admitted using the knife which she gave up. She added, "I did not think ,it was so had. I was in drink at the time —Superintendent I Leah said the prosecatrix would be unable to appear for several days, and applied for a remand.—The prisoner was remanded to Tuesday next. CARDIN-AL MANNING will give an address on Temperance in the Drill Hall, Warrington, on Men- day night. His worship the Mayor will occupy the chair. There will doubtless be a large attendance, for his Eminence is a devoted worker in the tem- perance cause; while as a Prince of the Church he is highly esteemed. PROBABLE RETIREMENT OF MR. ECE;ERSLEY, M.P.—lt was announced on Friday morning that Mr. Eckersley, junior member for Wigan, who was unanimously adopted as the Conservative candidate for the Ince division, will most probably not contest the division. Several weeks ago he met with an accident which caused partial lameness, and his medical attendants enjoin perfect rest for the in- jured foot, or permanent mischief may result. The news has caused much surprise in the district. Tau SHIP CANAL.—The Co-operative Wholesale Society have decided to take up 1,000 £lO shares in the Manchester Ship Canal. At a meeting of the Central Spinning Company on Wednesday night, the directors were empowered to take shares to the value of over £2,000 in the Ship Canal. Numerous other concerns are to adopt a similar course, the Royton Industrial Co-operative Society taking shares to the value of £5OO. A meeting of limiteds is to be convened for the purpose of taking definite steps in the matter. THE INCE DIVISION OF SOUTH-WEST LANC.A.,- SHIRB.—Mr. C. M. Percy, the unanimously adopted Liberal and labour candidate, is pursuing a vigor- ous campaign. His election expenses are being borne by working-men and some leading Lanca- shire Liberals. Mr. Edward'Cross, the Liberal can- didate for Westhoughton, has sent a subscription of £2O, and expresses his belief that Mr. Percy's special knowledge of mining and labour questions, and great power of speech will make him an able member of the House of Commons. Mr. Percy was formerly lecturer on engineering at the Warrington School of Science. He spoke at the Wallington conference on Tuesday, and at the Overflow Meet-

ing. ALLEGED ROTO3ERY 71104 A HALTON HOUSE- KEEPER SINGULAR CASE.—At Warrington Borough Court, yesterday morning, two females named Anne Mahar and Annie Hodgson, well-known to the police, and William Johnson, alias "Spuddy" John- son, a private in the Bth (King's) Liverpool Regi- ment, stationed at Orford barracks, were charged with stealing, on the flay previous, in Rose-yard, Warrington, a double case gold hunting watch, alleged to be of the value of £6, from the person of Sarah Ann Moore, a housekeeper, residing at Halton; the male prisoner was also charged with receiving the watch, knowing it to have been stolen. From a statement given by the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) and evidence subsequently taken, it appeared that Mrs. Moore, a widow, came to Warrington on Monday on a visit to some friends—Mr. and Mrs. Wright, of the Rose Inn, Rose-yard, Dial-street. On Wednesday night, it was remarked by the Chief Constable, Mrs. Wright found fault with some i alleged undue familiarity on the part of her husband and Mrs. Moore. Mrs. Wright was then turned out of the house by her husband. Towards noon next day Mrs. Moore was going through Rose-yard to go to the station when Mrs. Wright met her and twice knocked her down. Mrs. Moore, whose dress had been disarranged, called for assistance, and prisoner Hodgson assisted her to put her jacket on. Whilst she was doing so Mahar came up, took the watch and decamped, while Hodgson kept the prosecutri* in conversation. Afterwards, it appeared, the two female prisoners sent to the Lower Angel for " Spuddy," who was there, and gave him the watch, which was subsequently recovered from him at the barracks and he, was taken into custody. From the information given to the police the female prisoners were also arrested. Prisoner Mahar, when appre- hended and charged by P.S. Jones, made reply, "I don't know nowt about the watch, and I never took it." Afterwards she voluntarily said " tell you. about the welch : I took it myself and gave it to, Spuddy '• Johnson, a soldier." Hodgson, apprehen- ded and charged by Inspector Spinks, replied "I wish to,say nothing; I know nothing at all about it, but we were all together." The.fitspector saw the male prisoner at the barracks, and he said that he never saw the watch', but would admit having been drinking with the girls. The Inspector insisted that the watch was in possession of the prisoner, who then took it from a place where it had been secreted, and handed it over. At the police station he said that he did not know how he came by the watch. The three were conjointly 'charged, when Mahar said she took it, and Johnson did not know that he had it. Ifodgson said she was in the crowd and saw Mahar take it, and the soldier said " I knew I had the watch, I found it in my breast."— Mahar and Hodgson were each sent to gaol for four months; and Johnson, who has served 20 years in the army, 18 years being abroad,. was sent to prison for one month. IVIOLUNT THUNDERSTORAt : A Cow KILLED.—A violent thunderstorm passed over the Earlestown district on Friday evening, accompanied by a heavy downpour of rain. No damage in Earlestown has been reported, but at Newton a valuable cow, belong- ing to Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park, was struck by the lightning and killed. The animal was in on of the fields, and the ground near where, it stood was torn up. Two men were out shootinqt Newton, and were overtaken by the storm. electric fluid struck a gun hela by one of the men, and the shock was so great that he was thrown to the ground. Fortunately, however, he was un- hurt. _... .

LANCASH/lIE ANNUAL SESSIONS. - The annual meeting of the Justices of Lancashire was opened on Thursday morning, in the County Hall, Preston. The chairman and vice-chairman forthe year having been re-elected there' were read rtports of various committees of the county for the past twelve months, including that of the Finance Committee. It was proposed that with the view of completing the new County Sessions House, at Islington, Liver- pool, a further sum of £4,000 be granted. It was also proposed that £2,200. should be spent in im- provements at the Lancaster County Asylum, and that .£5,000 be spent at the. Whittingliam, Asylum. A special commattee was appointed to secure an Act in the ensuing session to enable the county justices to appoint one executive for all the asy- lums in the county, and for other purposes. A num- ber of pensions and gratuities were passed tocounty and other officers.

RAILWAY Accineorr AT NEWTON.—A serious , accident, which occasioned a great delay in the passenger traffic, pccurred on the railway near New- ton Bridge Station, on Monday afternoon. About three o'clock a mixed goods train was shunted into the Golborne branch from the Manchester and Liverpool line to allow the passage of an express, tram. As the goods train was being shunted back, two, wagons, loaded with coals, left the rails. One' was overturned, and its contents scattered on both, the up and down main lines, which were both comz, pletely blocked. Information was conveyed to. Newton Bridge and Kenyon Junction stations, and Mr. Tabemer (station-master at Newton), Mr. Bat- tersby (Kenyon Junction), and Inspector Atkinson, from Bolton, were soon on the spot. In the mean- time a break-down gang from W arrington had been telegraphed for, and quickly arrived. With all speed one of the lines was cleared, and for over two hours the traffic was worked on the one-line system. Both lines were cleared about six o'clock. THE MARQUIS OP RIPON AT ST. HELENS.—On Tuesday next, as will be seen from our advertising columns, St. Helens will be visited by Lord • Ripon, late Viceroy of India. The primary object of his lordship's visit is to take part at a public meet- ing in aid of the funds of the Providence Hospital, a deserving institution in Hardshaw Fields, which will be held in the Volunteer Hall in the evening of the day named. It is expected that Colone/ Gam- ble, J.P. (Liberal Candidate), Mr. 11. Seton-Karr (Conservative Candidate), and other gentlemen, will also address the meeting. The announcement ,of Lord Ripon's visit gave rise to a strong feeling among all sections of the Liberal party, that the opportunity should be acted upon to present to his Lordship an address expressive of their high appreciation of his enlightened rule of the great Indian depen- dency. The matter received the careful considera- tion of the Council of the Liberal Association, and ' on Friday last Councillor Richard Pilkington, J.P., chairman of the Council, proceeded to Studley Royal, where he had an interview with the Marquis. Lord Ripon consented to receive an address of wel- come, and this will be presented at a banquet in the Volunteer Hall at noon on Tuesday. Great enthu- siasm is being manifested by local Liberals at the prospect of showing their personal approval of the policy of Lord Ripon. THE FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION AT EARLESTOWN. —On Thursday, Mr. J. E. Pardey, of Newton, agent to Mr. W. J. Legh, M.P., lord of the manor, and Mr. J. Duxbury, honorary secretary of the Earles- town Football Club, had legal notices served upon them in respect of the obstruction of the alleged public footpath across the Mesnes. The notices are dated the 10th inst., and are signed by Mr. Richard Brierley, civil engineer, surveyor to the Newton Improvement Commissioners. They state that in pursuance of the Act 4th and sth William IV., entitled an Act to consolidate and amend the laws relating to highways in England, Mr. Brier- ley, as the duly appointed surveyor of the Improve- ment Commissione-s, who are the highway authority for the district, "do hereby give notice forthwith to remove the wooden or other fences, erections, and obstructions placed by you, or under your direction and authority, or by your consent, approval, or permission, upon or across a certain public footway being the Queen's highway, lying between Crow-lane, in the parish of Newton afore- said, and thence crossing farm lands, and lands known as the Mains, to its junction with a certain other public footway or Queen's highway adjoining the London and North-Western railway to the obstruction and annoyance of the said high- way." .In the event of the obstruction not being removed, the parties mentioned will be summoned for causing an obstruction, and the case will come on for hearing at the next Newton Petty Sessions. A DANCING MASTER AND PUPILS.—At the Warrington County Court, last week, before Judge Ffoulkes, John Hall, a young man, belonging to Newton, sued C. Mess, a dancing master, 'for a debt alleged to be due.—Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the plaintiff, and stated that the claim was .E 2 2s, being the amount plaintiff had had to pay for the hire of the Newton Town Hall for two quarters for defendant's dancing class. Plaintiff, on behalf of , himself and others, had arranged fer defendant to I come over to Newton to teach dancing, and had hired the hall in his own name as the caretaker had declined to let it to Mr. Moss, he being a stranger to him. Plaintiff never expected to have to pay the .E 2 28 out of his own pocket, as he had no benefit whatever from the class beyond his own instruction. At this point Mr. Browne, who appeared for the de- fendant, said defendant had decided to admit the claim, and his Honour accordingly gave judgment for the amount with costs.—Mr. Browne then pro- ceeded with defendant's counter claim, which was for .C 2 7s, being .£1 for plaintiff's own dancing les- sons and LII 76 for balance owing from five of plain- tiff's friends whom he had introduced, and whose subscriptions he was expected to be responsible for, in support of which contention Mr. Browne called defendant, and put in several of plaintiff's letters. The defence was that plaintiff was only liable for a subscription of 15s, being 7s Gd per querter accord- ing to his original agreement, and he had never con- sented to the increased charge of lOs per quarter. And as to the subscriptions of his friends that he was not liable for them.—His Honour held that Hall must pay 15s subscription, that the class was fo • Hall's benefit, and that he was responsible for the subscriptions of four of his friends, amounting to 18s 6d, so that there would be judgment for the de- fendant on the counter claim for a 38 6. Mn. GLADSTONE'S RETURN.—Mr. Gladstone, ac- companied by Miss Mary and Miss Helen Gladstone, arrived at Perth shortly before noon on Monday, on his way from Fasque to Hawarden Castle. The right honourable gentleman was met at the station by Sir Andrew and Lady Clark and the Rev. Stephen and Mrs. Gladstone. Several hundred persons had also assembled. Mr. Gladstone proceeded to the stationmaster's room, it having been arranged that Sir Andrew should examine the ex-Premiefa throat. Mr. Gladstone was found to be in excellent health and spirits, and, though his voice is still a littlel hoarse,. it has much improved during his stay at Fasque. Mr. Gladstone was afterwards conducted to a, through carriage for Chester, walking bare- headed the length of the platforms the crowd, which had meanwhile considerably increased, continually cheering " Midlothian " and Mts. Gladstone. Al Carlisle, which was reached at 5-19 p.m., refresh- ments were supplied to Mr. Gladstone and his family. A large crowd pressed round the carriage, and the right honourable gentleman frequently showed himself at the window. Mr. Gladstone ar- rived at Bank Quay Station, Warrington, about 8-50 on Monday night. The right hon gentleman was cheered by the few person.; who had assembled on the platform, and he bowed his acknowledgments. The carriage was shunted into a siding, whilst the mail train passed, and afaerwards the saloon was at- tached to the train from Manchester to Chester. The party arrived at Chester at 9 15 p.m., and, amidst the cheers of a crowd of people, left by special train for Broughton Hall Station, en route to Hawarden. The Dairy News says :—" Mr. Gladstone caught a cold while travelling from Scotland to Hawarden Castle, and our correspondent was on Thursday informed that he was suffering from a slight attack of lumbago. Neither cold nor lum- bago was sufficiently severe to prevent Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone taking an enjoyable drive on Thursday afternoon in an open carriage. RECEPTION OF THE WESLEYAN MINISTERS AT RUNCORN. A meeting of Wesleyans in the Runcorn Circuit for the purpose at giving a hearty and cordial welcome to the ministers who have just taken up their residence amongst them was held in Brunswick School. on Monday evening.
(esten,

Besides the various chapels in the town, Halton, W. Weston Point, and Preston Brook were represented, and up- wards of 350 persons were present at the tea party, with which the proceedings commenced. Tables were given and presided over by Mesdames Hackett, Frith, P. Speakman, R. Shaw, Unswortb, Coventry, J. H. Harrison, Yarwood Leach, Handley, R. Norman, A. Riley; alleges Norman', Taylor (2), Simister, Peacock, Ellis, and Wilton. At the ,subsequent meeting the room was well filled, and Mr T. 'Simister occupied the chair. Amongst those present were the Revs. George Wood (formerly of Newport, Isle of ?Wight), A. Percy Watson (formerly of Wrexham), and Thomas Hackett ;Messrs. J. Simpson, T. Norman, R. Shaw, J. R. Frith, R. Norman, B. Kniveton, G. C. Beckett, J. W Kirkham. G. Bellanny, G. Yarwoed, C. A. Dawson, H. Fit: ton, W. Marsh, 8 Taylor, J. H. &arisen, E. Marshall' C. Littler, T. Leach. and W. Leathwood.—The Chairman ex- plained the object of the meeting, and called upon Mr. T. Norman. a circuit steward, who said he believed their new ministers God-sent men, and he gave them on behalf of the, circuit a cordial and hearty welcome. He moved a resolu- tion tendering the ministers a sincere and warm reception. Mr. J. Simpson seconded the motion, and spoke in favour of the Wesleyan System of appointing ministers. They re- ceived Mr. Wood and Mr. Watson, he said 'i in the name of Jesus Chriet and gave them a hearty welcome, trusting they would 5s useful whilst they remained in Runcorn. He that they might have the best men preaching to them, but they who professed to be working with the .ninisters were not living pure and hely lives they- could not expect that God would bless their &Arts. (Ap- plause.) He hoped their ministers would be happy and comfortable with them and that God would bless their ser- yiees.—The Rev. T. Hackett supported the resolution,. which was carrieal, by acelematon.—The Rest George Wood on rising to reply received a hearty greeting. Although he had been i 6 years in the ministry, this, he said, was the first formal recognition service he had had the pleasure of attending, so that be 2-,ardly knew in what dire- tion his speech ought-to travel. A conversaziene. he ' thought, would have been better than a speechmaking meeting, because then he could have moved among them and-talked with them pereenally. He believed he and his colleagues would work harmoniously together. There were many things the congregation would expect from hide ; and be would expect many things from them. Sermons prepared by reading, thought,end prayer—not mere " talks- tives "—they would have a right to expect, and he felt rather anxious upon this stihiect, forhe did not think he could fill the shoes of his predecessors. But Lie trusted that as they became more familiar with his habit and with his sensitive and nervous temperament, and as be became more acquainted with their relieiour • thoughts and necessities, his sermons would be to them profitalele, instructive, powerful, and saving. (Hear, hear.) , He referred to visiting, class meetings, and punctuality and regularity in attending chapel on Sunday. Let their motto • be "Earnest religious life and earnest religious work," and the success they anticipated would be realised.. (Applause). —The Rev. A. Percy Watson, who was received with ap- plause-, made some humouroes remark-s, and addressed those present upon unity and fidelity. He said he had great hope In young Methodism, but if progressive Methodism meant that thev were to turn their backs upon class-meetings, he Would prefer not to be a progressive Methodist. (Applause). —At this point the Chairman remarked that he believed the circuit fund would be enriched to the extent of £25 or £3O bytlrst meeting. (Applause.)—On the 11101019 of Mr. J. R. Frith, seconded by Mr. R. Shaw, a vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies and gentlemen who had contributed tables, and to all others who had assisted in the-success of the proceedings. A similar compliment having- been paid to the chairman, the meetieg terminated.

div.head: STRANGE DEATH AT HALEWOOD.'
div.p: STRANGE DEATH AT HALEWOOD.'

On Thursday afternoon the dead body of Joseph Birch, 50 years cf age, a collier from Wigan, was found under strange circumstances. Birch, who is a native of Halewood, had arrived in the village that day on a short visit? About eleven o'clock he dined at the house of his cousin, Mrs. Hunter, and about twelve o'clock started to walk to Aig- harth to see his brother, who resides there. Two hours later his dead body was found in the footway leading to Lyon's Home Farm, in Mackett's.lane, and it was removed to the Eagle and Child, kept by Mr. Wm. Crosby. The de- ceased when last seen was in the best of health, and was not known to be subject to heart disease, or any such com- plaint, and tbs strange occurrence has caused quite a sen- sation in the village. The deceased leaves a wife and seven children. An Inquest will be held.

(Continued from page 3.) seize the opportunity of getting a number of votes and a renewal of power at the general election, he could not be- lieve for one moment that their conduct was fair and just. (Applause.): They all would have to work very hard; and they would take ativant ige of what they had heard. Of course they were not all of the same mind—that had been clearly explained that night. There were crotchets, but they must endeavour to get rid of them, and to unite as one man for the grand objects they had in view; and if they did so he had not the least doubt they should carry them. (Rear, hear.) He would like to plead on behalf not only of the working classes generally, who had been spoken of by Mr. Chamberlain but he would allude to two particular sets who require the greatest care and consideration—men who contribute to their comfort, their happiness, and their prosperity—he meant those who go down into the bowels of the earth—the miners—(hear, hear)—and those who go down in ships into the deep—the sailors. (Hear, hear, and applause.) For these two claws of men undergo dangers day by day, and they require their sympathy very much indeed. (Hear. hear.) He would not detain them, but he would say that if they stood still in the present day they were in reality going back. but they were not going back ; they were going for the objects that were legitimate and righteous; they were going to endeavour to elevate those who have not had the opportunity of elevating themselves. (Hear, hear, and applose.) Looking back to what had been accomplished by their statesmen in the past, he would Venture to say that if they were all united for the object they had in view, they must endeavour to do their duty in assisting to mass such measures as would contribute to the happiness and the welfare of the great masses of the people. Let them work while they had an opportanity. "Be just and fear not "—and they should assist in hand- ing down our glor:ous Constitution and united country to future generations. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously amidst applause. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman, said: I have every pleasing duty to perform,which I will do as well as what remains of my voice will allow me. I have to propose that the best thanks of the meeting be given to our chairman, Mr. Rigby, for his services in the chair this evening. (Applause.) lam sure it is a matter of congratulation that Mr. Rigby has presided over so orderly and so patient and long-suffering a meeting, for I am afraid that some of you must have found Yourselves in the situa- tion in which patience was rather difficult. Gentlemen. I believe that Mr. Rigby has other claims upon your good feeling. lam told he has of late ceased to be your fellow- townsman.. If that is so he has come in as a young man from the country—(laughter and applause)—once more to appear on the scene of his former triumphs, to take part in a meeting of his fellow-citizens, in whom at all times he has taken very great interest. (Applause.) lam told also Mr. Rigby might have been, but would sot be, your repre- sentative in Parliament. I do not know what moved him to decline so great an honour. But it is sometimes a good thing that a constituency should be able to keep its best men in its centre at home in order to aid in every good work, to do the work which Comes nearest to their hand. I am glad to believe yen have many such citizens, and among them I believe Mr. Rigby inane of the foremost. (Applause.) I have very great pleasure in moving the vote of thanks. (Cheers.) Mr. F. MONKS briefly seconded the proposal. Mr. WILLIAM Lose, in putting the proposal to the meet- ing, said he could not put it wiithout expressing his great pleasure at seeing Mr. Rigby once more in his right place presiding over a Warrington audience. (Applause.) He did not know whether Mr. Rigby's appearance there was to inaugurate the coming fight, which he hoped would have even better results than the last one. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) The vote of thanks was then cordially carried, and Mr..' Rigby having briefly acknowledged the compliment, the -dings terminated.

As usual, Mr. Sutton had received a guinea for his attend ince, and Mr. Birker, Mr. Marshall, and Mr. Jones, also a guinea each ; Mr. Dutton tflia and a police- man ss. He bad also expended £1 Ss for refreshments for ' those in the booth. He thought a guinea a day besides the refreshments that were needed during the time the officials were in the booth was quite sufficient, but some persons outside had thought that something more should be done. It had been a teetotal election entirely, and be hoped it might continue so, and he thought it would have been a mistake to have, as vorne thought they ought to have done, adjourned to some public-house and there feasted after the election was over, tie asked the Board to pass his charges of Ld 4e —Mr. Speakman: How much last year ? —The Secretary : £ll 78.—A cheque for the amount was passed, on the motion of Mr. 6peakman, seconded by Mr Dokson, _

If the Board was incompetent or unwilling to deal with its husiness—to deal with acts of discipline which were believed to be beneficial to the due administration of the work of the Board, he could only ask them to appoint. another chairman in i his place. He did not consider the thing ought to remain where t was. The issue was per- fectly fair ad would have been acted upon without the in- terference of the Board had the decision of the committee been otherwise. As the duty was Perfectly cleared from any lying imputation they had to leave the Board to do its duty. He asked them to appoint a chairman in his - place.—Mr. Norman was sorry the chairman had come to .euch a conclusion, and suggested that the matter should be dealt with at a special meeting when all the members were present.—Mr. Lake said be quite sympathised with the chairman, and agreed in lhe course he was taking, because he did not see bow he could allow the matter to stand where it was. He suggested, however, that the subject should be left for consideration at the ordinary Board meeting.-- After some discussion as to whether the matter could be raised at the present meeting, the chairman consented to defer any action until the next Board meeting. div.head: OVERFLOW MEETING.
div.p: OVERFLOW MEETING.

For thou who were unable to gain admission to the Public Hall, and there were many hundreds ef such, an overflow meeting had been arranged for at the Co-operative Hall, in Cairo-street. Shortly after seven o'clock the com- modious room was filled almost to overflowing, and the audience waited with patience and good humour for the commencement of the proceedings. About half-past seven Mr. Diggle ascended the platform, and his appearance was the signal for an outburst of ironical cheering, and shouts of "What about the Ship Canal, Diggle?" Having fortified himself with a toffy, Mr. Diggle came to the front of the platform, and said if it were the desire of the audience that he should say a few words he had no objection. (Loud laughter.) What are von laughing at? (Renewed laugh- ter.) It was his intention to occupy that hall some time next week, if he could get it. (A voice: "Gas, Diggle.") I wish tha'd a meauttiful of gas. (Roars of laughter.) Shouts of "Take some water, Diggle," "What about the brick houses?" Pull that sweet out, and then tha CCM talk," and other cries assailed Mr. Diggle to such an extent that he could not proceed. At length, amid a roar of merri- ment, he took the toffy from his mouth and took a drink, and informed the audience that wss the "first water" he bad tasted for a month. He produced the draft of a bill he intended to issue, headed "Ship Canal Bubble." He intended, he said, to answer the speeches made in the Free Trade Hall by Mr. Adamson and Mr. Leader Williams. (A Voice " What port art' going to anchor in, Diggle?" and cries of "Chairman.") He said he wanted to address men, and not "chairmen." He ehoald charge an admission of 2d to this meeting; lads 3d, and roughs he would not have at all. ("Is it a tea party, Dig- gle ? " Laughter.) He was going to chew that the Ship Canal would not benefit Lancashire, and to answer the questions: Would they raise the money? Was it safe for people to invest their money in the scheme? And would it permanently benefit Warriogton ? (Cries of "Oh." A I Voice: " They roasted three bullocks at Manchester.") He wished they would roast a dozen, for there were plenty of folks that could eat them. (Laughter.) At this point Mr. Henry Roberts appeared on the plat- form, and Mr. Diggle resumed his seat. In a few minutes Mr. John Crosfield took the chair, and was supported by the various speakers mentioned below. The CHAIRMAN said : lam sorry that we have not in Warrington a public hall large enough to hold the people that want to hear the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain. (Hear, hear.) As you are aware that ball at the present moment is filled as full as it is possible. There is not room for another person, and the only thing that we could do was to engage this hall for an overflow meeting that you might have a chance of hearing Mr. Chamberlain speak after he had finished speaking in the Public Hall. (Hear, hear.) To-day is a great day for the Liberal patty in War- rington, and I hope that the effect produced by it will have a considerable influence whenever the General Election takes place. (Hear, hear.) We have in Mr. Chamberlain, as you know, one of the most prominent and cleverest statesmen living. (Hear, hear.) He was a leading man in Mr. Glad. stone's Government, and there is no doubt whatever that Mr. Chamberlain's opinion will have considerable influence upon the future of this country. (Hear, hear.) I may ven- ture to say, gentlemen, that we as a Liberal party still re- tain unbounded confidence and affectien in our great leader Mr. Gladstone. (Loud cheers.) We don't mean to say that the late Government never made a mistake, but I mean to _ .

say this, that England owes a great deal to Mr. Gladstone's Government during the last five years. (Hear, hear.) If there was nothing else that Oey did they passed the great- est Reform Bill that ever was, perhaps, passed, enfranchis- ing two millions of the people of this country ; and I shall be very meth mistaken indeed if these two million electors —a great majority of them at all events—are not found supporting the Liberal party at the coming General Elec- tion. (Hear, hear.) I look with great confidence to the next election. I believe that there will be a large majority of Liberal members assembled in the House of Commons, and that we shall again see that great man Mr. Gladstone leading the Liberal party in that House. (Cheers.) There have been difficult questions during the last five years for the Liberals to deal with, and perhaps the most difficult has been that unfortunate country Egypt. Well, you know, Egypt troubled Moses a good deal—(laughter)—and it has been a great trouble ever since. It is a problem that is not solved yet. (Hear, hear.) But let me remind you at the same time that the Immediate trouble that we have in Egypt was a legacy from the Tory party—(hear, hear)—and they have to deal with it still. There are other measures that were passed by the Liberal Government, and if the Liberals are in office again we shall see other important measures, es- pecially as effecting land, passed by them. (Applause.) You may depend upon this, that if you want any great re- form passed in this country you have no need to look to the Tories for it. The Tories never do anything except through fear. As far as I can remember they don't do anything from love to the people. (Hear, hear.) This I take it is the great distinction between the Liberal party and the Tory partY,.and I hope and trust that the Liberals of War- rington, and the Liberals throughout the kingdom, will send such a majority to the House of Commons as will give Mr. Gladstone power to carry out the reforms which we want. (Hear, hear.) Well, we are indebted also to Mr. Gladstone and his Government for the peaceable settlement of the Af- ghanistan question. I have no doubt in my own mind that had there been a Tory Government in office then that we should have bad, war with Russia—(hear, bear)—whereas the thing is quietly settled,and we have escaped the curse and evil of a tremendous conflict with that great nation. (Cheers.) I also think that we must look to Mr. Gladstone as being a much abler man and a much greater statesman than the Marquis of Salisbury or anybody on the Tory side hear)—and I hope and trust that every Liberal in Warrington, and in Lancashire, will feel it his bounden duty to do all he can for the Liberal party at the coming elec- tion. (Cheers). Mr. W. P. SINCLAIR, M.P. for county Antrim. said his friend Mr. Wm. Crosfield was going to carry the flag of the Liberal party in Warrington at the corning bittle in Novem- ber. He hoped they would allow him to say how much they as electors of Warrington were indebted to a man of the character of Mr. Crostield coming forward on their be- half, and how admirably he would look after their interests when they returned him to the Imperial Parliament as he felt sure they would do at the coming election. (Cheers.) He had had the honour and pleasure, and let him add, pro- fit of Mr. Crosfield's acquaintance for a considerable num- ber of years. and he could only say that he thought there were few men in LivPrpool who were better qualified to enter Parliament and to do his duty not only to the con- stituency that sent him, but to the 'Whole country at large. (Cheers.) On the day of election he expected to see every ens of those present—he hoped they were all voters—giving their votes to Mr. Crosfield in order that he might support

div.head: prJeeedii
div.p: prJeeedii

the great statesman at the head of the Liberal party—Mr. 1 Gladstone, who had done so much for the people of Eng- land. (Cheers.) Mr. Sinclair then moved a resolution giving a hearty welcome to Mr. Chamberlain, and expres- sing confidence in Mr. Gladstone and the members of the late Government, and gratitude for the Franchise and Re- distribution Acts. The speaker referred to these measures iat considerable length, and reply iig to the boast of Lord \Randolph Churchill respecting the measures passed by the present Conservative Administration, said they were one and all measures of a Liberal character, inaugurated by the Liberal Government. (Cheers.) Mr. J. T. BRUNNER, candidate for the Northwich Divi- sion, seconded the resolution, and proceeded to deal with the four L's—the Land Laws, Local Government, Liquor Laws, and House of Lords. He had been found fault with , by his Tory opponent for saying that the landlords had robbed the people for many generations. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared to stand by that assertion. In the conference that day they had condemned the law of entail, by which noble lords and great landowners could preserve their estates free from their creditors for the next heir. But how was it if a poor tenant owed his rent and did not pay it? (Laughter.) The landlords would take their beds into the street and sell them. From the reign of, Queen Anne up to 1835 no man could have a hand in malting laws who was not a freeholder to the tune of £3OO a year, and during the whole of that time the landlords had taken their tenants' goods for their debts in preference to the debts owing to all other creditors, and until very lately they took the lodgers' goods too, whether the lsdger shad paid his rent or not. (Laughter.) For all these generations they had taken the farmers' crops and stock in payment of rent, and if the butcher had put a few sheep on to grass on the way to mar- ket for half a day they sized these shsep too: (Laughter.) And worse! Many a time the landlord had hired a thrash- ing machine to thrash his corn for half a day, and then when that machine had travelled to the tenant's farm to thrash his corn, the landlord bad seized it for the tenant's rent. (Loud laughter.) Farmers bad been dumb dogs, but now, strange to say, when their numbers counted very little in a county con- stituency they were plucking up coarage and actually asking that landlords should no longer raise the rent upon a farmer's own improvements. They were asking in a very humble fashion that the landlords stiould cease to rob them. Well might Mr. Chamberlain say the landlords owed the people ransom for their hod. (Applause.) The Liberal party were aiming at free trade in land—(hear, bear)—and he felt convinced that when obtained it would reduce the pauperism of the country from one in3s to one in a thou- sand. (Cheers.) Alluding to local government, Mr. Brun- ner advocated the es'ablishment of authorities in villages that could receive gifts of land from liberal landowners ready to give commons to replace those that had been stolen in times gone by, and other gifts of citizens. They wanted to be able to buy a common if they could not get one given. Hitherto the great landlords had been able to steal commons, and no body had been able to say them nay. For a long time it had been true that The law conderrms the man or woman Who stea's the goose from off the common. But leaves the gr,a`er f.lon loose Who steals the commcni from the glom

(Loud laughter.) Speaking of the liquor Ime Mr. Brunner said the magistrates had done a rmschlef which was in- calculable by granting licenses to the occupiers of houses who were merely the temporary servants of great brewers, and to men who sold liquor and liquor alone. Gin, he said, was not victuals. (Laughter.) After dealing with the House of Lords he concluded by an eulogy of Mr. Chamberlain, and resumed his seat amid cheering, Mr. MALCOLM GUTHRIE, candidate for West Derby, Liverpool, supported the resolution, which was carried with- out a dissentient vote.

_ The Cut lIIIIAN said they would observe that he did not hesitate to ask them to vote. There was a gentleman in the town who was contesting a Scotch constituency. This gentleman said that out of consideration for the feelings of the electors he would not ask them to vote—(loud laughter) —the fact being that if he had put the resolution to the meeting the vote would have gone against him. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. PERCY, candidate for Ince division, said Dr. Mackie must be contesting that Scotch constituency as be conduc- ted his paper—" neutral in all matters political and religious.' (Loud laughter and applause.) He happened to be a Scotchman himself. (Laughter.) He believed Dr. Mackie was a Scotchman too. He had sufficient confidence in the Scotch people to know that they would have a poli- tician of one type or another, and that they would not have a man who conducted his ()pinions as he conducted his paper—" neutral on all matters political and religious." (Cheers.) Mr. Percy then moved a resolution approving the action of the Council and delivered a vigorous speech, during which he was frequently cheered. The Rev. S ARMSTRONG seconded the motion, which was carried with applause.

It was understood that Mr. Chamberlain would be able to attend the overflow meeting aed address a few remarks to those present, but after making his powerful speech at the Public Hall he was unable to do so. Towards the close of his speech it was apparent that the task of the right hon. gentleman in the cro*ded and hot room was telling on him. When the announcement was made to the overflow meeting that Mr. Chamberlain would not be able to give another address those assembled were naturally somewhat disappointed, but when Mr. Percy stated how lengthy and vigorous a speech Mr. Chamberlain had delivered in the Public Hall, hearty cheers were given for the right hon. gentleman. A vote of thanks was then passed to the chairman, and the proceed- ings terminated. It is due to Mr. Roberts, secretary of the Liberal Associa- tion, to say that the extensive arrangements for both meet- ings were carried out in a very satisfactory manner. Thanks are due to the volunteer stewards fer the admirable way in which they did their work. The policemen in attendance were equally obliging.
LIBERAL MEETINGS IN CHESHIRE.

Mr. I. S. Leadam, the Liberal candidate for the Altrin- chain division of Cheshire, who has for some time been assiduously pursuing the election campaign, has during the last few days addressed a series of i,ublic meetings in this neighbourhood. On Saturday and Monday he spoke at Lymm, and on Thursday, in conjunction with Mr. Bar- low, candidate in the Liberal interest for the Knutsford division of Cheshire, at Thelveall. At each meeting he was supported by local gentlemen who take an active interest in his candidature, and was received with an enthusiasm that gives promise of success. He dealt with a variety of sub- jects, and, as is usual with him, he was highly effective. Mr. Leadam and Mr. Barlow also found time to attend the Liberal Conference on Tuesday afternoon, and the great meeting that in the evening succeeded it, and the calls that were made for them to speak during the expectant time that the vast assamblage awaited the appearance of Mr. Chamberlain, was acceptable evidence of their popularity. Summarised reports of the meetings referred to are ap- pended.

div.head: SATURDAY.
div.p: SATURDAY.

*On Saturday evening Mr. Leadam addressed a meeting of electors at Sandy-lane, Lymm, when the chair was occupied by Mr. E. Brewtnall. Amongst those also present were Messrs. Swanwick, Mackey, Kendall, Cameron, Holt, Nixon, Leigh, ate.

The' Cumnatax, in a brief address, said that they owed all the blessings of popular education of to-day to the Liberal party. Indeed, in whatever direction they looked they would find that all the progress the country had made had been brought about by the efforts of Liberal politicians. What could Conservatism have te do with progress when all its interests were bound up in the past ? Conservatism meant, so far as he could see or appreciate it, a determina- tion, after having seized everything, to keep it as long as possible. It meant get all you can, and then at all hazards keep all you have got,. The Chairman cautdened his hearers to remember that though the franchise had been obtained, the Conservatives would still make a fight to retain the power which they felt to be slipping from them. The ex- tended franchise had admitted two million people to the rights of citizenship, and every effort would be made to thrust them through the Tory gate. It was incumbent upon them, therefore, if they valued their political duties and rights, to do what they could to promote the Liberal cause. They could not do that more effectually than by sending Mr. Leadam to represent the Altrincharn Division. (Ap- plause.)

Mr. LEADAVE, who was received with applause, recalled some of the great measures passed daring the last 50 years by the Liberal party, and proceeded to show what had to some extent been the conduct which had dictated the action of political parties in the past, and what would dictate their action in the future. By such a review he hoped to con- vince those who were in doubt, or had some Oisposion to call themselves Tories, by giving them an opportunity of knowing the history of those principles Liberals possessed. The first great measure of Liberal progress, which headed the measures of this century, was the Reform Act of 1832, Prior to which time the government of the country was in the hands of the nobility and landed gentry, the people hav- ing no part or share in it. The Tories tried to continue that state of things, but alter a fight of 50 yeara the Liberal party accomplished the change. Now, after another low, fight the franchise had been greatly extended by the Liberal party. After referring to the many beneficient works of the Liberal party, Mr. Leadam said that the aim of that party had ever been national interests rather than class in- terests.
_ The usual rote of thanks brought the meeting to a con- clusion.
MONDAY.

Oa Monday evening Mr. Leadara addressed a meeting, , large in number and enthusiastic in character, at the Mis- . lion Hall, Lymm. Mr. Swanwick occupied the chair, and amongst those also present were Councillor Broadbent, and Messrs. W. Long, We'ford, Skilling, &c., 4:c. The CHAIRMAN; in the course of his remarks, said that there could net be the slightest doubt that Mr. Leadam would head the poll at the next election if all the electors of the division who had the interests of the Liberal party at heart worked well for that ebject. He was glad of that oppor- tunity of bearing his willing testimony to the most earnest, unselfish, and energetic work that was being done ' by a certain section of their supporters. The only thing that remained to be desired in that division was that that strong body of active workers should be considerably added to during the next few weeks, as he had no doubt that it would be, and that. being the case there would he no doubt at all as to the result of the polling in that dis- trict. Whatever the result was in the end, he thought that the electors of that district would be able to say that they had made a very handsome subscription towards Mr. Leadam's majority. (Applause.) He did not think there ,

div.head: TliE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 12, 1885.
div.p: TliE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 12, 1885.

would be much intimidation' pressure. and inffuence used in that district. There would probably be less than before had been the case, for it was not of great advantage to inti- midate where the electors were so numerous. Nevertheless there wool I be certain instances. Some of their neighbours about there hid been accustomed to undue influence, and he was afraid that they would have some little of it. He wanted them all to look out for such cases—not to make a particular noise about it—but to take care that any case of intimidation or pressure that might occur was brought to the knowledge of some member of the active committee. No one, he could promise, would in consequence incur trouble, but it was most essential that such cases should be called attention to. If it was well known in the neigh- bourhood that everyone was vigilant, there would probably be very little of it. It must also be borne in mind that the punishment for intimidation was imprisonment, if the matter was thoroughly carried through. (Applause.) Let them try to crush out finally such sparks of intimidation as might appear. If it did show its head let it be forced back once and for all, and then they might be free of it in the future. He then proposed the following resolution : " That this meeting,while cordially thanking Mr. Gladstone and the late Government for the great boon of an extended franchise and for their many efforts in other directions to better the condition of the people, looks forward with con- fidence to their early return to power with a large majority at their backe, and to the consequent enactment of much needed measures of land law and county government re- form. It farther desires especially to express its entire con- fidence in Mr. Gladstone as leader, and its earnest hope that with renewed health and vigour he may be able to take his old place in the forefront of the fight." (Applause.) Councillor C. BROiDBENT rose to second the resolution. He remarked, as a representative of the district of Latchford, that he thought it would have been better had the Com- missioners adhered to their original plan, and allowed Lyman and Latchford to remain together. He was sorry that they had been separated, as he bad been looking forward with satisfaction to Mr. Leadam as candidate for the part of Che- shire in which he (the speaker) lived. But although sepa- rated their desires and ioterests were the same. They in the Knutsford division had a good and plucky candidate, and he hoped that they would have as great success as be hoped would result in the Altrincham division. (Hear, hear)" He'vvas certain that if there was success in the Alrrincham division—and in Lymm in particular—that in a large manner it would be owing to the energy of their chair- man. (Applause) • A few days ago an American Minister said that the condition on whic6 the extension of the fran- chise would be valuable and an advantage to the country would be proportionate as the electors endeavoured to. un- derstand the great questions that were brought before them. He (the speaker) knew no one among the present candidates who had taken more pains thoroughly to understand the great questions of the day, and who was more capable of in- telligently explaining them to his audience than Mr. Lea- darn—(applause)—and he thought that if the electors of that division listened carefully to his speeches they would be well qualified to give an opinion on the great and im- portant questions that would be before the next Parlia- ment. Speaking more closely to the resolution Mr. Broad- bent expressed the firm conyierion that at the next election the Liberal party would not fail to show a united front. (Applause.) Mr. Lneasse supported the resolution. He was received with cheers and a verse of " tie's a jolly good fellow," fol- lowed by still more cheers. Referring to the Tory and Irish alliance, he said that each of those two factions had had their own ends to serve. He was indisposed to say harsh things of the Irish. Ile recognised the treatment under which the Irish people had been governed, and he could not but feel that in.the past there had been cause for disoontent and exasperation. (Hear, hear.) They Liberals hoped that by a series of remedial measures that past might in time be effaced, but its traces yet lingered in Irish hearts and Irish recollections. The Irish had at any rate an in- telligible policy, which was, as Mr. Parnell had declared, to assert the independence of the sister kingdom and to sever its connection with this country. But what share of that interest had the English Tory party—the party which was fond of arrogating to itself the names of the constitutional, patriotic, and national party—in such a disintegration of the country. He took it that the interest of the Tory was not on all fours by any means with that of the Irish. Their first interest was to make government by the House of Commons impossitie—(applause)—to paralyse Liberal measures of reform. And the consequence of that, as con- templated by Lord Salisbury—whose relationship to Lord Randolph Churchill he sometimes' suspected was that of a monkey to a cat's paw—the outcome contemphated by Lord Salisbury was that by paralysing the power of the House of Commons there should be a transfer of influence to the House of Lords. (Applause) What were the real senti- ments ef the Tories before this alliance was concocted as to our relations to the Irish ? Why, when the Irish Land Act, to glYe the justice of a secure tenant right, was introduced, no language was too harsh for the Conservative party to employ against the Irish. No remedial measures were then in their minds—the necessary curative measures which the state of Ireland desiderated. On the contrary, no measures could then be too stringent, they thought, for dealing with the dissatisfaction prevalent amongst the Irish people. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Leadam, who was frequently cheered, then spoke at length of the benefits that have accrued from Liberal rule, and freely criticised remarks made in the neighbour- hood by his opponent, Mr. Brooks. The resolution was carried with applause. Mr. W. Loma, in proposing a vote of confidence in Mr. Leadam, remarked that he hoped the time had now come when in Cheshire they would have a Liberal victory, which remark elicited the observation, " We'll ' Lead 'em,'" from one of the audience.

Mr. WIMPORD seconded the resolution, which was enthu• elastically carried, and a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close. THURSDAY. On Thursday evening a meeting in support of the candi- dature of Mr. I. S. Leadam and Mr. J. E. Barlow was held ia the Temperance Hall, Thelwall. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Long, J.P.. and there were also present Messrs. I. S. Leadam, J. E. Barlow, Brewtnall, Watkin, Welford, Thornley, Dunkerley, and Swanwick. There was a good attendance.

The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, ex- pressed the pleasure he felt in seeing that a large majority of the audience was compesed of the new electors—a part of that two millions of voters who through the exertions of the Liberal party had been gives' a voice in the government of their own country. (Applause.) If he could say any- thing that would impress upon them the duty and responsi• bility that had been thrown upon them he should be glad to do it. To his mind the next most important thing to religion was political work, for upon:the choice of the men they put in power depended very inuch the welfare of the whole community. (Hear, hear.) He did not know how many men tnere might be there who had heard the magni- fieent speech of Mr.. Chamberlain—(loud oplause)—at Warrington a few nights ago, but he thought anyone who had heard that soul-stirring address must have felt the power there was in right principles rightly put befere the people. (Hear, hear.) fheir great leader, Mr. Gladstone —(loud applauee)—bad sad that the difference between the Liberals and Tories was that the Liberals trusted the people while the Tories feared them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Chamberlain's idea was this and he (the chairman had it from him in speaking mivately to him when he was in this neighbourhood—that he would rather trust the instincts of the people as a whole than trust the interests of the country to any one particular class—that he should consider those instincts of the people, as a mass, properly led and instructed, were truer and safer than any class utterances. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

lation of this country. He also deaounced the game laws, and expressed the opinion that the labourers would sweep away those game laws. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Referring to the question of the pension list, be said he thought they would find the new Parliament would ask for an inquiry into this list and not only ask for it, but have it. (Applause) He thought also that the next Parliament would wish to exercise a judicious oviasight over some of these funds which bad been left for various purposes which had become obsolete and which were now applied to various purposes not very nearly connected with the objects for which they were originally left. He was of opinion that some of these funds would be very much better applied in giving free education to children of the working people, (Applausse.) They did not expect that now that the working•man had got the franchise he was not going to have an opinion of his own. They knew that he would have an opinion, and they knew that he wanted that his children should have a better education than he had had himself in order that they might be able to better do their duty to the nation to which they belong. (Loud ap- plause.) In answer to a question, both Mr. Leadam and Mr. Bar- low expressed themselves in favour of conferring the power on localities to decide as to the keeping open of public-houses. Mr. DIINICERLBY moved a vote of confidence in Mr. L Leadam. and pledging those present to use all legitimate means of securing bis return to Parliament.

Mr. BEE SYTNAL seconded the proposal, which was car- ried by acclamation. A similar motion with regard to Mr. Barlow W. 113 moved by Mr. T. WALM-LEY, seconded by Mr. J. FAIRHURST, sup- ported by Mr. W ELFORD, and carried by acclamation. Mr. Leadam and Mr. Barlow having responded, and a vote of thanks to the chairman having been passed, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. Fusions DRIVING —A man named liolcroft, belonging to Appleton Thorn, Cheshire, was fined 20s and costs ler furiously driving a pony and trap in Bridge-street on the previous day. P.C. Turner proved the case. NEGLECY OF WIFE AND FAMILY.—A man named Good- head, described as a cooper at Atherton's Quay, was charged with having neglected his wife and three children, and on the evidence of Mr. Shearer, was committed to pri- son for a month.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Coun- cillor Greening, and Mr. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS —The following were fined for drunken- ness :—James Doyle. in Buttermarket-street, 2s : Thomas Garritty, in Market-place. 5s and costs ; Edward Sauce, in Scotland-road; lOs and costs; Ann Gore, in Dial-street, ss, including costs.—For fighting in Fennell-street, Thomas Berry was bound over to keep the peace.—Arthur Willett and Ambrose Foden were fined for neglecting to send their children to school.—Michael Callighan, for being drunk and disorderly in the Gun Inn, Scotland-road, for refusing to quit those premises, and for wilfully breaking a win- dow, was sent to prison for two months. It was his 13th appearance. _ . _

A DAttnartons Doo.— Joseph Wadsworth was summoned for being the owner of a ferocious dog not kept under proper control. It was shown that the animal knocked over a child and bit it. The Bench ordered that the dog should be kept under proper control and that defendant should pay the costs, 14s CU. Defendant said he would dispose of the dog. TUESDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, Alderman Holmes, Councillor Greening, Dr. Got- nail, and Messrs. Guest. Garnett, Fairclough and Monks. DEUNIEENNESS.—Margaret Percival, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Market-gate, was discharged ou promising to leave the town. NEGLECT OF FAMILY.—John Macadam was charged with neglecting his wife and child. He was sent to prison for 14 days.
kntheY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. R. Garnett.

Matilda Carlisle and Ellen Connor, young women, were each sent to prison for a month for drunkenness and dis- orderly conduct.—. Joseph Johnson was summoned at the Instance of the Guardians to show cause why be should not contribute to the maintenance of his mother. An order was made by consent.—Jenny Howard, Hollins Green, sum- moned for neglecting to send her child to school, was fined 2s 6d.—Several apprentices were summoned for neglect- ing work, and were ordered to return ; in one case an order for imprisonment for seven days was made. ALLEGED ASSAULT. Thomas Jones, a respectable- looking man, was charged with assaulting a woman named Alice Oxley, on the 3rd of September. On the evening of that day, complainant said, she crossed the street where she lived to see a neighbour, and prisoner abused her and thee struck her a violent blow on the side of the head. Defen- dant alleged that Mrs. Oxley was drunk and provocative, and denied having struck her.—A witness for the defence said that Mrs. Oxley was intoxicated on the day in ques- tion, and came home in a cab singing the "Union Jack of Old England." and another person described her as the most scandalous woman upon earth.—The Bench dismissed the case.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley. DRUNICENNESS.—George Towey, William Roscoe, John Molloy, William Hughes, James McFarran, James Hulse, and Mary O'Neil, were each fined for drunkenness. _

OBSCENE LANGIIAGIA—Ann Flannigan, for using obscene and profane language in Bridge-street on the 31st ult., was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' hard labour. INFRINGEMENT OF THE CANAL BOATS ACT. John Crewe, of Stoke-on-Tara, was, on the evidence of Mr. Far- rington, inspector to Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, fined ss, and costs us 63, for not having a canal boat marked as required by law. SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—John Clucas, Robert Gillies, and Richard Seymour were each fined 58 for not sending their children regularly to school. For a like offence at- tendance orders were issued against John Neild, Joseph Taylor, Eliza Maddock, William Shaw, and William Light- foot.

Mr. LEADAM, who was received with loud applause, referred to the statement of Mr. John Brooks, the Conserva- tive candidate for the Altrincham Division, and he had no doubt the same statement was made by Mr. Tattoo Egerton, that the new electors owed the privilege of the extended franchise to the Conservative party. He had no doubt they had heard of an ancient people called the Spartans, who were brought up from their youth never to make a state- ment which involved inaccuracy, and the consequence was that when the Spartans made a statement which staggered people it went by the name of a Spartan truth, or what vulgar people now-a-days called a "Salisbury "—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and when the Conservatives made the statement he referred to they were telling a "Spartan truth. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Leadam then quoted extracts from the speeches of Sir R. Cross, Mr. .W. H. Smith, Lord IL Churchill, and Lord Carnarvon, showing that those gentlemen had strongly opposed the extension of the fran- chise. The Conservative position was. that they ought never to have had the franchise, but now that they had it the Consetvatives would take care that it was used in the right way, and the consequence was that all over England they saw attempted what was described by a working•man living in South Westmoreland in a letter to the Times as a reign of terror. They had a political party who desired to float into office upon a reign of terror. He did not say that things had COrUs to that pass in Che- shire, but he did regret to have heard within the last few days of things which they might describe in language little short of that which was used to describe the state of things in South Westmoreland. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Leadam then went on to advocate the establishment of county boards, and warned the voters against putting too much trust in the very plentiful promises of Tory candidates. He ad- vised them if they wished to know which was the party that was likely to benefit them most to consult history. As an instance of the !tyranny practised by Tory squired in former times, he mentioned that within the past few days while visiting a house in Lymm an old lady said t 9 him that if her father had been alive he would have voted for him (Mr. Leadam.) On being &eked why she said this, she said that at one time her father and three or four other work- men combined to take a newspaper which were then very ex- pensive. They used to meet together, and one of the workmen read the paper until it got it rumoured about the village that a few Radical fellows had took to reading the news- papers aed, as it was considered a had sign when they took to reading, the squire of the next village sent for them and said that if they continued reading that newspaper he would send them to penal servitude. The newspaper was of course d:scontinued. (Hear. hear.) That story was corroborated to him (Mr. Leadan) by a man who happened to be in the cottage at the time, whose father happened to be one of the Barrisir Assocualoze.—The work of the sections of the three men who combined to take in the newspaper. That British Association meeting at Aberdeen was begun on story brought home to them the kind of treatment the Thursday. The Presidents of the several departments de- labourers received at the hands of the Consesvatives in livered addressee, the most notable of wnich was that of other days. (Hear, hear, and applause.) NOTES BY THE WAY.

1 So far as first-class matches are concerned the Scar- borough Cricket Festival came to an and on Wednesday. llt was a bright sunny day, but a bitterly cold wind was 'blowing nearly all the atternoon, to the discomfort alike of Ithe players and the few spectators on the ground. Mr. Grace was kept away by a private engagement, and up till about five o'clock it looked as though the M.C.C. would be beaten in a single innings. Following on against a major- ity of 157 runs, they lost five of their best men for 46, Bates, bowling on a sticky wicket, being very difficult to play. Gunn was out at 83, and then, by some fine cricket, Mr. Wright and Barnes saved the match,putting on 73 runs between them, and being still in when stumps were drawn. When he had scored about 12 or 15 Barnes gave a pal- pable chance of stumping, but apart from this one blemish, the batting was capital. At the finish the M.C.C. were one run behind, and, in Mr. Grace's absence, there were four wickets to fall. The festival has been very nnfortnnate in the matter of weather, but it produced some admirable cricket.

The two days' match between Lancashire 12 and 18 of East Lancashire district ended at Blackburn on Saturday in a draw, much in favour of the county team, only four runs being wanted to win, with nine wickets to fall. Less than four overs sufficed to bring the innings to a close, with a total score of 134. In the second innings of the District team Barlow and Briggs bowled unchanged, and Watson kept wicket. Barlow bad bowled eleven overs for seven runs and two wickets when Phillips hit him out of the around for six. The innings closed for 85. The fielding of the county team was of the finest description.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE CAROLINE ISLANDS.—RIVAL FLAGS HOISTED BY GERMAN AND SPANISH GUNBOATS. MADRID, SATURDA.Y.—Official telegrams have been re- ceived from the Caroline Islands, bringing news to a later date than that sent to-day. Two of the Spanish warships in those waters arrived off the island of Yap on August 21st, and the Spanish commander at once set about instal- ling the Spanish officers with him as governing the island. At seven o'clock on the evening of the 24th a German gun- boat arrived and immediately landed a force of Sailors and marines, and took possession of the island in Has name of Germany, hoisting the German flag in the most conspicuous position. The commanders of the Spanish vessels entered an energetic protest, stating that they had already occupied the island de facto. Telegrams were at once forwarded by the Spanish Commander to Manilla for transmission to Madrid, but in the meantime the close proximity of the rival warships at Yap may at any moment lead ts an out- break of hostilities, the consequence of which could only be disastrous. The news from the Caroline islands having now become generally known, the large crowds which gathered in the streets last night have doubled in numbers this morning, shouting "Down with Germany." One large crowd ran to the German Embassy, where a hostile demon- stration was made. Finally, a rush was made at the build- ing. Daring youths climbed the front of the house and tore down the German coat of arms amidst the enthusiastic plaudits of the mob. The yelling mob tore away to the Puerta del Sol, where the Government buildings stand. A fire was built opposite the office of the Minister of the In- terior, where the German coat of arms was burnt. The ex- citement was intense. The crowd ran thence to the French Emba_cf,' where they remained for a long time cheering londliThe expressions used showed that France was re- garded as a natural ally against crermany. Troops were called out, and a large military display was made in the streets, before which the excited people are now retiring. The serions character or the demonstration, and the news from Yap, has compelled the Ministers to call an immediate Council.

• MADRID, BIINDAY.—The Imparcial,'a leading Liberal organ, says that an ultimatam has been sent to Berlin re- questing the evacuation of the Carolines as a sine qud non, Spain offering in the meantime to refrain from material oc- cupation, so as to afford a basis for future negotiations, res- pective rights being reserved. This ultimatum was drawn up at yesterday's Cabinet Council, with the King's ap- proval, and despatched without delay. The excitement of the populace continues unabated, notwithstanding the vigo- rous action of the police, who have up to the time of tele- graphing made 184 arrests. The feeling in the capital is being reflected throughout the country. A telegram has just been received from Valencia, stating that the German Consulate in that city was last night attacked by an excited mob, and the German arms emblasoned over the door of the building subjected to the same treatment as those at the Embassy in this capital. At Saragossa popclar demonstra- tions have taken place, and the people had to be dispersed by the civil guard and police.

BERLIN, gLiNDAY.—The morning papers state that the ex- cesses of the Madrid populace have effected no change in the calm attitude and composure which have hitherto been uninterruptedly observed by Germany in regard to the question of the Caroline Islands. They express unbounded confidence in Prince Bismarck's policy, and consider it self-evident that the Spanish Government will give full satisfaction to Germany by punishing the guilty p.rsons.

MADRID, MONDAY.—The night has passed quietly. The streets are now deserted. An official telegram from the Spanish Minister in Berlin stttes that the German Minister for Foreign Affairs informed him that the German Govern. meet had ordered the commander of the gunboat sent to the Caroline Islands not to hoist the German flag if he found himself in the presence of the Spanish flag. MADRID, WEDNESDAY, 6 P.M.—Despatches from all parts of Spain to-day report that perfect tranquility pre- vails. It is officially known here that the German gunbut Iltis touched at Manilla on the 7th inst. and then continued her voyage to Singapore, and that she did not meet the Velasco, which remains anchored off the Island of Yap. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—SevetaI papers publish this morn- ing a letter from Don Carlos, autporising and even begging his friends to fight for Spain should her honour have to be defended by arms. THE SPANISH NOTE TO GERMANY. MADRID, THURSDAY, 2 P.M.—At a Cabinet Council held this morning, under the prisidency of the King, the tenour of the Spanish Note to be despatched to Berlin to-day was fully discussed. The document, which is stated to be couched in friendly terms, sets forth the facts on which Spain bases her claims to the Caroline Isfands, and de- mands the recognition of Spanish rights. The Queen wad Royal Family will return' here fro.n La Qranja this after- noon.

div.head: TEE CHOLERA..-.A FATAL CASE AT CARDIFF.
div.p: TEE CHOLERA..-.A FATAL CASE AT CARDIFF.

- . A Central News telegram dated Madrid, Thursday, says, —1,547 fresh cholera cases were registered throughout Spain yesterday. The deathe for the same period number 496. The returns for the past few days show a great diminution in the virulence of the epidemic, the figures for yesterday being the most satisfactory yet recorded. A sailor died on Friday night from cholera on board the steamer Craindau, of Newport, lying in East Bute Docks. The ship, on arrival in Penarth Roads, was examined and passed as healthy by the medical and sanitary officials, and was docked on Thursday. Four men were engaged on Frt- day afternoon to assist in loading the Craindau with coal for Cadiz. One of them, named Richards, from St. Dog- mael's, was observed drinking from a cask O. 'water under the fore bulkhead, which had been filled up at Barcelona. He shortly afterwards complained of griping pains and ex- cessive diarrkcea, to relieve which the chief officer gave him some cholera mixture. Richards, however, grew rapidly worse, and shortly after nine o'clock was found dead in the latrine. Dr. Paine considers that there need be no appre- hension of any farther sickness. MADRID, BAITED/Y.—The official cholera bulletin re- ports 2,196 cases and 776 deaths in Spain yesterday. MADRID, MONDAY.—The official bulletin reports 2,132 oases and 619 deaths in Spain yesterday. TOULON, SATIIRDAY.—TweIve deaths from cholera have been registered here since last night.--6 p.m. Five deaths from cholera have ocCurred here to-day.--Sunday. Six additional deaths have been registered. FOUR, FRIDAY.—Ten cases of suspected cholera are re- ported from Parma, Novara, and Genoa.

MADRID, WEDNESDAY —The cholera bulletin reports 1.,780 cases and 664 deaths throughout Spain yesterday. MARSEILLES. WEDNESDAY, 8-30 P.M.—The day's record Of the Pharr) Hospital shows 5 admissions, 2 deaths, 2 dis- charged as cured, and 38 still under treatment.

GIBRALTAD, WHDNESDAY.—The corporal in the Rifle Brigade who was seized with cholera on the 7th inst. has succumbed to the disease To-dav a child was taken ill with cholera. Twenty cases and line deaths have occurred during the last two days in the Spanish lines. ROMH, WEDNESDAY EVENING.—It is officially announced this evening that cholera has broken out at Palermo, and that five cases and two deaths occurred there yesterday. It is, however, reported that there were really 19 cases and five deaths.

div.head: PRINCE OF WALES.
div.p: THE PRINCE OF WALES.

S-rocKnonr, StI7M-LY:=-77f18 iCrinCe-OiViales was present yesterday with King Oscar and the Crown Prince and Princess at the regatta of the Swedish yacht clubs. In the evening there were illuminations and firework displays on an extensive scale on shore. THE ROYAL MEETING IN DENMARK. _ _

COPHNHAGEN, SUNDAY.—The Queen of Denmark.and the Princess of Wales, with her three daughters, arrived yester- day afternoon at Elsinore, where they were received by the Kings of Denmark and Greece, and an enthusiastic popu- lace.—Fvening Early this morning King Christian left on board his yacht Dannebrog to meet the Czar in the Baltic. At noon the Derjava, with the Czar and Czarina on board, accompanied by the Dannebrog and three Russian men-of- war, arrived in tt e inner roads, where they were received by the Princess of Wales, the King of Greece, the members of the Danish Royal Family, and a distinguished assembly, consisting of the Corps Diplamatique, the highest military and civil authorities, the town councils, and an immense crowd of the populace. After the official reception, the three Monarchs, with all the Royal personages and their train, drove in open carriages through the flag-decorated streets, being everywhere enthusiastically cheered by the population, to the railway station, from which an express train brought them to Fredensborg. The Russian Sovereigns are expected to remain here for three weeks.
