div.head: OF OSMAN DIGMA.
div.p: OF OSMAN DIGMA.

CAIRO, MONDAY.—Authentic news which has been re- ceived from Kassala, dated August 15th, states that the tribes beseiginT Kassala attacked each other, and during the fight the head Sheikh was killed. The conquerors then offered to fraternise with the garrison. Two delegates were permitted to enter, bringing cattle. A market was estab- lished outside, at which the inhabitants were purchasing goods. The Mudir is unable to leave, because the Haden- dowas are at Filik. The Gheeri garrison are fed and clothed by the Abyssinians, who, with their Iylussulman allies, are advancing on Kassala. Osman Dignia, in trying to coerce four Sheikhs to attack Kassala, was shot in the back by a revolver, fired by a Gailin Arab in the Gash Valley, three days' march from Filik.

TERRIBLE DISASTER AT SEA.-40 LIVES LOST. ROME, MONDAY.—A terrible disaster at sea is repoited. The steamer Willa left Genoa last night for Malaga, when in consequence of a sudden storm it sank enuth of Savona. A boat with 15 men of the crew reached Genoa in a piti- able gate, where every kindness was 'shown to them. Steamers were without delay sent out from Genoa in the hope of saving some of the passengers, bet it is feared that 40 lives are lost.
DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT NANTES. NANTFS. SIINDIY. The extensive drapery establish- ments of M. garx in this city have been entirely des- troyed by fire. Tne losses are estimated at three million francs.

ISIMLA, SUNDAY.—The -1-71:e-rO; will leave here on Oc- tober 21et. The proposed increase of the Indian army is in course of arrangement. It is eetimated that there will be

an additional force of 10 000 British and 17,000 native • troops, exclusive of reserves. SIMLA, MONDAY.—The Viceroy will make a tour in Raj- putana, and will visit the principal cities of the north-west provinces, reaching Calcutta on December sth. LOSS OF AN AUSTRALIAN CLIPPER SHIP AND 45 LIVES. Information received from Lloyd's on Thursday morning states that the splendid iron clipper ship North American, of London, 1,676 tons register, has been poked on the loss book as missing with all hands. She sailed from Mel- bourne for London on the 19th February last, with a full cargo of wool and other produce, valued at £lOO,OOO, was spoken eight days later, all well, but has never been heard of since. Underwriters are of opinion that she has been lost in the ice off Cape Horn, the whole of the crew perish- ing with the ship. REPORTED CONVENTION WITH BELOOCHISTAN.. VIENNA, SUNDAY —lt is reported here that the agents of the Indian Government have succeeded in getting a Con- vention with the Khan of Beloochistan, which, in case of war with Russia, the latter would aid Afghanistan with a corps of 30,000 men. FRANCE AND TONQUIN. PARIS, SATURDAY.—Tite Minister of War has received a despatch from General de Courcy, dated from stating that he has returned to that place from Quinhon, and re- porting serious disorders in that province. A num- ber of Christians had been massacred and villages burnt. TERRIBLE CYCLONE IN OHIO. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY.—A. terrific cyclone has passed ever some parts of the State of Ohio. The village of Bloomingburg has been laid in ruins, and at Washington Courthouse, a Place with 4,000 inhabitants, 400 buildings have been totally wrecked, while a great number of other houses have suffered serious damage. Five bodies have been recovered from the ruins, and it is greatly feared others have perished. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY EVENING —Three hundred of the inhabitants of Washington Courthouse were injured, some very seriously, in the wreck of their town. The damage to property is estimated at a million dollars. THE ATTACK ON A BRITISH CON.WL. CONSTANTINOPLE, THURSDAY. Lienten int • Colonel Everett, the British Consul at Ezeroum, who was wounded during an attack upon his residence by Armenian marauders in April last, arrived here to-day. He is now convales- cent.

div.head: FOLNDATION STONE LAYING AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: FOLNDATION STONE LAYING AT LATCHFORD.

Oa Saturday afternoon the foundation stone of the new schools in connection with St. James's Church, Latchford, was laid by Sir Gilbert Greenall in the presence of a consi- derable gathering of spectators. The schools are to be built on a site adjoining the Old Road, Latchford, and will pro- vide accommodation for about 400 b•ys and girls and 200 infants. The building will be apportioned into a large room 91 feet long for the mixed school, a smaller room for the infants, two class morns, and other conveniences. The schools will be built of brick, tbe flooring consisting of wooden blocks, and altogether the building and furnishing is estimated to cost something like £2 500. The architect is Mr. R. R. Rowe. of Cambridge, and the builder, Mr. Gib- son, of Warrington. Several handsome contributions to- wards the building fund have already been made, including £l,OOO from Sir Gilbert Greenall and £lOO from Mr. W. Beament. The Site, which is valued at about £6OO, has been given by Mr. Lyon, of Appleton Hall. Amongst those present at the opening ceremony were Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, and the Misses Greenall, the Mayor and Mayoress (Aederman and Mrs. Harrison) Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, Mr. and Mrs. Stanton (Thelwall) the Rey. F. and Mrs. Slater, Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Rev. Morley Stevenson, trey. E. J. Wilcocks, Rev. G. Smith, Rev. E. C. E Carleton, Rev. M. Schonberg, • Rev. J. G. Richards and numerous others. The usual religions service having been gone through, the Vicar of St. James' (the Rev. F. Slater) said he was sure most of them would look back upon that day with feelings of satisfaction for many long years to come. There could be nothing excepting a church more important than a school. They had all felt what a great thing it would be to have a new school in Latchford, they had long wanted it, as everybody felt how inadequate there school accommodation was in that parish. Yet it seemed a very hopeless task, but their first encouragement came from Mr. Rowe, their architect, who offered to do all the architects' work gratuitously; the next help they got was from Mr. Lyon, of Appleton Hall, who was so good as to give them the ground on which they stood: and Mr. Beamont, the well-known patron of everything that was good, was, he believed, the Silt to subscribe. But still the work seemed very difficult till at length the burden was made possible by the very generous gift of Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.) They had now got so much pro- mised and given that they felt justified in commencing the work, but the whole of the money was not yet found, and they hoped that others would follow the good example Sir Gilbert Greenall had eet. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)— A handsome silver trowel was then presented to Sir Gilbert Greenall by a little daughter of the Rev. F. Slater, and the stone was formally laid. Sir Gilbert Greenall said he had heard with great pleasure with great pleasure what Mr. Slater had said. He listened attentively to what he had uttered, and all he said had his most hearty concurrence. He was very pleased to be there on that occasion. He came thine not with any desire to be present on an occasion like that; he was brought there by the feeling that it was his duty to give a willing help and a helping hand to those who were working in a right and a good cause. He con- gratulated Mr. Slater upon being the main means of the erection of that school, and he had the mast confident belief that the school would be a blessing to the parish in which he laboured. He (Sir Gilbert) desired that the (lineation given in their parishes should be founded upon God's Word and that the education that was given should be baeed upon religion. (Applause.) He cordially united with them in their work, and he hoped that God's blessing would rest upon that school and upon their labours. (Hear, hear, and applause,)—Mr. Beamont, in moving a'vote of thanks to Sir Gilbert Greenall, said that teaching and learning should be based upon religion. He believed if they did not couple the two together they did not do good, but they did harm, and therefore he thought that on that occasion they had great reason to be thankful that the means were being raised op to diffuse religion and learning in that parish, where as in most parishes which had grown populous, it was a crying necessity. (Hear, hear.)—The Mayor, in seconding the proposal, said he looked upon it as of the greatest import- ance that education should be diffused throughout the length and breadth of the country. When they considered that every man, whatever his position in life might be. had now a vote and could exercise hie influence over the des- tinies of this country, it was absolutely necessary that these people should be educated in order to know how to use that privilege aright. (Hear, hear.) It was to be hoped that the education received in those schools would be sufficient to enable them to judge aright and not to give their votes for the purpose of supporting a party, out from patriotic mo- tives, and from a love of country. (Applause.)—The vote of thanks was then carried by acclainrnatien, and Sir Gil- bert Greenall having briefly responded, the proceedings ter- minated.

MURDER IN PARIS OF AN ENGLISHMAN —A Lewes tele- gram states that the body of a Lewes man, named Frederick Smith, employed in France as a jockey, has been found in the Seine. He had evidently been mtadered, and a man has been arrested wearing the deceased's clothes The French polic have communicated with Smith's relations in Lewes, and at their request a brother or the deceased left for Paris on Thursday.

DEATH OE THE "MAID OF LLANGOLLEN." Mrs. Edwards, the aged proprietress of the Hand Hotel, Llan- gollen, died suddenly on Thursday morning. She engaged in her usual duties on Wednesday, but was taken seriously ill during the night and expired as stated. She was a celebrated Welsh beauty, and was the subject of the popular song, "Thl Maid of Llangollen" by Brindley Richards. She was widely known and greatly esteemed. JEWELLERY THEIre 'IN GLASGOW—Between Saturday afternoon and. Monday the premises of Mr. Semple, a jeweller, carrying on business in St. Enoch's-lane, Glas- gow, were entered by thieves. Two safes were forced open, and diamonds, gold, jewellery, and silver in bars to the value of several thousands of pounds were taken away. There is at present no trace of the robbers, who had ample time to leave the city before the loss was discovered. THE ULSTER CONSERVATIVES AND THE GOVERNMENT.— Mr. C. E. Lewis, M.P. for Londonderry, writes to The Times:—" The great Tory-Democrat oracle has now spoken —the first Minister who has done so since the declaration of Mr. Parnell of his Irish policy. Lord Hartington has also spoken, and great must have been the satisfaction of genuine Conservatives and Constitutionalists at his utter- ances in reply' to Mr. Parnell's plainly formulated demands —opposition, uncompromising opposition, in the interests both of England and Ireland. What has the Ministerial spokesman to say on the same subject I, Nothing—abso- lutely nothing. An apocryphal explanation of the decision of the Conservative leaders (not to ask for a re-maral of the I Crimea Act), said to have been arrived at long before they I had the responsibility of office, and a lame, insincere (not to say untrue) statement of the attitude of the Ministry on the Maamtrasna mcgiou, are all we get of Irish policy from Lord Randoipla Churchill. The good old Conservative party has, indeed, sunk very low to have such a leader ; but what I seek to learn as a Conservative of old standing, who thinks the integrity of the Empire worth preserving, is— bow can we appear as pledged supporters of a Government whose spokesman is disposed to keep silence on such a fun- damental question as the union between England and Ire- land? At the forthcoming election the Conservative party may be beaten, but, for Heaven's sake, let us praserve our self-respect." Hours of idolness—Sparking days. A grave charge—The sexton's fee. Dome+tic pets—Matrimonial sulks. Why is a little boy learning the alphabet like a postage- stamp? —Because he gets stuck on the letters. Soto.r passenger, angrily: "Look where you step, man!' Tipsy passenger, apologetically: "Y-yes, I do; the tr-trauble is to—hic—step where I look." Papa: "Ethel, you mustn't say 'I won't' to papa. It's nanAlity." Ethel: "Well but, papa, what must I say when I mean I won't ?" An absent husband telegraphed to his wife: "I send you a kiss." He received as reply: "Spruce young man called and delivered the kiss in good order." "What to do with wealth after one's got it? is a serious question," says the Brooklyn Eagle. This may be, but the question which strikes us as far more serious is, what to do without wealth when one has not got it? Perhaps the utmost extreme of intense agony has been reached when a woman dislocates her jaw, and her obliging neighbour comes in and informs her that Mrs. Jones says she's a mean, spiteful, gossiping old harridan. "Oh, Harry, what a beautiful birthday present! lam glad to know that you didn't forget me. Pure gold isn't it ?" Harry, her betrothed: "Yes, darling." "And the case is superb. It isn't a charm or an earring, for you would have bought me a pair. I never saw anything like it. What is it ?" "It is a thimble."

farmer, "that When I came .to measure those five barrels of apples I bought from you I found them nearly a barrel short ?" "Singular, very singular, for I put them up in some of your own flour barrels." "Ahem ! Did, eh? Well, perhaps I made a mistake. Fine weather, isn't it ?" "I don't want mother to marry again," said a little boy one day at breakfast. "Why not ?" was asked, with some surprise. "Because," said he, "I've lost one father, and I don't want the trouble of getting acquainted with another." A woman fell out of a woad storey window of an hotel and alighted on her/ head on the side walk below. They picked her up, and in due time she recovered her conscious- ness. "Oh ! my hat, my hat," she sobbed, "I can never get that feather to look like anything again." "I cannot sing the old songs," shrieked an amateur soprano; and while she took in breath for the next line, a • young man, who had looked on for a moment, was heard to remark, casually and emphatically, "That's no bloomhe error; you can't!" It broke up the concert on the spot, the prima donna refusing to vooalise further. Tun TRAINING OF CHILDIMN.—" Fanny, you should not beat your doll with that heavy stick. You will make all the sawdust come out of it," said a Texas mother to her little girl, who had placed her doll on the ground and was belabouring it with a base ball bat. "I don't care if all the sawdust does come out of her," replied Fanny; "I don't want people to say that my children turned out bad because I humoured them too mach."

A scientific writer says that to discover how an insect breathes, "take, say a wasp or hornet" He may mean well, but we shall take neither a wasp nor a hornet. The person who takes either a wasp or a hornet to discover how an insect breathes is pretty apt to do some very rapid and vigorous breathing himself before he proceeds far with the investigation. Better take an insect that doesn't violate the law against carrying concealed weapons.-2Vorristortm Herald.

ARTIBIIIS WARD AND YOUNG BRIGIIT.—Upon one occa- sion when Artemus Ward was in London, a children's party was arranged by the great humourist, and to which one of the sons of John Bright was invited. The boy returned home aglow with delight. "Well," said the English states- man to his son, "did you enjoy yourself, my boy ?" "Oh, indeed I did," replied the little Bright, "and Mr. Ward gave me such a nice name for you, papa." "What was that?' inquired the father. "Why, he asked me how that gay and festive cuss, the governor, was," replied the child. TEE FISH me JoNss' NET.—The other night, after the thunder shower, Jones dropped in on a neighbour and found about a dozen people assembled. a Well, well, you look cheerful after such a close call," growled Jones as he re- moved his hat. "What close call?" "Why, lightning struck the barn in the alley not a hundred feet away." "Oh dear!" said one of the women, "but I knew it all the time. One of my arms has been numb ever since." "And it affected my foot," said another. "And it set my heart to palpitating.' "And my elbow has felt queer ever since." Everyone in the room remembered to have been shocked, and everyone was thankful over the narrow escape. By and by a boy, who had been thinking deeply, gushed out: "Why, there's no barn in the alley r, Amidst the deepest silence everybody remembered this fact, aid the boy clinched in with: "And how could there be, when there is no alley ?" Jones had lied, but so had all the ethers. DIDN'T LET lILE FINISH THE SENTENCE.—An cold farmet -like chap came aboard a train down near Galesburg. He looked as if he was yearning to talk to somebody. Approaching a plug-hatted, dignified gentleman, he said: "Is it hot—" But here the plug-hatted gentleman turned his back upon the farmer. But the old gentleman was not discouraged. Accosting a flashily dressed drummer, he re- peated: "Is it hot—" But here the drummer raised his newspaper between his face and the questioner's. The old man made the rounds of the car, but everywhere met with the same rebuff. Finally he got mad and shouted: "I s'pose you smart-aleck fellers think I wanted to ask you if it was hot enough for you, but I didn't. I never ask no such questions o' no man. l've got some fine old 1867 whisky in my pocket here, an' I wanted to ask one o' you fellers if it was hot enough to make a good drink attractive. I never like to drink alone, but, seein's there's no other gentleman in the car, gum I'll have to." Hi DIDN'T Masarsurzn TREIL—The Rev. Mr. Windbag was taking dinner with Deacon Baldy, when the solemnity which Is usually prevalent on such occasions was broken by the Deacon's youngest exclaiming: "Say, Mr. Windbag, is you a mesmerizer ?" "No, Thomas, lam a minister of the gospel. Why ?" "'Camas I heard pap tell Deacon Jones that, whenever you opened your mouth, the congregation went to sleep, and I thought maybe you mesmerized them." (The Deacon and the Rey. Windbag never speak al they paw by.)

WARRING-TON LICENSING SESSIONS. The adjourned annual meeting of the Licensing Commit- tee of the justices of the borough of Warrington was held at the Sessions Rouse in Irlarmstrest on Tuesday, when the magistrates on the bench were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, Alderman Holmes, Councillor Greening, Dr. Gornall, and Messrs. Guest, Garnett, Monks, and Faircleugh. Considerable interest was taken in the proceedings. THE QUESTION OF FEMALE DRUNKENNESS. ' Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, addressing the justices, said that during an absence from home he had seen his native town held out in the newspapers as being a place notorious for drunken women. He knew that that statement had been felt very much by thousands of respeztable women in War- rington who were sober. He did think that it was certainly hard for old Warringtonians to see their native town pointed out up and down the country as a place for drunken women. Had he been present when that statement was made he should have demurred to it. It was made by a deputation of ladies and gentlemen actuated by the best motives, but, so far as he could see from the papers, not one of whom was Warrington born. Mr. Hunt entertained a great horror of female drunkenness and did all in his power to check it. He (Mr. Davies) wished to call the attention of the committee to the real facts of the case. During 1885 there had been 174 cases of female drunkeness, some of whom were probably the same females brought up at different times. He deducted from the total 53 cases that were dis- missed, which left 121 as against the thousands of respect- able women who lived in Warrington. He thought such statements as had been made were very unfortunate. He recollected something being said about the morality of Warrington when Mr. Rigby was sitting on the Bench on a similar occasion to the present, and they anew how careful he was as to the morals and religious training of those under his influence, and he spoke to him (the speaker) about it. He said he did not think Warrington was worse than other places, and he (Mr. Davies) felt a resentment at the time at the statement that Warrington was notorious for that vice. He afterwards made inquiries, and Mr. Sutton told him that so far as illegitimate& were concerned, tio number in War- rington was below the average. When a statement was amlsaodebe d t respecting these rash statements against the town for which they as g its a townHe trusted no one would make credit. like Warrington something should natives felt so much regard, so that it should be held up throughout the land ass vicious and immoral place. The Way to meet the evils complained of was to spread education and make religious efforts in the right directipn, and, if I Possible, find some substitute for public-houses. They could not repress them by the strong hand. He saw with pleasure that in ten years' time the number of charges of drunkenness had diminished from 1,033 to 718, and be thought he might say that Mr. Hunt was quite as strict as he ever was, and that all the people who deserved to be summoned were brought before the Bench Warrington, it should also be borne in mind, was the half-way town . between two large towns, and was much frequented by tramps. 'The Mayor, in reply, said that he had long felt Warring- ton was unjustly treated in being held up as containing an unduly large number of drunken females. Ile believed that the more the case was inquired into and the more fallacious it would appear. Yesterday there was a girl brought before the magistrates on a charge of drunkenness, and it was the 37th time she had been before the magistrates, and in the statistics she had been counted as 37 distinct cases. That showed how likely these statistics were to be misinterpreted. There were a number of others who had been several times convicted for female drunkenness. He thought they should do all they could to relieve Warrington from the odium that was most unjustly attached to it. He did not believe that there was so much female drunkenness in Warrington as in many towns, and he attributed the notoriety referred to in a great measure to their having a large staff of reporters attending the court, who were in direct communication with the Man- chester and Liverpool papers. Naturally they wished to make their communications as attractive as possible, and when there was a case of female drunkenness brought before the Bench, it generally occupied a prominent position, and was most conspicuously placed before the public, whereas similar eases brought before the Manchester and Liverpool

magistrates were absorbed amongst the number of other cases, and were not so conspicuously set forth. Hence wrong impressions were sometimes formed. Mr. R. Davies said that he was glad that the Mayor had confirmed what he had said for the honour of Warrington. It was an explanation that should go forth to the public, I because be felt sure that every gentleman on the bench had a pride in the town, and would rather see it famed for morality and religion than decried for the opposite. APPLICATIONS.

Mr. Robert Davies apTdie—d7tii-h-e.hralf ef Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. for a license for a new house to be built in Hoyle-street. It was practically, he said, the transfer of the Pelican, in Buttermarket-street—to remove the Pelican to a situation at the corner of Hoyle-street, where there was no licensed house nearer than the Three Pigeons. He thought that a respectably conducted house in that neigh- bourhood would not be objected to by the persons resident in the locality.—Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of the Rev. G. E. Cutting and others, opposed the application. He urged that there were sufficient houses to supply the neigh- bourhood.—He called the Rev. G. E. Cutting, who said that though he was not Warrington born, he had resided in Bewsey-road, and, environed as he was by opportunities for the public to get drink, he had a sufficient knowledge of Warrington to strongly oppose the granting of this new license. It seemed strange to be clashing with the interests of respectable men; but they lighted fires they could not al- ways afterwards control, although he believed they would wish to do so. He appealed to the Bench to do their utmost to quench these evil fires that were burning in War- rington. He was sufficiently acquainted with Warrington to have a deep interest in it, and he was glad to have heard words which somewhat explained matters that had troubled him much. He had met with young girls the worse for drink in Warrington and had heard remarks that seemed to be directed te him, such as be had never heard during a three years' residence in • Birmingham. He hoped the im- rovemetat that had been noted would continue.—The ap- -1 ication was refused. Mr. Robert Davies also applied for provisional license for premises te supplant the Roebuck Inn, after the Corpora- tion alterations, on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.—The application was withdrawn, the Bench being of opinion that under the exceptional circumstances of the case it was not necessary to apply for a new license, and that the renewal of the existing license would be sufficient. Mr. Wallhead, on behalf of Ralph Lamb, 21, Butter- market-street, applied for a license to sell beer, wines, and spirits off the premises.—Mr. Browne spoke in opposition. —The Bench refused the application so far as regarded a license to sell beer.

Mr. P. Davies, on behalf of Elijah Lawton, the Grove, Bewsey-road, applied for a full ale house license to sell off or on the premises. He called a number of witnesses, who Said that the house would be a convenience to the neigh- beurhood.—Mr. A. Browne, who was instructed to oppose, said that a similar application had been eight times refused. and there was no additional evidence to show that the house was required.—The Committee declined to grant the appli- cation.

An application made by Richard Price, of the Gardeners' Arms, Brick-street, to eell wine, was granted •, as was also an application by Richard Burchall, tea dealer, Scotland. road, for a public billiard licence. Mr. A. Browne supported both applications. This was all the business. -.....--.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Germany is in these latter days what France used to be during the hey-day of the Third Empire. It was necessary for the existence of Napoleon the Third that he should keep things going in lively fashion throughout Europe. With his fickle people he lived upon sufferance, and was to be endured only if he kept France in the front line, and from time to time gave the army something to do. Now it is Germany that at brief intervals disturbs Europe with threats and high-handed proceedings. Ever since Prince Bismarck conceived the notion of making Germany a colonial power there have been wars and rumours of wars. When the Liberal Gov- ernment were in power, the Conservatives trembled , with indignation because England did not straight-1 way go to war with Germany on the New Guinea question. Since Lord Salisbury presided at the Foreign Office, Germany has bullied the Sultan of Zanzibar into an arrangement seriously and dis- tinctly harmful to British interests. But Lord Randolph Churchill, Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Sir Hy. , Wolff, Mr. Chaplin, and all the rest who set up a I howl over New Guinea have said never a word over Zanzibar. Now it is Spain that has felt the weight of the 'heavy hand of Germany. German scouts, prowling 'over the Pacific, have picked up Yap, one of the klaroline Islands to which Spain lays claim. The incident found Spain in a state of political tension. The Conservatives were in office and wanted to keep in. The Liberals were out of office and wanted to I get in. Accordingly they, in true Ashmead Bart- lett style, raved and gnashed their teeth, denounced the Government as poltroons, andplainly indmated that if they were returned to office they would make war against Germany. Thus one touch of nature makes Spain and England kin. For a while the case looked, serious enough. The mob stormed the quarters of the German Consul in Madrid, tore down his flag, and trod the German coat of arms underfoot. Had the Germans lost their head war would have been inevitable. Prince Bismarck had certa'nly made a mistake, which is not strange. But he acknowledgedit, which is very strange indeed, and assurances have been given to Spain which at the present moment seem to avert all danger of war. In case of war one of the first things that would happen in Spain would be the pulling down of the Throne and the setting Up of a Republic, and that is a consummation which the German Emperor is not disposed to assist in bringing about. Mr. Gladstone has returned home after Os yacht- ing cruise, and according to all accounts is much improved in health. Still his voice is weak, and I much doubt whether he will be permitted to im- peril it by another Midlothian campaign. It is generally assumed that-he will -visit Midlothian in October. But, as a matter of fact, no arrangement has been definitely made. Mr. Gladstone has always put aside suggestions of that _character, leaving his course of action dependent upon the state of his health. It would be quite possible for him to ful- fil the ordinary conditions of candidature by issuing a manifesto addressed to the electors of Midlothian, and he may finally adopt that course. In any case there will be nothing like the triumphal progress of 1880, or even the briefer succession of speeches made in Midlothian last autumn. It was during one of these that Mr. Gladstone's voice sustained the injury that has hampered him throughout the session. Meanwhile the general campaign is steadily go- ing forward, increasing week by week in volume, intensity, and energy, Mr. Chamberlain is for the moment the most prominent orator on the Liberal side. Lord Hartington has delivered his speech and gone his way. Presently Sir William Harcourt will appear upon the scene. He contemplates deliver- ing several speeches which he is even now elaborat- ing. Lord Randolph Churchill is the only notable' speaker on the Conservative side, and his deliver- ances are remarkable chiefly for what he does not say. Addressing two meetings immediately after Mr. Parnell's pronunciamento, Lord Randolph signi- ficantly avoided all reference to the subject, leaving himself untrammelled for any new compact with the Parnellites that may be necessary within the next six months. But there are signs abroad that though Lord Randolph may be equal to the treachery of abetting Irish sedition, his party will not follow him. Even in Conservative circles, Mr. Chamber- lain's frank and uncompromising denunciation of Mr. Paniell's separatist policy has been warmly ap- plauded and contrasted with Lord Randolph Churchill's reticence. The trial of the defendants in the Eliza Armstrong case has attracted an extraordinary amount of public attention. On the days when the investiga- tion was proceeding Bow-street was besieged by a surging multitude fighting for the remote possibi- laof obtaining entrance to the court. There is no culty in ascertaining how public opinion runs in this matter. In the court itself applause of points made by the prosecution is with difficulty repres- sed. Outside the appearance of the defendants is the signal for a storm of hooting. Professor Stuart, M.P., and Mr. McArthur, M.P., pluckily stand by their convictions and associate themselves with Mr. Stead in his affliction to the extent of standing bail for him. But others, including some of the Bishops, are tailing off. The simple statement made by Eliza Armstrong and the practical admission of its accuracy indicated by the course taken by Mr. 'Charles Russell, have made a great impression on the public mind. The defence may finally succeed in placing the motives of Mr. Stead and his assis- tants in a favourable light. But how the hard fact of a breach of the Criminal Law is to be got over is not easy to be seen. It would be a curious episode if, after his uncompromising efforts to get the Criminal Law Amendment Bill passed, Mr. Stead should be one of the first to suffer from its stringent regulations. I have just heard, from a gentleman who was present on the occasion, a pretty little story in con- nection with the appointment of the present Ministry. When Lord Randolph Churchill, Sir M. 11. Beach, and Lord George Hamilton went down to Windsor to take the oath of office the Queen, look- ing at them after the first greeting, said " Dear me, how young you all look." This is quite true, and comparison with the former Ministry, or with any average Ministry, whether Liberal or Conservative, the application of the remark might be further ex- tended. The youngest man in Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet was Lord Rosebery, who is 38. Next in order came Sir C. Dilke 42, Mr Trevelyan 47, and Mr. Chamberlain 50, though no one looking at the member for Birmingham would imagine he was that age. Since he came into office he has aged considerably, but is still at a short distance younger looking than Sir Charles Dilke. Lord Randolph Churchill, as he boasted the other day, is the youngest member of the Cabinet, and indeed of the Ministry. He is only 36, Lord George Hamilton is 40, Colonel Stanley is 44, and Sir M. H. Beach 48. There is no member of the present Ministry as old as Earl Granville, much less Mr. Gladstone. The 'The present Premier is 55, as compared with Mr. Gladstone's 76 years The oldest members in the new Cabinet are Sir Stafford Northcote and Lord John Manners, who are each 67, though Lord John looks ten years older. Mr. Gladstone at 76 is a much younger looking man than Lord John, who nevertheless still affects with quaint results the sprightly manners of young England. I have been reading the cheap stereotyped edition , of "With Harp and Crown," and note the survival of a curious slip of the pen. In finally disposing of their characters Messrs. Besant and Rice write : " Dr. Chacomb is now Sir Joseph Chacomb, Bart., M.D. This distinction was acquired in pulling a certain exalted personage through an attack of gout which threatened to fly to the stomach. Dr. Chacomb never left the patient's bedside till the great man was safe. Then they knighted him." This apparent.ignorance of affairs is by no means un- common in modern novels. In a recent novel by Mr. Christie Murray, "A Piece of Human Nature," a principal episode in the story turns upon a Chinaman who sits down to a good English supper, and eats mutton chops and other things with the greatest zest. The Chinese, as most people know, never eat English food, whether in the form of chops or joints. In San Francisco, where they remain for years in domestic service, they religiously preserve their own ways of living, towards which eggs from five to ten years old, were contribute, It is the same in Hong Kong, w „ here a Chinaman would starve before he touched tile meat he himself skilfully prepares for the household. These references are, as Dr. Johnson explained to the lady who asked him why he had described a horse's fetlock as a pastern, "Sheer ig- norance, madam, sheer ignorance." But the genial and accomplished authors of "With Harp and Crown " cannot be supposed to lie under the im- pression that the knighting of a man gives him the right to add "Bart." after his name. Yet the error has snrvived many editions, and is now stereo.
typed. All sorts of strange statistics are given by which one may gauge the size of London. I think one of the strangest is that its cat population should be

so large. Half a million of cats sounds incredible but I am told the true number is within that figure, and that .E 150,000 a year is laid out in horse flesh on their food. One would be glad to know what the mouse population is, which acts as a sort of rate in aid to assist these cats to live. However, money is not only spent on them, but made by them. This week an eminent cats-meat-man died and left behind, as the result of his earnings in that business, the sum of £20,000. One might ex- pect that the West End would have been the scene of his successful labours. Kensington abounds with corpulent cats. But here again the mystery of London asserts itself. It was in the City that all this money was made, round about Gray's Inn Road and the purlieus of Clerkenwell.

THE VISIT OF CARDINAL MANNING. Sir,—l am glad to notice that the great Apostle of Tem- perance is about to visit Warrington. I also learn that the Mayor is annoy:neat to preside. I would suggest to the members of the League of the Cross that they furnish his Eminence with a copy of the report of the Mayor's re- marks at the recent Brewster Sessions. What a capi- tal subject it would make for Carctinal Manning to speak upon, and how nicely he might give a lesson to the chief magistrate.--Yours, &c., Warrington, Sept. 10.1885.

POLITICS AND ANTI-VACCINATION. Sir,—Under this heading the following letter appeared in .a Liverpool paper on Tuesday : Sir,—With reference ta your observations as to the shining lines imposed on anti-vaccinators by the Newton magistrates in yours of the 3rd September, it may late i est you to know that the Radical anti-vaccinators In Earlestown will command something like from 400 to 500 votes at the en suing election. The chairman of the Newton bench is the Liberal candidate for the Newton district in oppasition to Sir R. A. Cross His son is another magistrate, and a third is a very prominent supporter cf the Liberal Muse in the neigh- bcurbood. Your readers can draw their own conclusions.— Yours. dm A LOOKER-ON.—September 5, 1885." • This, sir, is worth preserving as an instance of Tory bigotry and party spite. When it is stated that the only magistrates on the Bench when the fines of Is and costs were inflicted were Colonel McCorqnodale and Mr. W. F. Gooch, the value of "A Looker-O' " comments can be easily judged. His gratuitous assertions that certain magistrates are Liberals are in accordaoca with the rest of his letter— only what they are worth? I could easily forward a list of Tory magistrates on other occasions; and could add "Your readers can draw their own conclusions," but such a course would be foolish, as it is in " LookerOn's " case.—Yonrs, Szc., • JUSTICE.

A RED-ROT "SALISBURY." Sir,—The other day, having a little time to •west*, I bethought me to take a glance at a speech made by the Con- servative (why not " neutral ?") candidate for Montrose aad I came across the following passage No matter what takes place between now and the e ection, I shall ga to the poll. lam not accustomed to changing my mind, and deserting my friends!" (The italics are mice.) Here I hastily threw the paper aside, fearing lest I might meet with the remark that • The speaker at this point turned deadly pale, and seemed ready to faint, but recovered him- self by a great effort !" Why, sir, not so many years ago no Liberal platform within a radius of six miles was considered complete without this Doctor of Defunct Dormitories; this LL.D. of a Yankee University! And now, as a candi- date for Conservative votes, is it not a" Salisbury" for him to say he "is not accustomed to change his mind ?"

Yes, "A merciful Providence fashioned him holler. 0' purpose that he might his prince! pies swolier." And his Conservative friends in the Association say that be has even deserted them. They rejoice, however, above all things that he will be away at Montrose when their own futile struggle comes on; and, like myself, are intensely curious to see how that Liberal-Neutral training be has undergone will enable him to acquit himself before the wide-a-wake folk " owre the border,' who don't like turn- coats, and who dislike still more a Tory in any shape. That the Doctor is " bold and brave" no one will deny ; but for his wild goose chase after Parliamentary honours at Montrose, nothing seems 80 appropriate as Pope's famous line—

Balmoral, September, 1885.
AN EXEMPLARY PARSON.

Sir,—lt is, and'al;;;;;;;--been-, a great novelty t hear a clergyman of the Established Church raising his voice in support of the liberties of the masses ; but it appears that there are some—like the Rev. W. Tuckwell, rector of Stockton, that do not fear the frowns of their parochial squire. If there were more of his stamp in our so-called " National Church," lam of opinion that the question that we hear sometimes raised by eur prelates of " how to reach the masses," would be solved, and perhaps we should hear less complaint about empty churches. The Rev. W. Tuck. well, In his address to the new voters of Rugby, strikingly pourtrays the important nature of the rights that have now devolved upon the working-man. In the following words he shows the power that the people will wield at the ap- proaching political conflict :—" I want you to observe the enormous power which this new franchise, as they call it, confers upon you. Out of every five men who vote at the next election four will Le working-nzen, that is to say, that your class has absolute power to create a parliament which shall be pledged, above all things, to attend and obey your bidding." Now, let us working-men ever keep this fact before us as the time of conflict approaches. Let every candidate who cemes to seek our suffrage be firsrasked if he will pledge himself to use his power to further the cause of labour, and should he not be candid on this one point, no matter what other fine premises he may make, let us de- nounce him. Let no be fooled no more by those who in order to distract our thoughts from this, by talking about "British interests in Africa and India," and of upholding "the honour of England." The latter with a Tory means nothing more or less than expending life and treasure in seeking quarrels ia dietant lands. Our foreign possessions, like India, are more for the benefit of the upper and middle class than the working class. I trust that the above clergyman's attitude towards the people will be copied by more of his brethren, who gener- ally, instead of enlightening them, tell them that they have great cause to be thankful and contented that they live in such a faveured land. Do they really believe what they say P If not, then they must be charged with duplicity.— I am, yours, etc., PLEBEIAN. Frodsham, Sep. 8, 1885.
THE ANTI-VACCINATORS' FIASCO. .

Sir,—The proceedings of the local Anti-Vaccinators at Earleetown last Friday will no doubt be reported, but per- haps you will permit me a little space, as an observer, to criticise their doings. I know they, are in the habit of boast- ing of their strength, and of the conscientious character of their principles, and up to Friday last I was willing to grant them all in that respect. But since then I must consider- ably alter my impressions. Yes, and everybody else who siw the miserable character of their "demonstration." Demonstration," indeed ? Yes, it was a dece,nstration of law and order against fanaticism and disorder. Speaking trnly, so far as an exhibition favourable to anti-vaccination was concerned, it was a failure, both miserable and discou- raging. " Discouraging " scarcely expresses the state of mind in which it placed the anti-law conspirators. In every

respect the lawful authorities gained the victory, if the assertion °Moe power of the law can be called a victory, while the anti•lawites were defeated all along the line. The antics of the latter were indeed amusing—well, perhaps I should say pitiful—to an extreme degree. Instead of con- demning the Anti-Vaccinators, I am sure all right-minded persons must think they were deserving of sympathy and pity. Who could view the so-called" procession" without feeling sympathetic towards the miserable few who followed the banner? Where were the 400 or GOO Anti-Vaccinators I had read and heard talked of ? I looked in vain for them —perhaps their representatives only attended. However, the "sale " was the most miserable part of the affair. The auctioneer was more than a match for his " persecutors," and the latter ultimately submitted to a defeat and dis- comfiture which was truly heartrending. I really pity them from the bottom of my heart. The " public meeting "at Earlestown in the evening, as well as the " sale," did not "come off" from a successful point of view. The " public " were represented by the representatives of the press—so I am informed—while the " Earlestown Branch of the Anti- Compulsery Vaccination Society (I think that is its title) were represented by about six or eight of the most earnest members and officers. Heaven help them. At the sale the Anti-Vaccinators were truly" sold,' while at the " meeting " they met with nothing but themselves and discouragement. However, the least said the hetter.—Yours, _
ANTI-VACCINATOR.
COERCIVE VACCINATION.

Sir,—The clerk to the Warrington persecutors, miscalled Guardians (Mr. Sutton) in his speech to his family friends, reported in your last issue, is not only remarkable for its frankness, but truth is most conspicuous by its absence. While he claims to have p6ceeded with moderation, he has Invariably, since the first trial in May last year. asked for the fullest penalties and costs. And this sot only in cases of determined opposition, but even in cases where the child has been vaccinated, the costs have been asked, pressed for, and obtained, as instance the case of Mr. Emmett, of Earle- street.

Then he would have us believe his absence from recent trials at Newton was due to his sense of uselessness. So some others may think, but anti-vaccinators know the greater reason was the comfortless position of having to fight for the (assumed) right of being heard, while his ab- sence was the marked reply to an intimation that he would be called upon to prove the statement that a certain letter affecting his assumed right to appear had been laid before the law officers of the crown. Further, his reference to Leicester is also very misleading. True, each person summoned and convicted for non-vaccina- tion is fined 10s, but he forgets to tell us this 10s includes all costs to the defendant. On the other hand, when orders are rendered nec,ssary, by the delay of proceedings, thus incurring two sets of costs, the Guardians, by order of the magistrates, are compelled to pay the costs in one instance. Thus at Leicester defaulters pay a total of 103, while at Newton the same defaulters must pay twenty-two shillings and sixpence, besides the amount of the fine. Can toe force of folly further go ? Mr. Thomas Littler wrote to correct the statement that the cellar at the Temperance Hotel had not been cleaned out for two years, and was a great nuisance. The cellar was regularly washed out and kept as clean as could be done, considering that frequently sewage entered to the depth of more than a, foot, and leaving a deposit of two or three inches of mud • The cellar at the Victoria Dining I Room was also kept clean. He expressed his willingness to connect the cellars with the main sewer if the Local Board would have the sewer made suitable.—The subject was re- ferred to the Highway Committee.

TEMPERANCE. Sir,—l want to say a few words on this very much abused question. To begin with,l am not like '• Rob Roy." who in your last issue deprecates the "interference of women at a Brewster Session." Whatever question comes to the front that is likely to influence society for its good, women have a right to take their part iJ . Having said this much in defence of the rights of women, allow me now, sir, to at once fall foal of their programme. I want to know, in the first place, what is meant by Temperance? Is it modera- tion, or is it downright abstinence ? If the former it shall have my support ; if the latter it will be treated with the indifference that kills. Suppose, in dealing with the drink question, we were to consider for a moment the side issues that it has. Do these young men and young women drink and lead mean lives for the mere love of the thing ? Or do they rush into evils, the immensity of which they know not, in order to escape the ever attending surroundings of their every day life? Suppose, again, you could make all the girls who now lead drunken and shameful lives into teetotallers. Can you fancy the monotonous existence that would be theirs? Brought up as they are, without any love for domestic life, knowing nothing, or very little of the various accomplishments that render the greatest charm to the home life of the beat of England's daughters, what would you have them do ? I could not speak of the good intentions of Mrs. Garnett and Miss Parker as being the out- come of " mock philanthrophy," but I must term it mis- directed zeal. To make a sober people, I must assert, is grand work, and it must also be allowed that while a thousand people may strive for the same object, it is not imperative that they should all be forced to go the same way, but ills desirable that none of the resources should be wasted. ' Allow me to point this out; that for all the money spent, and all the lablur devoted to "the cause." the result we have is a constantly increasing sense of dissatisfaction. I point to the modern feature of life in the streets, girl I drunkenness. I also, in all respect, ask the kind ladies to I fancy their lot to be from bell ringing at 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., confinement in a stifling factory, with the pleasant prospect of spending three or four hours each evening in a still more I stifling home? Situated in a street that reminds cue of the I ancient narrow thoroughfares, where in old times the Black I Death and the Plague had their homes, what would they Ido under these circumstances? lam afraid they would be. no better than their sisters. 'Tis not for the love of drink so many rush to the public. house ; it is as a resort to seek and to gain the company of what, I am sorry to sly, a vicious training has rendered a necessity. How shall it be remedied ? The answer to this is not yet found oat, only, I should say, in an abstract sort of way. I shonld think Mr. Chamberlain has done more than any other man to make Birmingham a sober town. He has cleared out rookeries where vice and drunken- ness abounded. Be has seen that if you render a house and its surroundings pleasant and agreeable to its inmates, the less will be the temptation to Stand at the bar of the gin shop To drink with the dregs of the people. You will do no good until the question of workmen's dwel- lings is taken up with spirit, until the question of Free Education is put to the front, and money that is paid in taxes and wasted on police and prisons diverted into other and better channels. I am strongly of opinion that free trade in drink Bening would brine; about its own cure. Throw it entirely open, and cease to make legislation responsible for the weaknesses of humanity. Trust to the people's own good sense for bring- ing the thing right in the end. The competition that would come about would do with publicans as it did with the Bir- migham screw makers; it would make them hail with pleasure the advent of one who could save them from the bankruptcy court. And so in the end publicans and drinkers, like screw manufacturers and their workmen, would mutually benefit by the Reformer's hand. ' CLIFFORD DI X.

div.head: TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
div.p: TRADES UNION CONGRESS.

The eighteenth annual congress of representatives of the trade unions of Great Britain was opened on Monday at Southport. Mr. J. S. Murchie, of Manchester, presided, and there wore present nearly 200 delegates. In his opening address the Chairman said that these congresses were mere representative than formerly, and possessed the confidence of the trades in a higher degree. They had grown out of the necessity for repeatedly defending unionist principles against attack into a position of great and increasing power and influence, which was constantly being exercised, not for the benefit of the trade unionist section merely, but in the interest of the masses. He said it was a common supersti- tion that trade societies spent their money on strikes alone, and quoted figures to prove that the amount spent on trakle movements was but a small proportion of the total expendi- ture, which was chiefly for benevolent purposes. At the close of the chairman's address the congress elected Mr. T. R. Threlfall, of Southport, as its president. The Parlia- mentary Committee in their report, which was read by Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., dealt with the legislation of the past year as affecting labour questions. The committee urged dele- gates to press their cause to the front at the general elec- tion.

At Tuesday's sitting of the congress Mr. Threlfall, the newly-elected president, delivered his inaugural address. He discussed various social and trade questions, and sub- mitted that the entire poor-law system of the country needed reforming, and that the people had a right to demand free education. On the consideration of the Parliamentary Committee's report, which as presented on Monday, a discussion arose with reference to recent appointments to inspectorships of mines, some of the mining delegates ex- pressing disappointment that working miners had not been appointed, as promised by the late Home Secretary. The new inspectors had been selected from among the class of managers. An amendment to the cemn'ttee's report em- bodying an expression of regret at the character of the ap- pointments was moved and seconded by delegates from Durham. Mr. Burt, M.P., said he believed that Sir Wm. Harcourt did all that was possible to carry out the promise be had made in the House of Commons. There were work- ing men present who had been offered inspectorsbips, but were unable to accept them because of their inability to pass the requisite examination. No doubt the appointments that had been made were open to criticism, but he was told on good authority that some, if no all, of those selected were practical men.—Mr. Broadhurst, M.P. also defended the action of the committee ; but the amendment upon be- ing put to the vote was carried by a large majority. A dis- cussion followed on the Royal Commission for Inquiring into the Depression in Trade. _ _

On Wednesday resolutions were adopted expressing sym- pathy with the operatives of Oldham in their efforts to prevent a redaction of wages unaccompanied by a measure for the restriction of output ; instructing the Parliamen- tary Committee to use its utmost efforts to secure the amendment of defects in the Employers' Liability Act by the new Parliament, and calling upon workmen generally to obtain pledges of support on this question from Parlia- mentary candidates ; insisting on the necessity of engine- men on land being compelled to hold the same certificates of competency as those at sea, and urging the desirableness of the appointment of additional working-men as factory in- spectors. Mr. Broadhurst submitted to the Congress, in view of the coming general election, an address to the workmen of the United Kingdom, detailing the questions to which, in the opinion of the delegates, candidates should be asked to give their support. Workmen were urged to make their influence felt in the assertion of the interests of labour in all its branches, whether organised or not. It was urged that the unprecedented increase in their political power carried with it a corresponding increase of responsi- bilities. Discussion on the address had not concluded when the Congress adjourned. _ _

On Thursday the delegates were engaged in the discus- sion of clauses in the election addrys submitted for ap- proval by the Parliamentary Committee. A resolution was carried in favour of such a change being sought in the law as will enable the relatives of persons killed in mines to be represented at coroners' inquests. Mr. Mnrchie (Manches- ter) moved a resolution expressing satisfaction that some constituencies had adopted working-men candidates for the next Parliament, and that some of the larger trade societies had adopted, and others had resolved to adopt, measures for providing the necessary pecuniary assistance. The resolu- tion was seconded by Mr. Forbes, a delegate from Glasgow; and whilst it was supported by the general body of the dele- gates and ultimately carried, one or two of the speakers deprecated the introduction of party politics into the deliberations of the Congress. A resolution on the question of land law reform was under discussion when the Congress adjourned. On Friday, the discussion of land law reform was con- tinued. There was before the Congress a resolution in favour of land reform, without pledging the delegatei to any particular scheme, and an amendment approving the principle of land nationalisation.—Ths resolution was car- ried by 69 votes against 44 for the amendment.—lt was re- solved that the law of Scotland, relating to sudden and accidental death, should be so amended as to provide for public inhairy in lieu of the present system.—The Congress discussed the place of meeting next year. Hall, Swan- sea, and Norwich were proposed by the respective dele- gates of those towns. On the vote being taken Hull was selected.

A Goons •I'muls ON Fiux. - About five o'clock on Tuesday morning a mixed goods train from Liverpool to Prestos and the north was discovered to be on fire on its arrival at St. Helens station. Smoke was issuing some- what densely from three waggons loaded with cotton, but, we are informed, there was nothing like a " mass of fire," as reported in one of the Liverpool evening papers. The smouldering loads of cotton were stopped beneath Sharp- Street bridge, and here water was poured on the waggons. The latter were subs.quently unhooked and shunted in a siding, while the rest of the train proceeded on its journey. The cotton continued to smoulder for some hours and great difficulty was experienced in extinguishing it. A good many of the bales of cotton were seriously damaged, the total loss being about £5O, and not "apparently £1,000" as stated in the report previously alluded to. The officials at St. Helens station.have been considerably annoyed by 'the alarming and exaggerated report of the affair.

MR; ‘SETON‘ KARR AND THE MINERS' PROGRAMME. Mr. Henry Solon Karr, the Conservative candidate for St. Helens, has forwarded to the Secretary of the Miners' I Association of Southwest Lancashire the following replies to the twelve questions put by that association to Parlia- mentary candidates : Question you vote for Mr. Burt's employers' liability act amendment bill? Answer.—Mr. Burt's act, as I understand, proposes chiefly to do away with the power that employers and workmen now have to contract them- selves out of the employers' liability act of 1880. Should Mr. Burt's act, be brought forward again I will give the matter nit:, best consideration ; and if any injustice to workmen is shown to exist under the act of 1880, for which injustice Mr. Burt's proposed amendment supplies an ads- quite remedy, I should consider it my duty to vote for such amendment. At the same time lam bound to say that the principle of interfering with the right of freedom of I contract may be a dangerous one, and such interference I would I think require a strong case in order to justify

it. Questions Relating to Mines.—Question 2.—Will you vote for necessary amendment of the mines regulation act, 1872. (a) That miners may have the power to seleet a check-weighman from any place they may choose, and not exclusively from the same mine or firm as at present. (b) That miners may be able to prosecute without having to get permission of the Home Secretary as at present. Question 4.—Will you vote for the Royal Commission to inquire into royalty rents paid for working mines with a view to reduction of the same? Question 9.—Will you vote for relatives of persons killed in or about mines to ap- pear personally, or by deputy, in the coroner's court to put questions to the witnesses, in order that a proper verdict may be come to. Answers to Questions relating to Mines : My technical knowledge of the working of the mines' regu- lation act, and the working of mines generally, is not suffi- cient to enable me at once and definitely to answer the above questions. As far as I understand at present I can only answer as follows :—(a) If the present system of ap- pointing a checkweighman is shown to be unfair on miners, any adequate remedy shall receive my support. (b) I am inclined to favour the removal of any unfair hindrances on the miners to prosecute, provided the danger of vexatious litigation by those who may be unable to pay costs if un- successful be guarded against. (c) As to royalty rents— unless some injustice is very clearly shown to exist—l do not see how legislation could well regulate or interfere with such a matter as this. (d) As to the Coroner's Court, the point of your question was, I believe' much discussed when the miners bill was in committee. The general feeling at the time was that such a question, if dealt with at all, should be dealt with in relation to accidents of all kinds. As regards miners, the case has often been met by the ap- pointment of a counsel to watch proceedings on behalf of the Home-office, who will always be ready to receive sug- gestions from relatives of the injured persons. Question s.—Will you vote for the entire abolition of the London coal dues? Answer.—As has been pointed out by Sir Richard Cress, these coal dues cannot at the present moment be abolished, because great public works have been undertaken on the strength of their being continued for a definite time, and money for such express purposes had been borrowed with the sanction of Parliament upon the security. Whether after that period they shall be renewed Is another matter, and one well worthy of consideration. Question 3.—Will you vote for thorough reform of the land laws of England, viz. : (a) Abolition of entail and primogeniture ; (I) Compulsory powers to cultivate ? Answer.—l am in favour of entire free trade in land ; that is, the removal as far as possible of all hindrances to its free sale and also the reduction as far as possible of the ex- penses connected with its conveyance. I am also in fav- our of encouraging peasant proprietorship by all legitimate and natural methods—such as co-operation ; particularly in those localities where it is found to pay. It may be pointed out that Conservative legislation (Lord Cairn's set- tled land act of 1882) has done more towards freeing the land than anything the Liberal party can show. By this act land has, to a very great extent, been freed from the restrictions of the law of entail. As to the abolition of the law of primogeniture—this seems somewhat unnecessary— though I have no strong objection to the proposal. In nearly every case land is left by will, and such a measure is not required. As for compulsory powers to cultivate, any measure of this kind would, as far as I understand it, do more harm than good. Land cannot be fertilised by act of Parliament. Moreover, any compulsory legislation in this direction would appear to be a serious infringement of the liberty of the subject and an encroachment on the rights of property. Questions of this kind are best decided by the natural laws of economy. I am, however, generally in fav- our of any legitimate proposal that would tend to bring land into the hands of those who will make the best use of it.

i3.—Will you vote for free education? Answer.—lf by free education is meant the whole extension of the Board School system with its costly machinery, division of re- sponsibility, and absence of religious education, I am op- posed to such a reform. Why should the ratepayers be compelled to pay for the education of the mass of the people, when the same work can be done in a better way; the pre- sent voluntary and denominational schools are doing a good work in a better and cheaper way than the Board Schools in many localities throughout the kingdom. It ap- pears, in reference to statistics, that free education through- out the kingdom would throw an additional burden of three millions on the country. The educational cost per child in Board Schools is 23 per cent, more than in volun- tary and denominatidnal schools. At present, therefore, I am unable to support the proposal cf what is called free education. 7.—Will you vote for payment of members of Parliament by the State? Answer.—This means payment of members of Parliament by the British taxpayer. I find very strong reasons for opposing such a measure. In the first place, we find very good men only too glad to do the work for nothing. Why therefore increase taxation unnecessarily? Secondly, it might have the pernicious effect of causing mep to take up politics as a trade, and for mercenary motives. Thirdly, if a constituency desires to pay its member it can always do so by voluntary contribution. Why, therefore, compel the taxpayer to do wkat can, where necessary, be very well done without him? B.—Will you vote for Mr. Broadhurst's bill—that rate- payers pay returniag officers' fees at elections, under certain specified conditions? Answer.—This seems to me a very reasonable proposal, and one that I am at present inclined to support. 9.—Will you vote for a thorough reform of the House of Lords, viz. :—(a) The exclusion of all archbishops and bishops ; (b) Suspension of all Peers for immoral offences ; (c) A specific limitation of their power to delay or prevent necessary legislation ? Answer.—l can see no good end to be attained by the exclusion of the lords spiritual from the House of Lords. They are a recognised part of our Con- stitution. Also any limitation of the free action of the House of Lords would impair its usefulness and efficiency. Such a reform of the House of Lords as an Increase in the number of life peers, and perhaps a transfer of the practical business of the House to a representative body of their own number, appears to be worthy of serious considera- tion.

SUPPOSED FENIAN OURTAGE AT WOOLWICH. A SENTRY OVERPOWERED AND STABBED.

The Press Association's Woolwich correspondent tele- graphs :—About one o'clock on Friday morning a sentry on duty at the Goverment Magazine, known as No. 1, in the Plumstead Marshes, situate below WJolwich Arsenal, was attacked by two men. He states that they came from be- hind a dark corner of the building, and seizing him by the throat and laying hold of his ride, demanded with threats of his life the keys of the magazine. He struggled with them, and attempted to raise an alarm, but they stifled his cries by filling his mouth with gravel, and heat and kicked him severely. He was also stabbed twice in the breast. He then became unconscious and his assailants decamped, and he was subsequently found insensible by his comrades. The affair is enveloped in mystery, but an inquiry is proceeding. The night was very wet and stormy, and it is not believed I that strangers would have teen on the marshes except on I evil intent.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. To this committee the inspector had reported that during the past month there were 87 births and 46 deaths, being at the rate of 38.7 and 20,1 per 1,000 respectively. Eight cases of diarrhoea had been reported, and of these five had proved fatal. It was recommended that the canal boats in- spector's salary be increased from £5 to £lO, and also that application be rdade to the Local Government Board to sanc- tion Mr. Cooper's reappointment as medical officer for the ensuing twelve months. The committee estimate of expen- diture for the half year ended March next was £559 10a 61—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

Another account says that the weapon with which the soldier was stabbed penetrated through his great-coat and clothes. Though the magazine is situated in a lonely part of the Thames, it is thought the would-be murderers must have taken alarm, for the sentry saw them decamp in the direction of Erith. He then became unconscious. The locality, which is far removed from env traffic, forbids the assumption of a drunken frolic, and the inclemency of the night, which was very wet and stormy, is opposed to any explanation of strangers being near the spot. The building is the nearest to the arsenal, and is used as a store for cart- ridges and other completed work. A telegram received late last night says it is believed at Woolwich that the sentry who says he was assaulted whilst guarding the powder magazine is suffering from delusion.

div.head: NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL AT FIVE
div.p: THE NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL AT FIVE

CROSSES. The new chapel at Five Crosses has now been completed. The building erected is In substitution for one built by the late Mr. liazlehurst, of Runcorn, more than a quarter of a century ago, and which has become inadequate for the increas- ing populations of the villages of Overton and Five Crosses. No better proof of the necessity of increased accommodation could be given than the fact of nearly all the sittings in the new chapel—which is intended to seat a congregation of 350—having been already taken. The style of architecture may be stated as 14th Century Gothic, and the building is pleasantly situated near the side of the road leading to Five Crosses, on the south-east side of Overton Hills, and forms a pleasing feature in the landscape. The walls are faced with buff bricks from the Ashton Hall Brick and Coal Company, Queensferry, with red stone dressings. The principal light is obtained from a four-light perpendicular , window over the front entrance, with tracery in local stone, and fitted with cathedral tinted glass of various shades. There is an ample porch, with a dado inside of glazed bricks, and payed with Staffordshire encaustic tiles in a neat design. There are also two side porches in addition to the main entrance. The boundary wall has been completed, and the walks in the chapel ground have been asphalted in a successful manner by Mr. Josiah Dale, of Northwich. The chapel consists of a nave and two transepts, with minister's vestry, lavatory, Jec. The seats and rostrum are pitch pine, by Messrs. G. and H. Wright, of Kelsall. The ventilation appears to be very complete, the windows having been arranged so as to secure efficient circulation without any perceptible draught, and there is also a chamber in the roof to carry off the vitiated air. The architect is Mr. John Wills, of Derby, and the contractor for the whole of the work, Mr. John Littler, of Five Crosses, Frodsham, who has done his part in a thoroughly conscientious manner, the 1 entire building hearing evidence of careful sunervision jn every detail. The sub-contractors under Mr. Littler, in ad- dition to those above mentioned, and deserving of notice, are Mr. Jones, of Temple-street, Manchester, for hot water apparatus; Messrs. Hedge and Co., Hatton Garden, Lon- don, gas fittings ; Mr. W. L. Price, Frodsham, stone work ; Mr. R. Hardman, Norley, plastering; Mr. John Barrow. Frodsharn, Painting and decorating ; and Mr, Me- shah Williams, of Chester, plumbing and glazing. The total cost of -the building, including fittings, ,tc., has been about £1,700. _ _ _ _

The first of a series of opening services of the above chapel was held on Thursday, when the Rey. Silvester Whitehead, of Manchester, preached in the afternoon and evening to large congregations, and a public tea meeting was held in the old chapel at five o'clock the same after- noon, at which upwards of 300 sat down. The collecti,ms in the afternoon amounted to £22 2s 2d. It is hoped to raise £2OO by the opening services.

About a dozen more new workmen arrived at Newcastle on Thursday morning from the North, to take the places of the men on strike at Elswick. They were received with op- probious epithets, but no violence was shown. The strike of factory and mill workers at Dundee, which affected more than 10,000 hands and caused the stoppage of several large concerns, has ended, the opera- tives accepting, the reduction in wages proposed by their employers. A letter from Mr. Gladstone is 7published in which the right hon. gentleman, referring to the disestablisbment question in Scotland, says the matter is one to be decided solely by the people of Scotland—that was to say, Parlia- ment should accept their expressed sense. MR. REDMOND AND DISINTEGRATION OF THE EMPIRE. —At a meeting of the National League in Dublin on Tues- day, Mr. J E. Redmond, M.P., said a number of landlords, disregarding warnings, had inaugurated a new eviction. In- stead of appealing to the landlords or the Government, he earnestly asked the people to combine as they did in the old Lard League days to put down eviction. If the question arose of disintegration of the Empire as against Home Rule, they would. in Grattan's words, say, "Perish the Empire live Ireland!" THE OLDHAM STRIKE.—The Masters' CY,mmittee held a meeting on Wednesday night to consider the position of affairs in connection with the strike. A report was received which stated that the cases were few and unimportant in which employers had abandoned the claim for a reduction in wages; and it was pointed out that the lifeless condition of ' the market, notwithstanding the prolonged stoppage of mil- lions of spindles, was proof that the " relief which capital insisted on from labour" was reasonable and necessary. The meeting resolved to throw open the mills on Monday next, to give the operatives an opportunity of returning to work at the proposed reduction. There is unhappily, great dis- tress in the town. At a representative meeting of operative cotton spinners in Bolton on Wednesday night, it was agreed to accept the masters' proposal for a reduction of 5 per cent, in wages.

div.head: AFGHAN SETTLEMENT.
div.p: THE AFGHAN SETTLEMENT.

PARIS, PRIDAY.—A telegram received here from London states that the Anglo• Russian protocol, concerning the set- tlement of the Afghan frontier, was signed at the British capital yesterday. REPORTED RISING IN SPAIN.

A Central News blegram, dated Paris, Friday morning, says :—rhe Matin publishes a despatch, said to have been received from Madrid, via the frontier, to the effect that a military rising has taken place in the provinces, one regi- ment already being in open revolt.

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

MADRID, FRIDAY.—The official cholera bulletin issued this morning, reports 1,729 cases and 542 deaths in Spain yesterday. TorioN, FRIDAY, 10-50 A.M.—Since last night three deaths from 2.holera have been registered in the city. The general situation remains unchanged. AN ENGLISH STEAMER SUNK AND FIFTEEN

div.head: MEN DROWNED.
div.p: MEN DROWNED.

COPENHAGEN, THURSDAY.—The German despatch vessel Blitz collided last night in the Cattegat, 8t- miles south- south-east and half-mile east from the lightship Trindeln, with the British steamer Oakland, of West Hartlepool, bound from Blyth for Stockholm, with a cargo of coals. The Oakland sank, and 15 of her crew were drowned, the remaining two, the mate Napier and the boatswain Charles Batty, being saved by the Blitz and landed at Frederiks- have.

CERTIFICATE OF ANALYSIS.— I hereby sertify that I have examined the samples of SODA WATER, LEMONADE, GINGER BEER. GINGER ALE. HOP BEER, and CIDER, received from Mr ISAAC STUBBS, MINERAL WATER MANUFACTURER, aRUNCORN, and find them all free from objectionable contami- nation, metallic or otherwise. In the present day where so many mses of Aerated Beverages po luted with lead come to light, the public will do well to be guaranteed as to the purity of the drinks the' consume, as the metal when taken into the system, even in the most minute quantities, gradually produ- ces dangerous and frequently fatal results. I ern, therefore, pleased to be able to report that Mr. Rubbs's preparations are PERFECTLY PURE AND OF EXCELLENT COMPOSITION. All the Aerated Waters made by him deserve to be well patro- nised. and the HOP BEER has seen WELL and SKILFULLY PREPARED The preparations that I have examined are well impregnated with carbonic acid gas. which imparts to them a refreshing and agreeable taste ALL I CAN OONFILENTLY RECOMMEND TO THE PUBLIC. RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending 31st March, 1888.—The GUARDIANS or the Peon of the liuNconN Wriox are desirous of receiving TENDE IS from parties willing to CONTRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Gro- ceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces. the price to include about 301bs. per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; Best Brand lsts American or English Bacon; Potatoes ; Wheat Straw ; Drapery and Clothing ; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples, to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate ss ith name, age and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before Monday, the 28th day of September, 1885, endorsed "Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 19th September, 1885, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if re- quired by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINAKER, Fredah'am, lith September. 1885. Clerk to the Guardians.
